Whether the age requirement is met
Whether at least one condition is false
questions.answer: Whether the age requirement is met
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions to be true.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A program must inspect every item in a known list once. Which approach directly fits?
options: Sort the list without inspecting its values
Loop through the list's items
Inspect only its first item
Repeat until an unrelated password changes
questions.answer: Loop through the list's items
questions.explanation: Traversal applies the required operation to each element of the collection.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A postcode begins with zero and is not used in arithmetic. Why store it as text?
options: To preserve its characters, including the leading zero
To make numerical addition faster
To force every postcode to have the same value
To prevent all invalid input automatically
questions.answer: To preserve its characters, including the leading zero
questions.explanation: An identifier's character representation matters; numeric conversion can discard leading zeros.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: The same calculation is needed in five places. What is an advantage of placing it in a function?
options: The function makes every caller's input valid automatically
It must run five times faster
The function cannot return different results for different inputs
Its logic can be maintained in one place
questions.answer: Its logic can be maintained in one place
questions.explanation: A reusable function reduces duplicated logic and centralises changes.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A list uses indices starting at zero and contains five items. Which index identifies its last item?
questions.explanation: Five positions beginning at zero are numbered zero through four.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: An age field permits values from 16 to 20 inclusive. Which pair best tests its permitted endpoints?
options: 0 and 100
16 and 20
17 and 19
15 and 21
questions.answer: 16 and 20
questions.explanation: The boundary values of the allowed interval are 16 and 20; adjacent invalid values are also useful in additional tests.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Two students have the same name. Why use a unique student ID as the primary key?
options: The ID distinguishes their records reliably
The ID makes every name unique
The ID removes the need to store any other field
Names cannot be stored in a database
questions.answer: The ID distinguishes their records reliably
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies a row even when descriptive attributes repeat.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A table contains many classes, but a report needs only class 12A. What should a query's WHERE condition do?
options: Rename every row as class 12A
Delete other classes from the stored table
Sort all names without filtering
Keep rows whose class equals 12A
questions.answer: Keep rows whose class equals 12A
questions.explanation: A WHERE condition selects qualifying rows for the result without itself deleting the others.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A report should show the highest marks first. Which ordering is appropriate?
options: Alphabetical order of student names
Insertion order regardless of marks
Descending order of marks
Ascending order of marks
questions.answer: Descending order of marks
questions.explanation: Descending numerical order places larger values before smaller ones.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: An enrolment row stores a course ID that refers to a course table. What does this link allow?
options: The course table to be replaced by one large text field
Related course details to be retrieved without repeating them in every enrolment
Every course to have only one student
The enrolment's student ID to become its course name
questions.answer: Related course details to be retrieved without repeating them in every enrolment
questions.explanation: A reference connects related records while allowing shared details to be maintained separately.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A message must reach a particular device on an IP network. Why does it need destination addressing information?
options: Network equipment uses it to direct the message toward the destination
It determines the font used in the message
It guarantees that the message contains no errors
It proves that the sender is trustworthy
questions.answer: Network equipment uses it to direct the message toward the destination
questions.explanation: Destination addresses support delivery; addressing alone does not establish integrity or trust.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A user types a website name instead of its IP address. What does name resolution help provide?
options: A guarantee that the site's claims are true
A copy of the user's password
Extra storage space on the user's device
The network address associated with the name
questions.answer: The network address associated with the name
questions.explanation: DNS resolves domain names to relevant network addressing information.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Two otherwise comparable links carry the same large file. Why can the higher-bandwidth link finish sooner?
options: It eliminates every propagation delay
It changes the file's meaning
It can transfer more data per unit time
It must reduce the number of bits in the file
questions.answer: It can transfer more data per unit time
questions.explanation: Higher available throughput can reduce transmission time for the same amount of data.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A message urgently asks a student to enter a password on an unfamiliar sign-in page. What is the sound response?
options: Forward the password in a reply instead
Verify the request through a trusted route before entering credentials
Trust it because the message is urgent
Use the same password but change its capitalisation
questions.answer: Verify the request through a trusted route before entering credentials
questions.explanation: Urgency and a sign-in request can be used to steal credentials; independent verification checks the destination and request.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A document exists only in working memory when power is lost. Why might unsaved changes disappear?
options: Working memory is volatile
The processor deletes all saved files when it stops
Secondary storage requires continuous power to retain every file
The keyboard stores the document permanently
questions.answer: Working memory is volatile
questions.explanation: Volatile memory does not retain its contents without power; saving to persistent storage protects the work.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A school must store names from several writing systems. Why use a suitable Unicode encoding?
options: It makes all characters occupy exactly one byte in every encoding
It translates every name into English
It encrypts the names automatically
It supports characters beyond a narrow single-language character set
questions.answer: It supports characters beyond a narrow single-language character set
questions.explanation: Unicode provides a broad character repertoire, while the chosen encoding determines how characters are represented as bytes.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: An archive must recover a program's original bytes exactly. Which compression property is essential?
options: A fixed reduction to half the size
Replacement of text with an approximate image
Lossless reconstruction
Removal of less noticeable instructions
questions.answer: Lossless reconstruction
questions.explanation: Program files generally require exact recovery; lossy changes can alter their behaviour or make them unusable.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Students should read a timetable but only staff should edit it. Which design fits?
options: Use a longer timetable title as the only protection
Give students read access and authorised staff edit access
Give every user full edit access
Hide the filename while allowing all writes
questions.answer: Give students read access and authorised staff edit access
questions.explanation: Permissions should match each role's required operations.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A program sums a list but starts its total at 1 instead of 0. What error results?
options: The final sum is one too high
The final sum is multiplied by one
Only the last item is counted
The result is correct whenever the list has more than one item
questions.answer: The final sum is one too high
questions.explanation: The initial value is included in the accumulation, creating a constant extra one.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A value must be at least 10 and at most 20. Why is x>=10 OR x<=20 an incorrect validation condition?
options: It rejects every real x
It accepts only 10 and 20
It checks exactly the same condition as AND
It accepts every real x rather than only the intended interval
questions.answer: It accepts every real x rather than only the intended interval
questions.explanation: For any real number, at least one of those two inequalities holds; the interval requires both.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A loop runs while count<10, but count never changes inside it. If count starts at 0, what is the main problem?
options: The condition becomes false automatically after one pass
The loop must skip its body
The loop does not reach a terminating condition
The loop necessarily executes exactly ten times
questions.answer: The loop does not reach a terminating condition
questions.explanation: Without a change to the controlling state or another exit, the true condition remains true.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A function displays a calculated value but returns no usable result. Why can a caller struggle to use that value in another calculation?
options: A displayed value is always converted into a database row
Displaying output is different from returning a value to the caller
Printed values automatically become the caller's variables
Functions cannot both display and return values
questions.answer: Displaying output is different from returning a value to the caller
questions.explanation: A return communicates data through the function interface; displaying it serves a different purpose.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: An unsorted list may contain a target anywhere. Why may a linear search need to inspect every item before reporting absence?
options: Any uninspected item could still be the target
Absence can be proved by checking only the middle item
The first nonmatching item proves absence
Unsorted lists cannot be searched at all
questions.answer: Any uninspected item could still be the target
questions.explanation: Without ordering information, unchecked positions cannot generally be ruled out.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A search should treat School and school as equivalent. What preparation helps?
options: Convert only one string to uppercase regardless of the other
Compare their first characters only
Compare their lengths as proof of equality
Apply the same case normalisation to both strings
questions.answer: Apply the same case normalisation to both strings
questions.explanation: A consistent normalisation removes the intended case distinction while retaining the rest of the text.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Two variables refer to the same mutable list. One variable is used to change an element. Why does the other show the change?
options: Assignment necessarily copied every element into a new list
The other variable has become a number
Both names refer to the same underlying object
Every list in the program shares all elements
questions.answer: Both names refer to the same underlying object
questions.explanation: Aliasing means different references can access one mutable collection.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A user enters letters where a number is required. Why catch the specific conversion error?
options: The handler makes all later calculations error-free
The program can explain the invalid input and request a correction
The handler converts every word into the intended number
Catching an error proves the original input was valid
questions.answer: The program can explain the invalid input and request a correction
questions.explanation: Handling the expected failure allows a controlled recovery rather than an abrupt termination.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A school wants the average mark for each class. What does grouping by class achieve?
options: A separate aggregate is computed for each class
The table becomes sorted by every student's mark automatically
Only one student from each class is retained in storage
Each student's mark becomes the whole-school average
questions.answer: A separate aggregate is computed for each class
questions.explanation: GROUP BY partitions rows into groups for aggregate calculations.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: In SQL, some email fields are NULL. Why can COUNT(email) be smaller than COUNT(*)?
options: COUNT(*) counts only rows with missing emails
COUNT(email) removes duplicates automatically
COUNT(*) counts columns rather than rows
COUNT(email) excludes NULL email values
questions.answer: COUNT(email) excludes NULL email values
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows, while counting an expression excludes rows where that expression is NULL.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: One course has several enrolments. Why can joining courses to enrolments return the course details several times?
options: Every join must return exactly one row per course
The database has physically duplicated the course table
The join produces one result row for each matching enrolment
The course's primary key has necessarily become invalid
questions.answer: The join produces one result row for each matching enrolment
questions.explanation: A one-to-many relationship can repeat parent details in a query result without duplicating the stored parent record.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A teacher's phone number is copied into every class record. What problem can arise when it changes?
options: Repeated storage guarantees consistent updates
Some copies may be updated while others remain stale
Every copy must change automatically without a relationship
The number can no longer be queried
questions.answer: Some copies may be updated while others remain stale
questions.explanation: Duplicated facts require coordinated changes; separating shared details helps maintain consistency.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Packets from one message arrive out of order. What information helps reconstruct their intended order?
options: Sequence information
Only the display colour of each packet
Only the message's total storage cost
The alphabetic order of router names
questions.answer: Sequence information
questions.explanation: A receiving protocol can use sequence information to place data in the intended order.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A link's bandwidth rises, but a small request still waits on a long round-trip delay. What distinction explains this?
options: Greater bandwidth guarantees zero latency
Latency is determined only by file size
Small messages require no network travel
Transfer capacity and travel delay are different properties
questions.answer: Transfer capacity and travel delay are different properties
questions.explanation: Higher bandwidth can speed bulk transmission while propagation and response delays remain.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Data are encrypted in transit to a correctly authenticated server. What does this primarily protect against?
options: All malicious actions by an authorised recipient
Every false claim on the website
An eavesdropper reading the transmitted content
Every mistake made by the receiving application
questions.answer: An eavesdropper reading the transmitted content
questions.explanation: Transport encryption protects data on the connection, not every aspect of endpoint behaviour or content quality.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Two computers on the same local network exchange a shared file successfully while the internet connection is down. Why is this possible?
options: The internet and the local network are necessarily the same connection
Local communication need not pass through the external internet link
Every local file transfer is stored on a public website
The computers must be using identical IP addresses
questions.answer: Local communication need not pass through the external internet link
questions.explanation: Devices can communicate within a functioning LAN independently of internet access.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: An unsigned fixed-width binary field gains one extra bit. How does the number of representable patterns change?
options: It doubles
It increases by one
It stays unchanged
It is squared
questions.answer: It doubles
questions.explanation: Each old pattern can be paired with either value of the extra bit.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Several applications appear to progress on a processor executing one instruction stream at a time. What can explain this?
options: Every application owns a separate physical processor necessarily
All instructions execute at the exact same instant
Task switching converts programs into permanent storage
The operating system switches execution between tasks
questions.answer: The operating system switches execution between tasks
questions.explanation: Scheduling can share processor time among tasks, producing concurrent progress without simultaneous execution of all instructions.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A program runs without crashing but applies a discount twice. Which response is most useful?
options: Reinstall the keyboard driver first
Treat every numerical output as valid
Trace the calculation and compare it with the intended rule
Assume success because there is no syntax error
questions.answer: Trace the calculation and compare it with the intended rule
questions.explanation: Logical mistakes can produce incorrect results even when code is syntactically valid and executes successfully.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A backup exists but has never been restored in a test. What remains unverified?
options: Whether storing a backup always eliminates all data loss
Whether the saved data can actually be recovered as needed
Whether the file has a name
Whether the original data once existed
questions.answer: Whether the saved data can actually be recovered as needed
questions.explanation: A restore test checks the usability and completeness of the recovery process.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A maximum-finding algorithm starts its current maximum at zero. Why does it fail on a nonempty list containing only negative numbers?
options: Zero can remain the result even though it is not in the list
Negative numbers cannot be compared
The largest negative number is always zero
Initialisation does not affect a maximum search
questions.answer: Zero can remain the result even though it is not in the list
questions.explanation: The initial candidate must be compatible with the input domain, for example the list's first element.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: Discount rules use an if-elif chain: spend>=100 gets 10%, then spend>=200 gets 20%. Why does spending 250 receive only 10%?
options: Both discounts are always added
The comparison 250>=200 is false
An elif branch always overrides the first branch
The first true branch prevents the later branch from being checked
questions.answer: The first true branch prevents the later branch from being checked
questions.explanation: An if-elif chain selects its first satisfied condition, so more restrictive thresholds should be considered appropriately.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: An algorithm compares every list item with every other list item. If list length doubles, how does the number of comparisons grow approximately?
options: By one extra comparison
It remains constant
By a factor of four
By a factor of two
questions.answer: By a factor of four
questions.explanation: A pairwise nested traversal has a comparison count proportional to the square of the number of items.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A loop removes matching items from a list while advancing to the next index. Why can it skip an item?
options: Every removal restarts the loop automatically
Removal shifts later items left while the index still advances
Removing an item makes all remaining values equal
Indices remain attached permanently to their original elements
questions.answer: Removal shifts later items left while the index still advances
questions.explanation: An item can shift into the just-processed index and then be bypassed by the next increment.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A list contains mutable inner lists. Copying only the outer list does not isolate all later edits. Why?
options: The two outer lists can still refer to the same inner lists
The outer lists must have the same identity
A copy operation always makes data immutable
Nested data cannot be copied by any method
questions.answer: The two outer lists can still refer to the same inner lists
questions.explanation: A shallow copy duplicates the outer collection but preserves references to its nested objects.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: With left-to-right short-circuit AND, why check index<len(items) before accessing items[index]?
options: The index is automatically changed to a valid value
AND evaluates both sides regardless of the first result
A length check proves every list element is numeric
A failed bounds check can prevent the unsafe access from being evaluated
questions.answer: A failed bounds check can prevent the unsafe access from being evaluated
questions.explanation: Short-circuiting skips the second operand when the first is false, provided lower bounds and other preconditions also hold.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A function's result depends on a hidden global value that another function changes. Why is testing harder?
options: Global state guarantees every test is independent
The return type must change on every call
The same explicit arguments may produce different results as hidden state changes
Functions with global values cannot execute
questions.answer: The same explicit arguments may produce different results as hidden state changes
questions.explanation: Hidden dependencies make behaviour depend on more than the arguments visible at the call site.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A sorting program passes tests containing only distinct positive values. What is still poorly checked?
options: Whether the program's title is unique
Its behaviour on duplicates, negative values and empty input
Whether positive numbers can be represented at all
Whether every programming language sorts identically
questions.answer: Its behaviour on duplicates, negative values and empty input
questions.explanation: Successful tests establish behaviour for tested conditions, leaving other relevant input classes unresolved.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A query must show only classes whose average mark exceeds 70. Why use a condition on the grouped result?
options: The criterion concerns a group aggregate rather than each original mark
Filtering individual marks above 70 gives the same class averages
Averages cannot appear in database queries
Grouping automatically discards every class below the threshold
questions.answer: The criterion concerns a group aggregate rather than each original mark
questions.explanation: Filtering rows before averaging changes the data used; aggregate conditions are applied after groups are formed.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: An SQL field is NULL. Why is comparing it with =NULL not the proper test for missingness?
options: NULL is always identical to the number zero
NULL is always identical to an empty string
An equality comparison converts every NULL to false data permanently
NULL represents an unknown value and needs an IS NULL test
questions.answer: NULL represents an unknown value and needs an IS NULL test
questions.explanation: Ordinary comparisons with NULL evaluate to unknown in SQL's three-valued logic; IS NULL explicitly tests missingness.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A table has two rows matching a key, and another has three rows with that key. How many pairings does an equality join produce for that key?
options: Three
One
Six
Five
questions.answer: Six
questions.explanation: Each of the two rows pairs with each of the three matching rows, producing six combinations.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A database update is intended for one student but omits its WHERE condition. What is the main risk?
options: The update automatically guesses the intended student
Every row in the target table can receive the update
No row can change without a WHERE condition
Only the row with the smallest primary key changes
questions.answer: Every row in the target table can receive the update
questions.explanation: Without a restricting condition, an UPDATE applies its assignments to all rows in the target table.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A packet network can route around a failed link. Why does this not guarantee uninterrupted delivery in every failure?
options: Alternative paths may also be unavailable or congested
Rerouting requires all links to fail simultaneously
Every message must use one fixed physical path forever
Having two routers eliminates all possible failures
questions.answer: Alternative paths may also be unavailable or congested
questions.explanation: Redundancy improves resilience only while usable alternative capacity exists.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A connection includes a very fast local link and a much slower external link. Why may upgrading only the local link barely improve large downloads?
options: End-to-end speed equals the sum of every link's capacity
The fastest link alone sets the full download speed
A local upgrade automatically upgrades remote infrastructure
The external link can remain the limiting stage
questions.answer: The external link can remain the limiting stage
questions.explanation: Throughput is constrained by bottlenecks along the path, so improving a nonlimiting stage can have little effect.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A user signs in successfully but is denied access to staff records. Why is this not necessarily an error?
options: Permission checks apply only to anonymous users
The password must therefore have been incorrect
Identity verification does not imply permission for every resource
A successful login must grant all database rights
questions.answer: Identity verification does not imply permission for every resource
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorisation determines what that identity is permitted to do.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: An attacker cannot read an encrypted connection but controls the receiving device after decryption. What remains possible?
options: The connection must have been unencrypted because an endpoint was compromised
The attacker can access plaintext at that endpoint
Encryption prevents all endpoint access forever
The endpoint never needs plaintext to use the message
questions.answer: The attacker can access plaintext at that endpoint
questions.explanation: Protecting transmission does not protect data from a compromised endpoint that processes the decrypted content.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: The largest value in an unsigned fixed-width integer field is incremented without overflow checking. Why can the result be incorrect?
options: The required value needs more bits than the field provides
The operation automatically increases the allocated bit width in every system
The largest value is followed by an exactly represented fraction
Unsigned fields cannot represent zero
questions.answer: The required value needs more bits than the field provides
questions.explanation: Fixed-width representations have a finite range; the outcome beyond that range depends on the system's overflow behaviour.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A lossy process removes image detail judged visually unimportant. Why might the output still be unsuitable for later scientific measurement?
options: Visual similarity guarantees identical numerical information
Lossy compression always preserves each original pixel
A smaller file automatically improves measurement precision
The discarded detail may matter to the measurement even if it is hard to notice
questions.answer: The discarded detail may matter to the measurement even if it is hard to notice
questions.explanation: An acceptable viewing approximation does not guarantee preservation of information needed for quantitative analysis.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A cache is enlarged, but a program rarely reuses recently accessed data. Why may the speed gain be small?
options: Cache size alone determines performance regardless of workload
A cache permanently increases the processor's instruction count
The access pattern may yield few useful cache hits
Larger caches necessarily slow every program
questions.answer: The access pattern may yield few useful cache hits
questions.explanation: A cache helps when requested data are present; benefits depend on workload and locality as well as capacity.

questions.subject: Computer Science
questions.q: A school system blocks legitimate users so often that they share one powerful staff account. What design problem should be addressed?
options: Stricter lockouts always improve actual security regardless of user behaviour
Access rules and recovery should support legitimate work without encouraging shared privileges
Shared administrator access is the safest solution for every user
Removing all authentication is the only possible improvement
questions.answer: Access rules and recovery should support legitimate work without encouraging shared privileges
questions.explanation: Security controls should provide workable authorised paths; shared privileged accounts weaken accountability and access separation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A student uses a free hour for paid work instead of their next-best option, study. What is the opportunity cost?
options: Every activity the student could imagine
Only the bus fare, even if no bus is used
The wage earned from working
The value of the study opportunity forgone
questions.answer: The value of the study opportunity forgone
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative sacrificed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An economy moves from an inefficient point inside its production frontier to the frontier. What can explain this?
options: A guarantee that new resources were discovered
A change in the units used on the graph only
Better use of existing resources
A necessary reduction in every output
questions.answer: Better use of existing resources
questions.explanation: Reducing unemployment or inefficiency can increase output without shifting productive capacity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An extra hour of tutoring brings a benefit greater than its additional cost. What does marginal analysis support, other things equal?
options: Taking unlimited hours regardless of later costs
Taking that extra hour
Rejecting it because a cost exists
Ignoring the additional benefit
questions.answer: Taking that extra hour
questions.explanation: An additional activity is worthwhile while its marginal benefit exceeds its marginal cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Consumers' incomes rise and a good is normal. With other factors unchanged, what happens to demand?
options: It shifts right
It shifts left
There is only movement along an unchanged demand curve
Supply must shift left
questions.answer: It shifts right
questions.explanation: A normal good is demanded more at each price when income rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A production method reduces unit costs. What happens to supply, other things equal?
options: It shifts left
Demand necessarily falls
Quantity supplied is fixed at every price
It shifts right
questions.answer: It shifts right
questions.explanation: Lower production costs make more output worth supplying at a given price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A maximum legal price is set below the market-clearing price. What is the standard competitive-market prediction?
options: No effect because every ceiling is nonbinding
An automatic increase in supply
A shortage
A surplus
questions.answer: A shortage
questions.explanation: At a binding ceiling, consumers demand more than producers are willing to supply.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Producing one extra unit adds 8 to total cost. What is the marginal cost of that unit?
options: The average of all past prices
The entire previous total cost
The selling price in every case
questions.explanation: Marginal cost measures the additional cost of extra output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A baker buys flour and sells bread to a household. Why count the final bread value rather than adding both sales to GDP?
options: The bread value already includes the flour used
Flour has no market value
Only imported ingredients count in GDP
All business purchases are excluded from production
questions.answer: The bread value already includes the flour used
questions.explanation: Counting intermediate inputs again would double-count value embodied in the final product.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country produces the same quantities at higher prices. Which measure can rise without greater production?
options: Real GDP measured at unchanged base prices
Physical output of every industry
Labour productivity measured as real output per hour
Nominal GDP
questions.answer: Nominal GDP
questions.explanation: Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP adjusts for price changes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Households become more optimistic and increase planned spending at each price level. What is the initial aggregate-demand effect, other things equal?
options: A movement caused only by a lower price level
A necessary leftward shift of productive capacity
A rightward shift
A leftward shift
questions.answer: A rightward shift
questions.explanation: Higher planned consumption raises aggregate demand at each price level.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A bank grants a loan by crediting a customer's deposit account. What happens initially on the bank's balance sheet?
options: Its owner's equity necessarily increases by the full loan
A loan asset and a deposit liability both increase
Only its physical cash stock increases
Its loan liability and deposit asset both increase
questions.answer: A loan asset and a deposit liability both increase
questions.explanation: The borrower owes the bank while the bank owes the depositor access to the credited funds.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A resident purchases an imported consumer good. Where is the goods transaction recorded?
options: As a current-account import debit
As an export credit
Only as domestic government borrowing
Only as a capital transfer
questions.answer: As a current-account import debit
questions.explanation: International purchases and sales of goods belong in the current account.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A training programme teaches workers to use more efficient machinery. How can this support development?
options: It converts every worker into physical machinery
It guarantees equal wages in all occupations
It reduces all need for investment
It improves productive skills
questions.answer: It improves productive skills
questions.explanation: Skills can improve workers' ability to use resources and technology productively.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A farmer must sell a crop cheaply immediately because a high-cost loan is due. How could accessible institutional credit help?
options: It removes all price risk from agriculture
It eliminates the need to repay borrowed funds
It can reduce dependence on costly borrowing and distress sales
It guarantees that every harvest is larger
questions.answer: It can reduce dependence on costly borrowing and distress sales
questions.explanation: Affordable credit with suitable repayment conditions can ease financing pressure and improve farmers' selling choices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Two family members leave a farm and its output does not fall, with other inputs unchanged. What does this suggest?
options: The farm's physical capital must have doubled
Some labour was contributing no additional output
The farm had no labour before they left
Every remaining worker is openly unemployed
questions.answer: Some labour was contributing no additional output
questions.explanation: Labour in excess of productive requirements can be disguisedly unemployed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An industry no longer needs some previously required production licences. What economic channel does this reform target?
options: Lower administrative barriers to entry and expansion
A legal guarantee that every entrant earns profit
A complete ban on private investment
An automatic rise in every import tariff
questions.answer: Lower administrative barriers to entry and expansion
questions.explanation: Liberalisation reduces selected restrictions on economic activity without guaranteeing business success.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A region raises crop output by extracting groundwater faster than it is replenished. What concern follows?
options: Higher output proves resource use is sustainable
Groundwater use cannot affect later farming
Only the market price of the crop matters for sustainability
Current gains may undermine future production capacity
questions.answer: Current gains may undermine future production capacity
questions.explanation: Using a renewable resource faster than replenishment can deplete the stock needed for future production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A survey codes travel mode as 1 for bus, 2 for walking and 3 for car. Why would the mean code be unhelpful?
options: The codes make travel mode a continuous measurement
The mean would equal the most common travel mode
The numbers label categories rather than measure an amount
The categories cannot be counted
questions.answer: The numbers label categories rather than measure an amount
questions.explanation: Changing arbitrary category codes would change their mean without changing students' actual travel modes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: One unusually long delivery delay is added to an otherwise tightly grouped set of delivery times. Which centre is usually less affected?
options: The sum divided by the number of observations
The median
The mean
The midpoint of the minimum and maximum
questions.answer: The median
questions.explanation: The median depends on ordered position and is less sensitive to a single extreme value than the mean or midrange.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A school randomly selects student IDs from a complete enrolment list. Why is this preferable to asking only students near the office?
options: It gives students throughout the school a chance of selection
It guarantees that every selected student responds
It guarantees a sample mean equal to the population mean
It eliminates all measurement errors in the answers
questions.answer: It gives students throughout the school a chance of selection
questions.explanation: Random selection avoids restricting the sample to a convenient location, although nonresponse and measurement problems can remain.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A bowed-out production frontier shows that making more of one good requires giving up increasing amounts of another. Why?
options: All resources have identical productivity in both activities
Opportunity cost is always zero
The economy must be operating inside the frontier
Resources are not equally suited to both activities
questions.answer: Resources are not equally suited to both activities
questions.explanation: Shifting progressively less suitable resources raises the opportunity cost of additional output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A producer is more productive in both goods. Why can trade still benefit both producers?
options: Only the less productive producer has any opportunity cost
Trade requires identical production ratios
Their relative opportunity costs can differ
Absolute advantage eliminates every possible trade gain
questions.answer: Their relative opportunity costs can differ
questions.explanation: Specialisation can be based on comparative rather than absolute advantage.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A consumer can move spending toward a good that gives more marginal utility per unit of currency. Why can this improve total utility?
options: Marginal utility increases forever for every good
The same spending can obtain a larger marginal benefit
Every purchase must have the same total utility
Price has no role in comparing purchases
questions.answer: The same spending can obtain a larger marginal benefit
questions.explanation: Allocating a limited budget compares additional benefit per unit of expenditure.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A good's own price falls, with demand determinants unchanged. Which description is correct?
options: Quantity demanded rises along the existing demand curve
The demand curve necessarily shifts right
Supply becomes demand
Income must have risen
questions.answer: Quantity demanded rises along the existing demand curve
questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price causes movement along its demand curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Demand is inelastic over a price rise. What happens to total revenue if the expected response occurs?
options: It necessarily falls
It stays constant by definition
It becomes equal to production cost
It rises
questions.answer: It rises
questions.explanation: The percentage fall in quantity is smaller than the percentage increase in price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Marginal cost is below average total cost at the current output. What does one more unit tend to do to average total cost?
options: Leave it unchanged necessarily
Make total cost negative
Reduce it
Increase it
questions.answer: Reduce it
questions.explanation: An additional unit costing less than the existing average pulls that average down.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: At the current output, marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost. What does increasing output slightly do to profit under the usual smooth model?
options: Make fixed costs disappear
Increase it
Decrease it
Leave it unchanged by definition
questions.answer: Increase it
questions.explanation: The added unit contributes more revenue than cost while marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Real GDP rises while unpaid household care falls and pollution rises. What is the sound conclusion?
options: GDP growth alone does not establish improved overall welfare
Overall welfare must rise by the GDP growth rate
Unpaid household care is fully counted in GDP
Pollution automatically reduces measured GDP by its full harm
questions.answer: GDP growth alone does not establish improved overall welfare
questions.explanation: GDP measures market production broadly, not every contribution to or cost of well-being.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Government cuts household taxes while purchases stay unchanged. Why is the first increase in consumption typically smaller than the tax cut?
options: Taxes are counted directly as private investment
Every household must repay the full cut immediately
A tax cut cannot change disposable income
Households save part of the extra disposable income
questions.answer: Households save part of the extra disposable income
questions.explanation: With a marginal propensity to consume below one, only part of additional disposable income is initially spent.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Two otherwise identical economies receive the same spending injection. One has a higher marginal propensity to save. Which has the smaller simple expenditure multiplier?
options: Both necessarily have the same multiplier
The economy with higher initial government spending regardless of saving
The economy with the higher propensity to save
The economy with the lower propensity to save
questions.answer: The economy with the higher propensity to save
questions.explanation: More saving from each income increase means less spending passed to the next round.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An improvement in technology raises output possible from the same inputs. How is it represented in an AD–AS model?
options: Potential output remains unchanged by definition
Long-run aggregate supply shifts right
Only a movement along an unchanged long-run supply curve
Aggregate demand must shift left by the same amount
questions.answer: Long-run aggregate supply shifts right
questions.explanation: Better technology expands the economy's sustainable productive capacity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country buys more abroad than it earns in current-account receipts. How can it finance the gap?
options: By net borrowing, selling assets or reducing external assets
Only by recording the imports as exports
Only by increasing current receipts on paper
By making all financial transactions disappear
questions.answer: By net borrowing, selling assets or reducing external assets
questions.explanation: A current-account deficit is matched by financing transactions, subject to the accounting convention and statistical discrepancy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Education spending rises but disadvantaged students still cannot attend regularly. What should an evaluation examine?
options: Only the number printed in the spending budget
Whether all school buildings have the same colour
Whether expenditure itself proves equal learning outcomes
Whether improved access lets intended learners acquire useful skills
questions.answer: Whether improved access lets intended learners acquire useful skills
questions.explanation: Expenditure is an input; access, participation and learning determine whether human-capital benefits are realised.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A farmer combines crop production with dairy activity whose returns fluctuate differently. Why might this help?
options: It necessarily raises the price of the original crop
It turns all agricultural income into government transfers
It can spread income risk across activities
It removes every production and market risk
questions.answer: It can spread income risk across activities
questions.explanation: Diversification can reduce dependence on the performance of a single activity, though risks remain.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Employment grows mainly through work without stable contracts or social protection. Why is job growth alone an incomplete indicator?
options: The employment count proves universal social protection
Job security and employment quality may remain weak
Every additional job must reduce national output
Informal workers produce no goods or services
questions.answer: Job security and employment quality may remain weak
questions.explanation: Employment quantity does not reveal earnings stability, working conditions or access to protection.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A public monopoly becomes a private monopoly without new entry or effective oversight. Why might consumers not benefit?
options: Ownership change alone does not create competitive pressure
Private ownership guarantees lower prices in every market
A monopoly has no influence over its prices
Public ownership always prevents production
questions.answer: Ownership change alone does not create competitive pressure
questions.explanation: Efficiency and consumer outcomes depend on incentives, competition and regulation as well as ownership.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Two countries have similar income per person but different schooling and life expectancy. What follows?
options: Their overall development must be identical
Schooling cannot affect productive capacity
Life expectancy is measured directly by GDP
Income alone misses important dimensions of development
questions.answer: Income alone misses important dimensions of development
questions.explanation: Health and education contribute to development beyond the average value of measured income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Most repair times are short, with a few very long repairs. Why might the mean exceed the median?
options: The mean ignores the largest values
Right skew requires more than half the observations above the mean
The long upper tail pulls the mean upward
The median gives extra weight to the largest values
questions.answer: The long upper tail pulls the mean upward
questions.explanation: The mean uses each numerical value and is pulled toward a long right tail more strongly than the median.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A survey asks whether students support the school's excellent new lunch plan. What change most directly reduces response bias?
options: Report the result to more decimal places
Remove the evaluative word excellent
Double the number of identical leading questions
Ask only students who already support the plan
questions.answer: Remove the evaluative word excellent
questions.explanation: Neutral wording avoids suggesting a preferred response to participants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.topic: Statistics for Economics: units and correlation
questions.q: All heights are converted from centimetres to metres before calculating correlation with arm span. What happens to correlation?
options: It stays the same
It is divided by 100
It changes sign
It becomes closer to zero automatically
questions.answer: It stays the same
questions.explanation: Correlation is unchanged by a positive linear change of measurement units.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An allocation maximises total surplus but leaves one group with very little income. What follows?
options: Maximum surplus guarantees equal income for everyone
An unequal allocation can never be efficient under any definition
Distribution is measured only by total surplus
Efficiency alone does not establish an equitable distribution
questions.answer: Efficiency alone does not establish an equitable distribution
questions.explanation: Efficiency concerns total gains or resource use; equity concerns how benefits and resources are distributed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Technology improves only in the production of one of two goods. Why might the frontier rotate outward rather than shift equally everywhere?
options: The improvement must move production inside the old frontier
Opportunity cost disappears for both goods
The maximum output of one good rises while the other intercept need not change
Every technological improvement must expand both intercepts equally
questions.answer: The maximum output of one good rises while the other intercept need not change
questions.explanation: A sector-specific productivity gain affects production possibilities asymmetrically.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm must decide whether to produce one more unit. A past setup cost cannot be recovered or changed. Why exclude that cost from this marginal decision?
options: The extra unit must be produced regardless of its variable cost
It is unchanged by producing the extra unit
All fixed costs are zero in accounting
Past costs always increase future marginal revenue
questions.answer: It is unchanged by producing the extra unit
questions.explanation: Relevant marginal decisions compare costs and benefits altered by the additional action.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Demand and supply both increase in a competitive market. Without knowing their relative sizes, what can be concluded?
options: Equilibrium quantity rises, but the price change is ambiguous
Price necessarily rises and quantity is ambiguous
Price necessarily falls and quantity is ambiguous
Both price and quantity must remain unchanged
questions.answer: Equilibrium quantity rises, but the price change is ambiguous
questions.explanation: Both shifts increase quantity, while their effects on price oppose each other.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A price ceiling is set above the unregulated equilibrium price. Why does it not change the standard market outcome?
options: Every price ceiling creates a shortage regardless of level
The ceiling increases supply by definition
Buyers must pay the ceiling even when sellers offer less
The market-clearing price already satisfies the ceiling
questions.answer: The market-clearing price already satisfies the ceiling
questions.explanation: A control has no direct effect when the unconstrained equilibrium is permitted.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A straight downward-sloping demand curve has constant slope. Why does its price elasticity still vary along the curve?
options: Quantity is constant along every straight line
Elasticity depends only on the currency symbol
Elasticity also depends on the price-to-quantity ratio
Slope and elasticity are always numerically identical
questions.answer: Elasticity also depends on the price-to-quantity ratio
questions.explanation: Point elasticity combines the curve's slope with the local price and quantity values.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A competitive firm's fixed cost rises while its marginal-cost schedule and price are unchanged. What happens to its short-run profit-maximising positive output, if it still operates?
options: Marginal cost rises by the same amount at every unit
It is unchanged, although profit falls
It must rise by the fixed-cost increase
It must fall to zero regardless of variable costs
questions.answer: It is unchanged, although profit falls
questions.explanation: An unchanged marginal comparison leaves the optimal operating output unchanged, while higher fixed cost reduces profit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country has positive gross investment but depreciation is larger. What follows for its produced capital stock, other changes excluded?
options: It declines because net investment is negative
It rises because gross investment is positive
It stays fixed because depreciation is only a price index
It becomes identical to current consumption
questions.answer: It declines because net investment is negative
questions.explanation: Net investment subtracts depreciation from gross investment; a negative amount means capital is not fully replaced.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm produces goods this year but sells them next year. How should the production be treated in expenditure-based GDP?
options: It enters GDP only next year as new production
It enters neither year's GDP because no immediate sale occurred
Its full value is counted as new output in both years
This year's unsold output enters inventory investment
questions.answer: This year's unsold output enters inventory investment
questions.explanation: Inventory investment accounts for current production not yet sold, preventing omission and later double counting.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In the simple closed-economy model with lump-sum taxes and idle resources, government raises purchases and taxes equally. Why can equilibrium output rise?
options: The tax rise is recorded as an equal increase in private consumption
The result requires a marginal propensity to consume greater than one
Purchases enter demand fully while households reduce consumption by only part of the tax rise
The equal changes necessarily cancel every spending round
questions.answer: Purchases enter demand fully while households reduce consumption by only part of the tax rise
questions.explanation: With a marginal propensity to consume between zero and one, the initial net demand effect is positive.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A simple deposit multiplier assumes no cash leakage and no excess reserves. What happens to realised deposit expansion if households retain more cash from loans?
options: The retained cash automatically becomes a new bank deposit elsewhere
It can be smaller than the simple maximum
It must exceed the simple maximum
It becomes independent of redepositing
questions.answer: It can be smaller than the simple maximum
questions.explanation: Cash leakage leaves less funding circulating through repeated bank deposit and loan expansion in the simple model.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A central bank defends a currency facing downward pressure by selling foreign reserves and buying domestic currency. What constraint can eventually bind?
options: Its available foreign reserves can be depleted
Its purchases create unlimited foreign reserves automatically
The exchange rate no longer needs any supporting transactions
A fixed rate guarantees investors cannot sell domestic assets
questions.answer: Its available foreign reserves can be depleted
questions.explanation: Defending the rate in this direction uses foreign assets, so persistent pressure can exhaust the reserve buffer.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Agriculture's share of output falls much faster than its share of employment. What disparity may persist?
options: Every farm worker must become unemployed
Agricultural output must fall in absolute terms
Employment shares and output shares must always be equal
Average output per agricultural worker may lag other sectors
questions.answer: Average output per agricultural worker may lag other sectors
questions.explanation: A large workforce producing a relatively small output share implies lower average output per worker in that sector.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Farmers pool produce in a cooperative to negotiate prices, but poor storage still forces rapid sales. What limits the reform's effect?
options: Storage is irrelevant to perishable produce
Cooperation prevents any negotiation with buyers
Stronger bargaining is constrained by inadequate complementary infrastructure
Collective selling guarantees freedom from all time pressure
questions.answer: Stronger bargaining is constrained by inadequate complementary infrastructure
questions.explanation: Marketing institutions and storage can complement each other; weak infrastructure can restrict farmers' selling choices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Export opportunities grow after integration with world markets, but some domestic firms close. How should the reform be assessed?
options: Treat every foreign transaction as a welfare loss
Compare gains, adjustment costs and their distribution across groups
Count only export growth and assume universal benefit
Count only closures and assume nobody gains
questions.answer: Compare gains, adjustment costs and their distribution across groups
questions.explanation: Integration can create opportunities and competitive pressure simultaneously, with uneven effects on workers and firms.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: More graduates are trained, but their skills do not match expanding industries. Why may educated unemployment persist?
options: Education quantity can rise without matching labour-market capabilities
Any educational qualification guarantees immediate employment
Industry demand is unrelated to the skills workers possess
Educated people cannot participate in the labour force
questions.answer: Education quantity can rise without matching labour-market capabilities
questions.explanation: The fit between skills and employment opportunities matters alongside years of education.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A project raises current income while causing costly, long-lasting ecosystem damage not charged to the producer. What makes GDP growth an insufficient assessment?
options: Every increase in GDP already subtracts all future damage
Future welfare is identical to current market revenue
The absence of a price proves that ecosystems have no value
Unpriced future costs may offset some current production benefits
questions.answer: Unpriced future costs may offset some current production benefits
questions.explanation: A production measure alone does not weigh external environmental costs borne over time.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.topic: Statistics for Economics: graphical representation sensitivity
questions.q: Two histograms of the same data look different because their bin widths differ. What should a reviewer infer?
options: The sample means must differ between the histograms
Narrower bins always provide the only correct summary
Apparent detail can depend on grouping, so inspect the bin choices and underlying data
One graph necessarily uses fabricated observations
questions.answer: Apparent detail can depend on grouping, so inspect the bin choices and underlying data
questions.explanation: A histogram groups observations into intervals; changing those intervals can reveal or obscure features without changing the data.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Two districts have different population sizes. Why is simply averaging their mean household incomes usually unsuitable for the combined mean?
options: Both district means must first be converted into medians
The district means need weights reflecting their household counts
A combined mean must always equal the larger district mean
A mean cannot be calculated for household income
questions.answer: The district means need weights reflecting their household counts
questions.explanation: Each household should contribute equally, so district means must be weighted by the numbers of households they represent.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A fixed-basket consumer price index rises while households substitute toward cheaper alternatives. What limitation should be considered?
options: The fixed basket may not reflect the changed spending pattern
The index necessarily measures no price change
Every household buys the fixed basket in identical amounts
Substitution proves that all prices fell
questions.answer: The fixed basket may not reflect the changed spending pattern
questions.explanation: An index using unchanged quantities does not fully capture consumers' changing purchases in response to relative prices.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: Students regularly complain that the only lunch queue is too slow. Why could this suggest a business opportunity?
options: It guarantees that any proposed service will be profitable
It proves that students will pay any price
It removes the need to investigate demand
It identifies an unmet customer need
questions.answer: It identifies an unmet customer need
questions.explanation: A repeated customer problem can suggest an opportunity, but demand and feasibility still require investigation.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A new business sets a target to reach monthly break-even within six months. Why is this more useful than simply saying do well?
options: It makes cash planning unnecessary
It means growth no longer matters
It provides a measurable result and a time frame
It guarantees the target will be achieved
questions.answer: It provides a measurable result and a time frame
questions.explanation: A specific measurable objective supports planning and assessment of progress.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A founder estimates sales, costs, staffing and delivery arrangements before opening. What does combining these in a plan help reveal?
options: A guarantee that competitors will not respond
Whether the proposed activities and resources fit together
The exact future profit with certainty
A way to avoid all future decisions
questions.answer: Whether the proposed activities and resources fit together
questions.explanation: A plan links the idea to its operational and financial requirements while exposing assumptions.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: Demand for a new product is uncertain. Why might a small pilot launch be useful?
options: It gathers evidence before a larger commitment
It eliminates every possible future loss
It proves nationwide demand from any pilot size
It replaces the need to calculate costs
questions.answer: It gathers evidence before a larger commitment
questions.explanation: A pilot tests important assumptions on a limited scale before more resources are committed.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A shop offers lightweight bags to cyclists and large bags to families. What is it responding to?
options: A requirement that every customer buy both types
A guarantee that both groups pay identical prices
A rule that markets cannot contain several segments
Different needs in different customer groups
questions.answer: Different needs in different customer groups
questions.explanation: Segmentation recognises groups with differing needs and helps tailor the offer.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A founder interviews potential customers about a proposed service. Why is this primary research?
options: The respondents have already bought the service
The information has no collection cost
The data are collected directly for the current investigation
The data must be more accurate than every published source
questions.answer: The data are collected directly for the current investigation
questions.explanation: Primary research gathers new evidence for a particular purpose, though quality depends on its design.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: Two cafés charge the same price, but one promises quick collection for commuters. What is the second café highlighting?
options: A requirement that every customer travel by train
A customer benefit that can distinguish its offer
A guarantee of lower production costs
A change in legal ownership
questions.answer: A customer benefit that can distinguish its offer
questions.explanation: A value proposition explains why a target customer might choose that business.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A popular product is difficult for customers to obtain because stockists are too far away. Which part of the offer needs attention?
options: Distribution and availability
The colour of the accounting ledger
Only the product's production cost
Only the number of shareholders
questions.answer: Distribution and availability
questions.explanation: A good product still needs a convenient route to its intended customers.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: An advertisement introduces an unfamiliar product and explains its use. What is its immediate purpose?
options: Record the business's liabilities
Guarantee customer loyalty permanently
Replace the product's quality checks
Build awareness and understanding
questions.answer: Build awareness and understanding
questions.explanation: Informative promotion helps potential customers recognise an offering and understand its benefits.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A business charges less than the variable cost of making each extra unit. What happens as it sells more of those units, all else equal?
options: Fixed costs disappear automatically
The selling price becomes the unit contribution
Each extra unit increases the loss before fixed costs
Every extra sale necessarily improves profit
questions.answer: Each extra unit increases the loss before fixed costs
questions.explanation: Negative unit contribution means additional units do not cover their own variable costs.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A shop's sales revenue rises, but its costs rise by a larger amount. What can happen to profit?
options: It is unaffected by costs
It can fall
It must rise by the revenue increase
It must equal revenue
questions.answer: It can fall
questions.explanation: Profit is revenue minus costs, so faster cost growth can reduce it.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A profitable sale is made on credit, with payment due next month. Why might it not help pay today's wages?
options: The cash has not yet been received
Credit sales can never generate revenue
Profit and cash receipts are always simultaneous
Wages can be paid only from cash sales
questions.answer: The cash has not yet been received
questions.explanation: Recognising a sale and collecting its cash can happen at different times.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A business needs to pay suppliers before customers pay it. What does this create?
options: A guarantee of accounting profit
A reduction of every future expense
A reason to stop recording receivables
A need to finance day-to-day cash commitments
questions.answer: A need to finance day-to-day cash commitments
questions.explanation: The timing gap between payments and receipts creates a working-capital requirement.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: An owner uses retained profit to fund a small expansion. What is one consequence?
options: Ownership must be sold to every customer
The funding has no alternative possible use
The business avoids borrowing that amount from an external lender
The retained profit becomes a new loan
questions.answer: The business avoids borrowing that amount from an external lender
questions.explanation: Retained profit is an internal funding source, although using it still has an opportunity cost.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A manager gives a trained employee authority to handle routine refunds within a limit. What is being delegated?
options: Authority to ignore the stated limit
A defined decision-making responsibility
Ownership of the entire business
Every duty of the manager permanently
questions.answer: A defined decision-making responsibility
questions.explanation: Delegation assigns specified authority and work while overall accountability remains with management.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: New staff make errors using unfamiliar equipment. What response directly addresses the skills gap?
options: Relevant practical training
Changing the business name
Increasing sales targets without instruction
Removing every performance measure
questions.answer: Relevant practical training
questions.explanation: Training develops the knowledge and skills needed to perform the task correctly.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: Employees say they do not know whether their work is useful or successful. Which response directly addresses that concern?
options: Withholding all information about results
Changing working hours at random
Increasing the number of unexplained rules
Clear goals and constructive feedback
questions.answer: Clear goals and constructive feedback
questions.explanation: Goals and feedback clarify expectations and help employees understand their contribution.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A bakery's ovens are fully used at peak time, and orders are delayed. What is the immediate operational constraint?
options: The age of its logo
The total number of products advertised elsewhere
Available oven capacity at the peak
The number of entries in its customer database
questions.answer: Available oven capacity at the peak
questions.explanation: A fully utilised limiting resource can prevent the business from meeting additional demand promptly.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A manufacturer checks finished items against specifications before dispatch. What does this help do?
options: Prove that every customer wants the product
Identify products that do not meet the standard
Guarantee that defects can never occur
Replace the need for clear specifications
questions.answer: Identify products that do not meet the standard
questions.explanation: Quality checks detect departures from requirements so defective output can be addressed.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A business reduces wasted raw material while producing the same acceptable output. What direct benefit follows?
options: Less material is required per acceptable unit
Sales revenue must double
Every fixed cost disappears
Product demand becomes unlimited
questions.answer: Less material is required per acceptable unit
questions.explanation: Reducing waste improves resource productivity and can reduce material costs and environmental impact.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: Many customers like an idea, but few will pay enough to cover its costs. What does this suggest?
options: Positive opinions guarantee commercial demand at any price
Costs cease to matter when an idea is popular
The idea must have no social value
Interest alone does not establish a viable business model
questions.answer: Interest alone does not establish a viable business model
questions.explanation: Viability requires a workable relationship between willingness to pay, demand and the resources needed to deliver.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A firm extends opening hours to increase sales, but employees object to the new shifts. What must managers balance?
options: A requirement that all stakeholders have identical objectives
A rule that longer hours always increase profit
Potential customer and revenue benefits against workforce effects
Only the preferences of whichever group is larger
questions.answer: Potential customer and revenue benefits against workforce effects
questions.explanation: Business decisions can affect stakeholders differently, requiring consideration of benefits, costs and implementation.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A fast-growing firm buys more stock and offers more customer credit. Why might it need extra finance despite rising sales?
options: Offering credit immediately increases cash receipts
Growth can tie up cash before receipts arrive
Rising sales guarantee a positive cash balance at every date
Inventory purchases have no cash effect
questions.answer: Growth can tie up cash before receipts arrive
questions.explanation: Expansion can increase inventory and receivables, creating a funding need before customers pay.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A repair service moves from one-off payments to subscriptions. Which issue should it reassess?
options: Whether recurring income covers the expected service demand and costs
Only whether the company name sounds modern
Whether subscriptions eliminate all customer cancellations
Whether every subscriber will require the same work
questions.answer: Whether recurring income covers the expected service demand and costs
questions.explanation: Changing the revenue model changes both income timing and the obligations that must be funded.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A business surveys only its most loyal customers before entering a new market. What is the main limitation?
options: Loyal customers cannot express preferences
A large loyal-customer sample necessarily represents noncustomers
Primary research cannot use existing customers
Their preferences may not represent the new target customers
questions.answer: Their preferences may not represent the new target customers
questions.explanation: The usefulness of research depends on how well respondents match the population relevant to the decision.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: Demand is price elastic over a proposed price reduction. What happens to revenue if the expected response occurs?
options: Quantity does not respond to price
Costs must fall by the same percentage as price
The percentage rise in quantity exceeds the percentage price fall, raising revenue
Revenue necessarily falls because the price falls
questions.answer: The percentage rise in quantity exceeds the percentage price fall, raising revenue
questions.explanation: With elastic demand, the quantity response more than offsets the lower price in revenue terms.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A premium brand cuts prices sharply and advertises only bargains. What strategic concern arises?
options: All customers value only the lowest price
The message may conflict with its quality-based position
Lower prices always strengthen a premium image
Price cannot influence how customers interpret a brand
questions.answer: The message may conflict with its quality-based position
questions.explanation: Marketing choices should form a coherent position; a price-led message can change perceived value.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: Selling directly online increases the producer's margin per sale but requires delivery and support. What comparison matters?
options: The extra margin against the added costs and responsibilities
The margin alone, with all new costs ignored
Only the number of intermediaries removed
A presumption that direct sales are always cheaper overall
questions.answer: The extra margin against the added costs and responsibilities
questions.explanation: Removing intermediaries can transfer their functions and costs to the producer.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: An existing product is entering a market with different user needs. Why test an adapted version?
options: To establish that all markets have identical preferences
To avoid measuring demand
To prove the original version had no value
To check whether the changes fit the new customers' requirements
questions.answer: To check whether the changes fit the new customers' requirements
questions.explanation: Adaptation should respond to evidence about the target market rather than assuming one version fits every context.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A campaign gets many views but few enquiries from the intended customers. What should be examined?
options: Only the duration of the advertisement
Whether a larger audience always contains more suitable buyers
Whether the reach converts into the campaign's relevant outcomes
Views alone as proof of commercial success
questions.answer: Whether the reach converts into the campaign's relevant outcomes
questions.explanation: Promotional activity should be assessed against its objective and target audience, not only exposure counts.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: Unit contribution rises while fixed costs stay unchanged. What happens to the break-even quantity?
options: It becomes equal to the selling price
It falls
It rises
It stays unchanged regardless of contribution
questions.answer: It falls
questions.explanation: Each unit contributes more toward the same fixed-cost total, so fewer units are needed to cover it.

questions.subject: Entrepreneurship
questions.q: A firm buys equipment expected to serve for several years. Why can relying entirely on a repayable short-term facility be risky?
