questions.q: A cork bobs as a water wave passes. What does this illustrate?
options: The cork must move permanently forward
Energy can travel without the cork travelling with the wave
All water travels at the wave speed
The wave carries no energy
questions.answer: Energy can travel without the cork travelling with the wave
questions.explanation: The disturbance propagates while material particles oscillate about local positions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two initially neutral objects become oppositely charged by rubbing. What was transferred between them?
options: Protons between nuclei
Whole positive nuclei only
Gravitational mass
Electrons
questions.answer: Electrons
questions.explanation: Charge separation in ordinary rubbing results from electron transfer.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A positive test charge is released in a uniform electric field, with no other force. Which way does it initially accelerate?
options: Perpendicular to the field
It cannot accelerate
Along the field
Against the field
questions.answer: Along the field
questions.explanation: The electric force on a positive charge points along the electric field.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One branch of two resistors in parallel is removed from an ideal battery. What happens to current in the remaining branch?
options: It stays the same
It doubles automatically
It falls to zero
It reverses direction
questions.answer: It stays the same
questions.explanation: The remaining branch still has the same battery voltage across the same resistance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal wire is made longer without changing material, temperature or cross-sectional area. Why does resistance increase?
options: The wire gains a larger cross-section
Its resistivity must decrease
Electrons stop carrying charge
Charge carriers encounter a longer conducting path
questions.answer: Charge carriers encounter a longer conducting path
questions.explanation: For fixed resistivity and area, resistance is proportional to length.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A magnet is held stationary inside a stationary coil. What induced emf results from this unchanged arrangement?
options: An emf that alternates automatically
Zero
A steady emf set only by magnet strength
An emf that grows with time
questions.answer: Zero
questions.explanation: Induction requires changing magnetic flux, not merely the presence of a magnetic field.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Why does an ordinary transformer need changing current in its primary coil?
options: It needs changing magnetic flux
Its core must rotate
Direct current has no charge carriers
The secondary must touch the primary
questions.answer: It needs changing magnetic flux
questions.explanation: A changing primary current produces flux changes that induce an emf in the secondary.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A converging lens forms an image of a very distant object. Where is the image approximately formed?
options: At the lens centre
On the object's side as a virtual image
At the focal plane
At twice the focal length always
questions.answer: At the focal plane
questions.explanation: Nearly parallel incident rays converge near the principal focal plane.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coherent light waves meet with crest aligned to crest. What happens locally?
options: Their wavelengths halve
Their amplitudes reinforce
Their frequencies cancel
Their speeds double
questions.answer: Their amplitudes reinforce
questions.explanation: The displacements add constructively when the waves are in phase.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radioactive sample contains fewer undecayed nuclei after one half-life. What happens to its activity?
options: It increases
It stays fixed until the last nucleus decays
It becomes independent of the number of nuclei
It decreases
questions.answer: It decreases
questions.explanation: Activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei for a fixed decay constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A velocity-time graph crosses from positive to negative values. What occurs at the crossing?
options: Its distance travelled returns to zero
Its mass changes sign
The object reverses direction
Its acceleration must be zero
questions.answer: The object reverses direction
questions.explanation: The velocity changes sign, indicating reversal; acceleration is determined by the graph's slope.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two balls are launched horizontally from the same height with different speeds. Ignoring air resistance, which lands first?
options: They land together
The faster ball
The slower ball
The heavier ball regardless of speed
questions.answer: They land together
questions.explanation: Their initial vertical velocities and vertical accelerations are identical.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two touching blocks accelerate together on a smooth floor when one is pushed. Why are their net forces unequal if their masses differ?
options: Contact forces violate Newton's third law
The lighter block has no net force
Their velocities must be different
They share acceleration, so net force is proportional to mass
questions.answer: They share acceleration, so net force is proportional to mass
questions.explanation: Newton's second law gives different net forces for different masses at the same acceleration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball moves upward after being thrown, ignoring air resistance. Which description is correct?
options: Gravity does positive work during ascent
Kinetic energy decreases while gravitational potential energy increases
Both energies increase
Mechanical energy decreases because speed decreases
questions.answer: Kinetic energy decreases while gravitational potential energy increases
questions.explanation: Gravity converts kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy while total mechanical energy stays constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A skater pulls in their arms while experiencing negligible external torque. Why do they spin faster?
options: Their moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum stays constant
Their angular momentum increases spontaneously
Their mass decreases
Their rotational kinetic energy must remain constant
questions.answer: Their moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum stays constant
questions.explanation: Conservation of angular momentum links smaller moment of inertia to greater angular speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two satellites have circular orbits around Earth. Why is the lower satellite faster?
options: The higher satellite is beyond gravity
The lower satellite must have greater mass
A smaller orbital radius requires a larger circular-orbit speed
The lower satellite has no gravitational potential energy
questions.answer: A smaller orbital radius requires a larger circular-orbit speed
questions.explanation: For a circular orbit, speed is proportional to the inverse square root of orbital radius.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Steady incompressible flow enters a narrower section of a pipe. What happens to average flow speed?
options: It must become zero
It increases
It decreases
It stays constant while volume flow increases
questions.answer: It increases
questions.explanation: Conservation of volume flow requires area times average speed to remain constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vacuum flask reduces heat transfer through its evacuated gap. Which process can still cross that gap?
options: Conduction through air
Convection of trapped gas
Bulk flow of liquid
Thermal radiation
questions.answer: Thermal radiation
questions.explanation: Radiation does not require matter, whereas gas conduction and convection are suppressed by the vacuum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas expands adiabatically while doing work. Why does its temperature decrease?
options: Its number of molecules decreases necessarily
Adiabatic expansion means constant temperature
The work comes from its internal energy
Heat flows into it faster than work leaves
questions.answer: The work comes from its internal energy
questions.explanation: With no heat input, work done by the gas reduces its internal energy and temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal spring oscillator's amplitude doubles while its mass and spring constant stay fixed. What happens to its period?
options: It stays the same
It doubles
It halves
It becomes four times larger
questions.answer: It stays the same
questions.explanation: The ideal spring period depends on mass and stiffness, not amplitude.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its second harmonic. What appears in addition to the end nodes?
options: An antinode at its midpoint
No internal nodes
A travelling crest fixed at one end
A node at its midpoint
questions.answer: A node at its midpoint
questions.explanation: The second harmonic contains two loops separated by a central node.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge moves along an equipotential surface. What work does the electric field do?
options: Work equal to charge times field strength
Zero
Positive for every charge
Negative for every charge
questions.answer: Zero
questions.explanation: Electric work depends on the potential difference, which is zero along an equipotential.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An isolated conductor reaches electrostatic equilibrium. Why is its interior electric field zero?
options: Free charges redistribute until the internal field cancels
The conductor contains no electrons
The conductor's potential must be zero
All external electric fields disappear everywhere
questions.answer: Free charges redistribute until the internal field cancels
questions.explanation: A nonzero internal field would keep free charges moving, contradicting electrostatic equilibrium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A real battery supplies a larger current. Why can its terminal voltage fall?
options: External resistance creates charge
The battery's internal current becomes zero
More voltage is lost across its internal resistance
Its emf must instantly become zero
questions.answer: More voltage is lost across its internal resistance
questions.explanation: Terminal voltage during discharge equals emf minus the internal voltage drop.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At a junction, one entering current becomes two outgoing currents. Why must their sum equal the entering current in steady state?
options: Both outgoing currents must be equal
Charge does not accumulate at the junction
Energy is created at the junction
Resistance is always equal in both branches
questions.answer: Charge does not accumulate at the junction
questions.explanation: Current conservation follows from charge conservation when there is no accumulating charge.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A magnet approaching a conducting loop experiences resistance to its motion. What explains this?
options: The loop creates energy from nothing
The loop always attracts every magnetic pole
Induced current cancels the magnet's mass
The induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux
questions.answer: The induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux
questions.explanation: Lenz's law makes the induced effect oppose the flux change, requiring mechanical work.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal capacitor is driven by a sinusoidal supply of unchanged voltage amplitude but higher frequency. What happens to current amplitude?
options: It remains zero
It reverses into direct current
It increases
It decreases
questions.answer: It increases
questions.explanation: Capacitive reactance decreases as frequency rises, allowing greater current amplitude.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A magnifying glass is used with an object inside its focal length. What image does the eye view?
options: An upright magnified virtual image
An inverted reduced real image
A real image at the lens centre
An upright image on a screen behind the lens
questions.answer: An upright magnified virtual image
questions.explanation: A converging lens used inside its focal distance produces an upright enlarged virtual image.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a double-slit experiment, the screen moves farther away while wavelength and slit spacing stay fixed. What happens to fringe spacing?
options: It decreases
It stays fixed
All bright fringes vanish
It increases
questions.answer: It increases
questions.explanation: Fringe spacing is proportional to the screen distance under the small-angle approximation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A p-n diode is forward biased. How does this promote conduction?
options: It turns both regions into insulators
It reduces the junction barrier
It removes all charge carriers
It widens the depletion region indefinitely
questions.answer: It reduces the junction barrier
questions.explanation: Forward bias lowers the potential barrier, allowing more majority carriers to cross the junction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ruler has a fixed positive zero error. Repeating a length measurement many times gives closely grouped results. What remains unresolved?
options: The systematic offset
Random scatter only
Whether the ruler has markings
The object's physical length changes
questions.answer: The systematic offset
questions.explanation: Repeated readings can improve precision without removing a fixed systematic error.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person stands on a scale in a lift moving upward but slowing down. How does the reading compare with their weight?
options: It equals weight because motion is upward
It is zero in every slowing lift
It is smaller
It is larger
questions.answer: It is smaller
questions.explanation: Upward motion with decreasing speed means downward acceleration, so the normal force is below weight.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two isolated carts stick together after colliding. Which statement is generally correct?
options: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy may decrease
Both momentum and kinetic energy must decrease
Kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
Neither quantity can be tracked
questions.answer: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy may decrease
questions.explanation: Sticking is inelastic: internal deformation can reduce kinetic energy while total momentum is conserved.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite is moved into a larger circular orbit. Which combination describes its new state?
options: Lower speed and lower total mechanical energy
Unchanged speed and unchanged total mechanical energy
Lower speed and greater total mechanical energy
Higher speed and greater total mechanical energy
questions.answer: Lower speed and greater total mechanical energy
questions.explanation: Larger circular orbits have lower orbital speed but less negative total mechanical energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal plate with a circular hole is heated uniformly. Which prediction is consistent with uniform expansion?
options: The hole enlarges as though the missing metal also expanded
The hole shrinks because metal expands inward only
The hole area stays fixed
The hole closes if the plate is thick
questions.answer: The hole enlarges as though the missing metal also expanded
questions.explanation: All linear dimensions scale upward under unconstrained uniform expansion, including the hole diameter.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two reservoirs remain at different fixed temperatures. Why can an engine between them not convert all absorbed heat into work in a cycle?
options: A gas cannot return to its initial state
The hot reservoir must have zero internal energy
Some heat must be rejected to satisfy the second law
Energy conservation alone requires all heat to be wasted
questions.answer: Some heat must be rejected to satisfy the second law
questions.explanation: A cyclic engine cannot take heat from a single reservoir and convert it entirely to work; heat rejection is required.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In ideal spring motion, when is acceleration magnitude greatest while kinetic energy is least?
options: At every position equally
At either extreme displacement
At equilibrium only
Halfway in time between equilibrium and an extreme always
questions.answer: At either extreme displacement
questions.explanation: Restoring acceleration is proportional to displacement, while speed is zero at the extremes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two equal pulses on a string, one upward and one downward, completely overlap and cancel momentarily. What happens afterward in the ideal model?
options: Their energy is destroyed
The string can never move again
Only one pulse survives
They pass through and reappear
questions.answer: They pass through and reappear
questions.explanation: Superposition is temporary; wave energy is not destroyed by momentary displacement cancellation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A closed surface encloses equal positive and negative charges. What follows from zero net enclosed charge?
options: No field line crosses the surface
Net electric flux is zero, but local fields need not be zero
The field is zero at every point on the surface
Potential is zero everywhere inside
questions.answer: Net electric flux is zero, but local fields need not be zero
questions.explanation: Gauss's law constrains net flux, not the field at each location.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical resistors are first in series and then in parallel across the same ideal voltage source. Which arrangement uses greater total power?
options: Series
Both use equal power
Neither can dissipate power
Parallel
questions.answer: Parallel
questions.explanation: Parallel connection has lower equivalent resistance, so total power V squared divided by resistance is greater.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an ideal series RLC circuit at resonance, which statement is correct?
options: The circuit stores no energy at any instant
Inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving impedance R
Each reactive component has zero voltage
The resistance becomes zero
questions.answer: Inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving impedance R
questions.explanation: Equal opposite reactances cancel in the total impedance even though individual components still exchange energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sample is chemically combined into a new compound. In the standard school model, what happens to its nuclear half-life?
options: It halves because bonds form
It doubles because electrons are shared
It follows the compound's boiling point
It remains essentially unchanged
questions.answer: It remains essentially unchanged
questions.explanation: Ordinary chemical changes affect electronic bonding, not the nuclear decay constant in this model.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two strings make slow beats. Slightly reducing the tension of string B makes the beats faster. If its frequency has not crossed that of A, what follows about B's original frequency?
options: It equalled A's exactly
Its frequency was independent of tension
It was lower than A's
It was higher than A's
questions.answer: It was lower than A's
questions.explanation: Lowering tension lowers B's frequency; a growing frequency difference therefore places B below A under the stated no-crossing condition.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged isolated conducting sphere is observed at two points outside it, one twice as far from its centre as the other. What comparison follows for electric-field magnitude?
options: The farther point has twice the field
The farther point has one quarter the field
The farther point has half the field
The fields are equal
questions.answer: The farther point has one quarter the field
questions.explanation: Outside a spherically symmetric charged conductor, the field follows an inverse-square dependence on distance from the centre.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal emits electrons under light only slightly above its threshold frequency. The frequency is halved and the intensity is doubled. In the single-photon model, what happens?
options: Emission stops despite the greater intensity
Maximum electron energy doubles
Current must double because brightness doubles
The metal's threshold frequency halves
questions.answer: Emission stops despite the greater intensity
questions.explanation: The new photon energy falls below the work function; more subthreshold photons do not produce ordinary photoemission.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two unequal hanging masses accelerate on an ideal pulley. Equal extra masses are added to both sides. What happens to acceleration magnitude?
options: It increases
It stays the same
It reverses direction
It decreases
questions.answer: It decreases
questions.explanation: The driving weight difference stays fixed while the total mass being accelerated increases.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a double-slit setup, slit separation is halved while screen distance is doubled, with wavelength unchanged. What happens to fringe spacing?
options: It halves
It stays the same
It becomes four times as large
It doubles
questions.answer: It becomes four times as large
questions.explanation: Fringe spacing is proportional to screen distance and inversely proportional to slit separation, so the two factors multiply.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A dielectric raises an isolated charged capacitor's capacitance. Which combined change follows?
options: Voltage rises and energy rises
Voltage falls and stored electrical energy falls
Voltage stays fixed and charge rises
Charge falls and capacitance falls
questions.answer: Voltage falls and stored electrical energy falls
questions.explanation: Isolation keeps charge fixed, so both Q/C and Q squared divided by twice capacitance decrease.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two narrow capillary tubes have the same wetting conditions, but one has twice the radius. How does the mass of liquid raised compare ideally?
options: It doubles in the wider tube
It halves in the wider tube
It is unchanged
It becomes four times larger
questions.answer: It doubles in the wider tube
questions.explanation: Rise height is inversely proportional to radius, while column area is proportional to radius squared; their product is proportional to radius.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Electrons start from rest and are accelerated through a potential difference. If that potential difference is quadrupled in the nonrelativistic regime, what happens to their de Broglie wavelength?
options: It quarters
It doubles
It stays fixed
It halves
questions.answer: It halves
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to the accelerating voltage, so momentum grows with its square root and wavelength varies inversely.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A flood-warning system benefits residents even when individual users cannot easily be charged. Why might collective provision be considered?
options: It has no production cost
Only its operator can benefit
Individual charges may not capture the shared benefit
Every resident must value it identically
questions.answer: Individual charges may not capture the shared benefit
questions.explanation: Some services have shared benefits and are difficult to provide solely through individual purchase.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Two groups accept parts of each other's proposals to reach an agreement. What does this illustrate?
options: A decision made without participation
A negotiated compromise
Complete agreement on every original demand
The absence of conflicting interests
questions.answer: A negotiated compromise
questions.explanation: Compromise can reconcile competing aims through concessions rather than identical preferences.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A constitution allocates authority to national and regional governments. What feature does this illustrate?
options: A constitutional division of governing powers
All authority belonging to one local official
The absence of national institutions
A requirement that every policy be identical everywhere
questions.answer: A constitutional division of governing powers
questions.explanation: Federal arrangements divide authority between levels of government under constitutional rules.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A constitution protects expression even when officials dislike criticism. What purpose does the protection serve?
options: Guaranteeing that every statement is accurate
Making all political disagreement disappear
Giving officials unlimited control over opinions
Limiting how public power may be used against individuals
questions.answer: Limiting how public power may be used against individuals
questions.explanation: Rights protections can constrain government action and preserve space for criticism and participation.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A campaign uses petitions, public meetings and lobbying to seek a reform. What do these activities show?
options: Public opinion cannot influence representatives
Every campaign automatically achieves its goals
Participation can extend beyond voting
Elections are the only means of expressing political demands
questions.answer: Participation can extend beyond voting
questions.explanation: Citizens and organised groups can pursue political change through several forms of engagement.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: An article openly states the political position from which it argues. What can readers do with that disclosure?
options: Stop checking factual claims
Consider how the stated perspective shapes its selection and interpretation of evidence
Assume every statement is false
Treat disclosure as proof of complete neutrality
questions.answer: Consider how the stated perspective shapes its selection and interpretation of evidence
questions.explanation: Identifying a perspective helps readers evaluate framing while still examining the evidence.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A poll asks whether respondents support a proposal described as obviously sensible. What is the concern?
options: The wording may lead respondents toward a preferred answer
The wording guarantees a representative sample
The phrase makes every answer more accurate
A leading phrase affects only the survey's length
questions.answer: The wording may lead respondents toward a preferred answer
questions.explanation: Evaluative wording can introduce response bias rather than neutrally measuring opinions.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Voters are asked to approve or reject a specific policy proposition directly. What distinguishes this from electing a representative?
options: It removes every role for public institutions
It means every voter agrees on the proposal's meaning
It guarantees that the proposal protects all rights
The vote concerns a policy decision rather than selecting a person to decide
questions.answer: The vote concerns a policy decision rather than selecting a person to decide
questions.explanation: A referendum puts a proposition to voters, whereas representative elections choose officeholders.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Several apparently separate news outlets have the same parent owner. What should an analysis of media diversity consider?
options: One owner guarantees identical reporting on every issue
Ownership makes the content impossible to examine
Common ownership may affect how independent their editorial choices are
Different outlet names prove complete independence
questions.answer: Common ownership may affect how independent their editorial choices are
questions.explanation: Ownership structure is relevant to potential influence and diversity, though actual editorial practice also matters.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Reporters examine documents to investigate the misuse of public funds. What democratic function can this support?
options: Removal of the need for evidence
Public scrutiny of those exercising power
Automatic proof of every accusation
Replacement of all courts by newspapers
questions.answer: Public scrutiny of those exercising power
questions.explanation: Investigative reporting can reveal information that helps people hold public authorities accountable.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: In a party-list proportional system, seats are distributed broadly according to parties' vote shares. What is the intended relationship?
options: Representation should reflect the distribution of votes more proportionately
Every party must receive the same seats
The largest party must win every seat
Votes are irrelevant once parties submit lists
questions.answer: Representation should reflect the distribution of votes more proportionately
questions.explanation: Proportional allocation aims to connect the share of seats to electoral support, subject to the system's rules.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: An organisation presents evidence to lawmakers in support of its members' interests. What activity is illustrated?
options: A judicial verdict
A constitutional amendment by itself
A referendum of all citizens
Lobbying
questions.answer: Lobbying
questions.explanation: Lobbying seeks to influence public decisions through communication with decision-makers.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A volunteer joins a campaign because they care about its cause, without expecting personal material reward. What motivates participation here?
options: An absence of political preferences
A requirement to obtain public office
Commitment to the policy aim
A guaranteed financial payment
questions.answer: Commitment to the policy aim
questions.explanation: People can participate because they value a collective or policy objective.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: District boundaries are deliberately drawn to favour one party's chances. What is the main representational concern?
options: Population geography has no connection to representation
Boundary choices can distort how votes translate into seats
Boundaries automatically reveal every voter's preference
Every district must then have identical turnout
questions.answer: Boundary choices can distort how votes translate into seats
questions.explanation: Partisan boundary design can give one side an advantage beyond its overall vote share.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A representative prioritises an area's transport problems after hearing from residents. What relationship is illustrated?
options: Responsiveness to constituency concerns
A guarantee that every resident has identical priorities
Complete independence from constituent interests
A transfer of all legislative power to one resident
questions.answer: Responsiveness to constituency concerns
questions.explanation: Constituency representation involves responding to the interests and concerns of the people represented.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A legislature increasingly includes people from backgrounds previously excluded. Which change is directly described?
options: Proof that every group's policy aims are achieved
The end of all political disagreement
A necessary change to every constitutional rule
Greater descriptive representation
questions.answer: Greater descriptive representation
questions.explanation: Descriptive representation concerns who representatives are, which differs from what policies they pursue.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: In a system authorising judicial review, a court examines whether a law conflicts with the constitution. What role is it exercising?
options: Conducting a public opinion poll
Choosing the next election's winner
Checking legislation against higher constitutional rules
Writing every future law on its own
questions.answer: Checking legislation against higher constitutional rules
questions.explanation: Judicial review assesses the compatibility of public acts with constitutional requirements in systems that provide it.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: One institution makes laws while another implements them under the constitutional arrangement. What distinction is illustrated?
options: Two identical tasks with different names
Legislative and executive functions
Public and private speech only
National and foreign currency
questions.answer: Legislative and executive functions
questions.explanation: Making general rules and administering or enforcing them are distinct governing functions.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A policy is described as successful. Which evidence is most relevant to evaluating that claim?
options: Reliable outcomes compared with the policy's stated objectives
Only the popularity of its name
The size of the report's cover image
The number of times officials repeat the claim
questions.answer: Reliable outcomes compared with the policy's stated objectives
questions.explanation: Evaluation requires evidence about whether intended results were achieved and what other effects occurred.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A government's spending exceeds its revenue in a particular year. What does this describe?
options: The entire accumulated public debt
A budget surplus
A guarantee that every public service has expanded
A budget deficit for that period
questions.answer: A budget deficit for that period
questions.explanation: The annual deficit is a flow, distinct from the stock of debt accumulated over time.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Many groups are allowed to participate, but a small wealthy group has consistently greater access to decision-makers. What should political analysis distinguish?
options: Wealth from influence as necessarily unrelated
The number of group names from all actual outcomes
Formal opportunities to participate from unequal practical influence
Legal participation from the complete absence of power
questions.answer: Formal opportunities to participate from unequal practical influence
questions.explanation: Equal formal access does not establish equal resources, attention or influence in practice.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A respondent gives an immediate answer about an unfamiliar issue, then changes it after learning more. What should a poll analyst consider?
options: All opinions are fixed before people encounter information
Some expressed preferences may be weakly formed or sensitive to information
Every changed answer is deliberate dishonesty
The first answer must be the only genuine preference
questions.answer: Some expressed preferences may be weakly formed or sensitive to information
questions.explanation: Opinions vary in strength and familiarity, so a response need not represent a settled position.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: One chamber represents population while another gives regions equal representation. What tension can this design address?
options: Representation of people alongside representation of constituent regions
The need to give every region the same population
The elimination of every legislative disagreement
A requirement that both chambers always have identical members
questions.answer: Representation of people alongside representation of constituent regions
questions.explanation: Different representation rules can balance population-based and territorial interests.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A higher government requires a new regional service but supplies no additional funding. What issue arises?
options: The service is necessarily cost-free
Regional budgets automatically rise by the required amount
The requirement guarantees uniform local capacity
Responsibility can increase without matching financial resources
questions.answer: Responsibility can increase without matching financial resources
questions.explanation: A mandate can impose costs that the implementing authority must find resources to meet.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Regional governments choose different policies and have unequal revenue bases. What consequence is possible?
options: Regional choice guarantees equal economic resources
A constitution makes all implementation differences impossible
Service provision may vary across regions
Every resident must receive identical provision
questions.answer: Service provision may vary across regions
questions.explanation: Decentralised choices and unequal capacity can produce variation in public services.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A right binds national authorities but is not effectively protected against equivalent regional action. What gap remains?
options: Written national rights automatically resolve every enforcement issue
Protection depends on which level exercises the power
The right is necessarily protected equally everywhere
Regional authority can have no effect on individuals
questions.answer: Protection depends on which level exercises the power
questions.explanation: Effective rights protection requires attention to the authorities bound by the rules and the means of enforcement.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A rule is written identically for everyone but creates severe barriers for one group. What must an equality analysis examine?
options: Its practical effects as well as its formally equal wording
Only whether the same font is used
Whether every rule must have identical effects in all circumstances
Whether unequal effects make evidence unnecessary
questions.answer: Its practical effects as well as its formally equal wording
questions.explanation: Formal uniformity does not settle whether a policy creates unjustified or discriminatory disadvantages.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A policy protects one group's interests while restricting another group's liberty. What should a reasoned assessment consider?
options: Only which group is larger
A rule that every restriction is justified by popularity
An assumption that interests can never conflict
The justification, effects and proportionality of the competing claims
questions.answer: The justification, effects and proportionality of the competing claims
questions.explanation: Political judgement often requires weighing rights and interests rather than treating one benefit as decisive by itself.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A popular top-level candidate attracts voters who also support other candidates from the same party. What effect is illustrated?
options: A change in the legal voting age
An absence of party influence
A coattail effect across linked contests
Proof that every candidate has identical personal popularity
questions.answer: A coattail effect across linked contests
questions.explanation: Support for one prominent candidate can benefit other candidates sharing the party label.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: An officeholder has greater name recognition and a record of constituency service than a new challenger. Why can this matter electorally?
options: Voters are legally required to support incumbents
Existing office can provide advantages separate from the merits of a new proposal
Holding office guarantees re-election
Challengers cannot communicate with voters
questions.answer: Existing office can provide advantages separate from the merits of a new proposal
questions.explanation: Visibility, established networks and service records can contribute to incumbency advantages.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Two reports use the same statistics, but one foregrounds individual stories and the other institutions and long-term trends. What differs?
options: The framing of the issue
Necessarily the arithmetic of every statistic
The existence of the event being reported
The legal status of both publishers
questions.answer: The framing of the issue
questions.explanation: Framing selects which aspects and explanations receive attention, even when some underlying facts are shared.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A small party has substantial national support spread thinly across many single-member plurality districts. Why might it win few seats?
options: National vote share automatically guarantees equal seat share
Every district must reserve it a seat
The system counts only the opinions of party leaders
It may rarely finish first in any district
questions.answer: It may rarely finish first in any district
questions.explanation: Geographically dispersed support can translate poorly into seats where winning each district is decisive.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A campaign's success would benefit supporters and non-contributors alike. Why may it struggle to recruit contributions?
options: Non-contributors must receive no benefit
A shared aim guarantees equal contributions
People may hope to benefit from others' effort without contributing
The benefit cannot be shared by definition
questions.answer: People may hope to benefit from others' effort without contributing
questions.explanation: Free-rider incentives can make collective organisation difficult even when the outcome has broad value.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A system requires both chambers to approve the same bill, but they pass different versions. What must happen before enactment under that rule?
options: The two texts can be treated as identical because their titles match
The disagreement must be resolved so both approve a common text
Either version automatically becomes law without further action
The larger chamber's version always prevails regardless of the rule
questions.answer: The disagreement must be resolved so both approve a common text
questions.explanation: Requiring concurrence gives both chambers a role in agreeing the legislation's actual content.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A proposed constitution makes the executive entirely dependent on a single legislature for appointment and removal. What concern might critics raise?
options: Insufficient institutional independence to check that legislature
A guarantee that the executive cannot be influenced
The disappearance of all legislative authority
A necessary increase in judicial power in every case
questions.answer: Insufficient institutional independence to check that legislature
questions.explanation: The arrangement may concentrate effective control unless other checks and accountability mechanisms operate.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: An executive appeals directly to the public to build support for a policy that legislators resist. What resource is being used?
options: A judicial power to invalidate legislation
A guarantee of automatic legislative approval
The right to cancel every future election
The visibility and persuasive platform of executive office
questions.answer: The visibility and persuasive platform of executive office
questions.explanation: Public communication can create political pressure even when it does not supply a formal power to legislate.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: An executive nominates an official, but another institution must approve the appointment. What is the intended check?
options: Approval is unnecessary once a nomination exists
The public has no possible interest in appointments
More than one institution participates in selecting the official
The nominee automatically chooses all approvers
questions.answer: More than one institution participates in selecting the official
questions.explanation: Shared appointment powers can limit unilateral control, while also creating opportunities for disagreement or delay.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A judge gives weight to the choices of elected institutions when the legal framework permits discretion. What approach does this illustrate?
options: The abolition of constitutional rules
Judicial restraint
A claim that courts never interpret law
A power to replace every elected decision automatically
questions.answer: Judicial restraint
questions.explanation: Judicial restraint emphasises limits on judicial intervention and respect for other institutions' legitimate roles.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A national grant is available only if a regional government adopts specified practices. How can it influence regional policy?
options: Financial conditions can encourage choices beyond an unconditional transfer
The region receives the funds regardless of every condition
Funding conditions have no influence on incentives
The grant removes all need for regional administration
questions.answer: Financial conditions can encourage choices beyond an unconditional transfer
questions.explanation: Conditional grants can shape decisions by linking resources to compliance with policy requirements.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Public employees are selected through job-related qualifications rather than personal party connections. What principle is emphasised?
options: Political patronage as the only criterion
Inheritance of every public position
Selection by the largest private donation
Merit-based recruitment
questions.answer: Merit-based recruitment
questions.explanation: Merit systems aim to connect recruitment with competence rather than personal or partisan favour.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Everyone values a shared benefit, yet voluntary contributions remain low because people expect others to pay. What explains the gap?
options: Shared benefits automatically produce full cooperation
The outcome cannot have any public-good characteristics
Individual incentives can obstruct a collectively desired outcome
Low contributions prove nobody values the outcome
questions.answer: Individual incentives can obstruct a collectively desired outcome
questions.explanation: Collective value does not remove incentives to free ride when benefits cannot easily be withheld from non-contributors.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Two powerful groups reach a compromise that imposes substantial costs on people excluded from negotiation. What remains to assess?
options: Whether excluded people can have legitimate interests
Whether the agreement fairly considers affected non-participants
Only whether the negotiating groups are satisfied
Whether compromise automatically guarantees justice
questions.answer: Whether the agreement fairly considers affected non-participants
questions.explanation: Agreement among participants does not establish legitimacy or fairness for everyone affected.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A constitution makes amendment much harder than ordinary lawmaking. What trade-off does this create?
options: Stability and protection against sudden change versus adaptability
A guarantee that all existing provisions are just
The ability to change every rule without consent
An absence of any future constitutional dispute
questions.answer: Stability and protection against sudden change versus adaptability
questions.explanation: Entrenchment can protect foundational rules but can also make needed reform more difficult.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Two states give regions similar practical powers, but only one constitution protects those powers against ordinary national revocation. Why is the distinction important?
options: Practical delegation is always constitutionally identical to federalism
A written guarantee proves that no disputes will occur
The number of regions alone determines their legal security
Similar current arrangements can rest on different guarantees of regional autonomy
questions.answer: Similar current arrangements can rest on different guarantees of regional autonomy
questions.explanation: The source and protection of regional authority matter alongside the powers currently exercised.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Regional policy experiments reveal useful results, but some effects cross regional borders. What must an evaluation include?
options: An assumption that regional boundaries stop all effects
A rule that variation prevents any useful comparison
Learning benefits alongside spillovers affecting other jurisdictions
Only outcomes inside the experimenting region
questions.answer: Learning benefits alongside spillovers affecting other jurisdictions
questions.explanation: Decentralised experimentation can generate information while creating external effects requiring coordination.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A large voluntary poll has many responses but attracts mainly highly motivated supporters. Why is size alone insufficient?
options: A narrow numerical margin proves random recruitment
Selection bias can persist despite a large sample
A large poll must represent every group equally
More responses necessarily remove every wording effect
questions.answer: Selection bias can persist despite a large sample
questions.explanation: Precision from many observations does not repair systematic differences between respondents and the target population.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A clear majority supports a measure restricting a minority's protected rights. Why does the vote alone not settle legitimacy?
options: Democratic decisions must also be assessed against rights and constitutional constraints
A majority can never make any legitimate decision
Minority rights require unanimous agreement on every policy
Popularity automatically eliminates constitutional limits
questions.answer: Democratic decisions must also be assessed against rights and constitutional constraints
questions.explanation: Majority rule is one democratic principle and operates alongside protections against misuse of public power.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Incumbents win often, but stronger candidates also tend to become incumbents. Why is the win rate alone not the causal effect of holding office?
options: The win rate proves office has no possible effect
All incumbents and challengers must be equally strong
A causal conclusion requires no comparison
Candidate selection and office advantages may both contribute
questions.answer: Candidate selection and office advantages may both contribute
questions.explanation: Separating incumbency's effect requires considering differences that existed before the office was held.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A market has many outlet brands but concentrated ownership and similar source dependence. What would best assess viewpoint diversity?
options: Assume one owner forces identical coverage in every article
Treat audience size as the only measure of diversity
Examine ownership, editorial practice and the actual range of coverage
Count brand names and assume each is independent
questions.answer: Examine ownership, editorial practice and the actual range of coverage
questions.explanation: The number of labels alone does not reveal independence or variation in the information supplied.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Readers see the same event framed either as individual failure or as a result of institutional conditions. Why might their preferred responses differ?
options: Only the article's publication date can matter
Different causal emphases can make different remedies seem appropriate
Framing must change every underlying fact
Readers' preferences cannot respond to interpretation
questions.answer: Different causal emphases can make different remedies seem appropriate
questions.explanation: Explanations of why a problem occurs influence which policy responses appear relevant or justified.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: Two electoral systems produce different seat shares from the same distribution of votes. What follows?
options: Rules translating votes into seats affect representation
The voters must secretly have cast different ballots
One numerical outcome proves every other system undemocratic
Electoral rules have no substantive political consequences
questions.answer: Rules translating votes into seats affect representation
questions.explanation: District structures, thresholds and allocation rules can produce different representative outcomes from similar support.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: An oddly shaped district benefits one party, but settlement patterns are also geographically uneven. What is needed before attributing the result solely to manipulation?
options: A rule that every unusual shape proves partisan intent
An assumption that population geography explains every boundary
Only the colour used to draw the map
Evidence about boundary choices and plausible alternatives given population geography
questions.answer: Evidence about boundary choices and plausible alternatives given population geography
questions.explanation: Assessing gerrymandering requires more than shape alone and should consider the design process and relevant alternatives.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A legislature becomes more socially diverse, but policy outcomes for excluded groups barely change. What distinction matters?
options: Diverse membership guarantees every desired policy
Policy outcomes can be inferred from appearance alone
Who holds office and whose interests policy serves are related but distinct
Social diversity has no possible political relevance
questions.answer: Who holds office and whose interests policy serves are related but distinct
questions.explanation: Descriptive representation does not automatically establish substantive representation in decisions and outcomes.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A proposal has broad support but must pass several independent approval stages. Why can it still fail?
options: Only the proposal's title determines its passage
Each stage can create a veto point or bargaining obstacle
Popular support automatically overrides all procedures
Multiple stages guarantee faster agreement
questions.answer: Each stage can create a veto point or bargaining obstacle
questions.explanation: Institutional procedures shape which preferences become policy and can block measures despite substantial support.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A court can invalidate an elected legislature's law under constitutional rules. What tension must an analysis consider?
options: Protecting constitutional limits while respecting democratic accountability
A choice between having any law and having no law
Proof that elections have no value
A guarantee that courts never make contested interpretations
questions.answer: Protecting constitutional limits while respecting democratic accountability
questions.explanation: Constitutional review can constrain majorities, raising questions about both rights protection and the legitimate scope of judicial power.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A commentator praises judicial restraint only when it helps their preferred policy and demands intervention otherwise. What weakens the argument?
options: Every change of opinion is necessarily dishonest
No judicial decision can be evaluated
A preferred outcome makes consistency irrelevant
The stated institutional principle is being applied selectively
questions.answer: The stated institutional principle is being applied selectively
questions.explanation: A principled institutional argument needs reasons for different treatment beyond whether the outcome is personally favoured.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: An agency is judged only by the number of cases processed and begins prioritising easy cases over urgent complex ones. What problem is illustrated?
options: Measurement removes every need for judgement
Complex cases must be outside the agency's responsibility
A performance measure can redirect effort away from the underlying public purpose
Higher counts prove better service for every group
questions.answer: A performance measure can redirect effort away from the underlying public purpose
questions.explanation: Narrow targets can create incentives that improve the metric while weakening the outcome it was meant to represent.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A public service is contracted to a private provider, but government remains responsible for access and standards. What follows?
options: Ownership alone resolves every access concern
Contracting changes delivery without removing the need for public oversight
Private delivery automatically ends all public responsibility
A contract guarantees quality without monitoring
questions.answer: Contracting changes delivery without removing the need for public oversight
questions.explanation: Accountability requires arrangements for standards, monitoring and remedy even when a different organisation delivers the service.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: An outcome improves after a reform while several other relevant conditions change. What is the strongest evaluation approach?
options: Compare credible alternatives and account for the other changes before attributing the effect
Assign the full improvement to the reform because it came first
Reject all evidence because circumstances are complex
Use only supporters' descriptions of success
questions.answer: Compare credible alternatives and account for the other changes before attributing the effect
questions.explanation: Temporal sequence alone cannot isolate a reform's causal contribution when other influences are changing.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.q: A deficit grows during a downturn even though tax rules and spending programmes are unchanged. Why not assume a new discretionary stimulus?
options: An unchanged programme guarantees an unchanged budget balance
Every deficit increase proves a new law was passed
The public budget is independent of economic conditions
Automatic changes in receipts and some payments can widen the deficit
questions.answer: Automatic changes in receipts and some payments can widen the deficit
questions.explanation: The fiscal balance can respond to the cycle without a deliberate change in policy settings.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A researcher links changes in hippocampal cells to memory formation. Which perspective is most directly used?
options: Psychodynamic
Biological
Humanistic
Sociocultural
questions.answer: Biological
questions.explanation: The explanation connects mental functioning with processes in the nervous system.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A researcher studies how job demands match workers' abilities. Which application of psychology fits?
options: Industrial-organizational psychology
Clinical psychology
Sport psychology
School counselling
questions.answer: Industrial-organizational psychology
questions.explanation: Industrial-organizational psychology examines people and behaviour in work settings.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A psychologist studies one person's unusual memory difficulties in great depth. Which method is illustrated?
options: A census of every adult
A randomised national experiment
A meta-analysis of hundreds of experiments
A case study
questions.answer: A case study
questions.explanation: A case study provides intensive information about a particular individual or small unit.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A researcher records how children share toys during ordinary playground activity without assigning conditions. What method fits?
options: Random allocation to treatments
A test of a drug's biological effects
Naturalistic observation
A laboratory experiment
questions.answer: Naturalistic observation
questions.explanation: The behaviour is observed in its usual setting without an experimental manipulation.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Students who report more television time tend to receive lower exam marks. What relationship is described?
options: Identical marks for all students
A negative correlation
A positive correlation
Proof that television causes lower marks
questions.answer: A negative correlation
questions.explanation: The variables tend to move in opposite directions; the association alone does not establish causation.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student deliberately moves their hand to pick up a pencil. Which system controls the relevant voluntary skeletal-muscle activity?
options: The somatic nervous system
Only the digestive system
Only the endocrine glands
The parasympathetic system alone
questions.answer: The somatic nervous system
questions.explanation: Somatic motor pathways carry commands to skeletal muscles involved in voluntary movement.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A faint tone is detected on about half the presentations under defined conditions. What does its intensity approximate?
options: The maximum tolerable intensity
A difference threshold between two loud tones
The highest frequency a speaker can produce
The absolute threshold
questions.answer: The absolute threshold
questions.explanation: The absolute threshold is conventionally defined by detection on half of presentations.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A room's unchanged smell becomes less noticeable after someone has been inside for a while. What process fits?
options: Proof that the smell has disappeared
A new conditioned fear response
Sensory adaptation
An automatic increase in the smell's concentration
questions.answer: Sensory adaptation
questions.explanation: Responsiveness can decline during continued exposure to a relatively constant stimulus.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Dots placed close together are seen as separate clusters despite sharing the same colour. Which grouping cue is most relevant?
options: A difference in genetic inheritance
Proximity
A change in sound frequency
A reinforcement schedule
questions.answer: Proximity
questions.explanation: Nearby elements tend to be grouped together in visual perception.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A broken outline is perceived as a complete circle. Which principle best explains this?
options: Closure
Negative reinforcement
Retroactive interference
Random sampling
questions.answer: Closure
questions.explanation: Closure describes perceiving a complete form despite gaps in the available visual information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A child learns to fear one furry toy and then responds similarly to other furry toys. What process is illustrated?
options: Complete extinction
Learning with no stimulus association
A fixed-interval reinforcement schedule
Stimulus generalisation
questions.answer: Stimulus generalisation
questions.explanation: A learned response can extend to stimuli resembling the original conditioned stimulus.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: An agreed privilege is removed after a behaviour, and that behaviour subsequently decreases. What is illustrated?
options: Negative reinforcement
Classical extinction alone
Negative punishment
Positive reinforcement
questions.answer: Negative punishment
questions.explanation: Removing a valued consequence to reduce a behaviour is negative punishment; negative refers to removal.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A coach first rewards a rough attempt, then rewards progressively closer versions of a target skill. What is the method?
options: Unconditional stimulus presentation only
Shaping
Random sampling
Sensory adaptation
questions.answer: Shaping
questions.explanation: Shaping reinforces successive approximations toward a desired behaviour.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Asked to picture a leader on a sports team, a student immediately imagines the captain as a typical example. What does the captain serve as?
options: A prototype
A randomised control
A sensory threshold
A conditioned reflex
questions.answer: A prototype
questions.explanation: A prototype is a representative example used to organise a category.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student follows a definite sequence of valid steps guaranteed to solve a particular class of problem. What approach is used?
options: A guess with no rule
A stereotype alone
An unrelated memory cue
An algorithm
questions.answer: An algorithm
questions.explanation: An algorithm specifies a procedure that produces a solution when correctly applied to a suitable problem.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A shopper uses a quick rule of thumb to narrow many choices, accepting that it may occasionally fail. What is used?
options: A randomised experiment
A sensory transduction process
A heuristic
A guaranteed exhaustive algorithm
questions.answer: A heuristic
questions.explanation: A heuristic reduces decision effort but does not guarantee a correct or optimal answer.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student knows a familiar word and can describe its meaning but temporarily cannot produce it. What does this illustrate?
options: Successful recall of the missing word
Retrieval blocking
Proof that the word was never learned
Permanent loss of all language knowledge
questions.answer: Retrieval blocking
questions.explanation: The tip-of-the-tongue experience reflects a temporary difficulty accessing stored information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A learner remembers a sequence using a sentence whose initial letters match the required items. What strategy is used?
options: An acrostic mnemonic
Random guessing
A placebo comparison
A punishment schedule
questions.answer: An acrostic mnemonic
questions.explanation: The sentence provides organised cues for retrieving the ordered information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A child uses precise finger movements to cut out a small paper shape. What type of skill is mainly involved?
options: Only gross locomotion
A purely hormonal reflex
A measure of language comprehension
Fine motor skill
questions.answer: Fine motor skill
questions.explanation: Fine motor skills involve controlled movements of relatively small muscles, particularly in the hands and fingers.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A learner completes a task mainly to receive a promised reward. What kind of motivation is emphasised?
options: An absence of any motive
Sensory adaptation
Extrinsic motivation
Intrinsic enjoyment alone
questions.answer: Extrinsic motivation
questions.explanation: Extrinsic motivation is directed toward an external consequence rather than enjoyment of the activity itself.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A researcher assesses the same children repeatedly over several years. What is a main advantage over comparing different age groups once?
options: It proves every change is caused by age alone
It can track change within the same individuals
It eliminates all effects of participants leaving
It guarantees that historical events have no influence
questions.answer: It can track change within the same individuals
questions.explanation: Longitudinal research follows individuals over time, though attrition and other influences still require consideration.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Participants with the greatest difficulties disproportionately leave a long study. Why can the final results be misleading?
options: The remaining sample may no longer represent the original group
Every remaining measurement becomes mathematically incorrect
Leaving necessarily improves the study's generalisability
A longer study automatically removes selection bias
questions.answer: The remaining sample may no longer represent the original group
questions.explanation: Selective attrition can change who is represented in the analysed outcomes.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Names are randomly selected from a complete school register for a survey. What does this procedure principally support?
options: Proof that any correlation is causal
Random assignment to different treatments
Identical responses from all selected pupils
A less selectively recruited sample of that school
questions.answer: A less selectively recruited sample of that school
questions.explanation: Random sampling concerns selection from a population; it is different from assigning experimental conditions.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A researcher varies study-noise level and measures recall accuracy. Which pairing is correct?
options: Both are necessarily uncontrolled confounders
Neither variable can be measured
Noise is the independent variable; recall is the dependent variable
Recall is the independent variable; noise is the dependent variable
questions.answer: Noise is the independent variable; recall is the dependent variable
questions.explanation: The independent variable is manipulated, and the dependent variable records the outcome of interest.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: An experiment compares an active intervention with an apparently similar inactive one while participants do not know their allocation. What is the purpose of the inactive comparison?
options: Ensure that the inactive treatment contains the active ingredient
Help distinguish intervention effects from participant expectations
Guarantee that every participant has identical expectations
Remove the need to measure outcomes
questions.answer: Help distinguish intervention effects from participant expectations
questions.explanation: A credible placebo comparison can help control expectancy-related influences on reported or observed outcomes.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: In a model synapse, a substance activates receptors normally activated by a neurotransmitter. What effect is most consistent with agonist action?
options: It mimics or facilitates signalling in that system
It necessarily destroys every receptor
It blocks all neurotransmitter activity by definition
It prevents the receptor from having any response
questions.answer: It mimics or facilitates signalling in that system
questions.explanation: An agonist can imitate or enhance activity associated with a neurotransmitter system.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A person distinguishes colour well in bright light but poorly in dim conditions. Which receptor difference helps explain this?
options: Rods provide equally detailed colour vision at every light level
Cones operate only when no light reaches the eye
The retina stops all signalling in dim light
Cone-mediated colour vision works best with sufficient illumination
questions.answer: Cone-mediated colour vision works best with sufficient illumination
questions.explanation: Cones support colour discrimination and function best in brighter conditions; rod-dominated dim-light vision has limited colour information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: After prolonged fixation on a green patch, a reddish afterimage appears on a white surface. Which explanation fits?
options: The eye has created a new external light source
Green and red are identical wavelengths
Adaptation within opposing colour-response systems
The white surface physically turns red
questions.answer: Adaptation within opposing colour-response systems
questions.explanation: Unequal adaptation in opponent colour mechanisms can produce a complementary afterimage.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Two lines cross, yet viewers perceive two smooth continuing paths instead of several sharply turning pieces. What principle is illustrated?
options: An endocrine feedback loop
Good continuation
Extinction of a conditioned response
Negative punishment
questions.answer: Good continuation
questions.explanation: The visual system tends to organise elements into smoothly continuing contours.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A tone previously paired with food is repeatedly presented without food, and salivation to the tone declines. What changed?
options: The learned predictive relationship is no longer reinforced by pairing
The tone was never a conditioned stimulus
Food has become biologically incapable of producing salivation
The animal has lost all learning capacity
questions.answer: The learned predictive relationship is no longer reinforced by pairing
questions.explanation: Repeated presentation without the unconditioned stimulus produces extinction of the conditioned response.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A response is rewarded after an unpredictable number of repetitions. Which schedule describes this?
options: Fixed interval
Fixed ratio
Variable interval
Variable ratio
questions.answer: Variable ratio
questions.explanation: Ratio schedules depend on response counts, and variable means the required count changes unpredictably.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student entering a familiar café expects to queue, order, pay and collect food. What is this organised expectation?
options: A genetic mutation
A difference threshold
An event script
An action potential
questions.answer: An event script
questions.explanation: An event schema or script represents the expected sequence of actions in a familiar situation.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A person judges an applicant solely by resemblance to a familiar occupational stereotype while ignoring the applicant's record. What shortcut is dominating?
options: A guaranteed deductive algorithm
Representativeness-based judgement
Careful use of all relevant individual evidence
Random assignment
questions.answer: Representativeness-based judgement
questions.explanation: Judging category membership by resemblance can overshadow more informative evidence about the individual.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A learner compares explanations against a dataset and evaluates which fits best. Which form of ability is most directly exercised in the triarchic model?
options: Analytical intelligence
Only practical familiarity with daily routines
Only generating novel ideas without evaluation
A fixed measure of physical strength
questions.answer: Analytical intelligence
questions.explanation: Analytical ability concerns examining, comparing and evaluating information or proposed explanations.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A test is normed only on a narrow, unusually selected group. What is a concern when interpreting scores from a broader population?
options: Norming guarantees fairness for every possible group
The test must contain no correct answers
A smaller reference group automatically gives universal validity
The comparison norms may not represent that population
questions.answer: The comparison norms may not represent that population
questions.explanation: Norm-based interpretation depends on the suitability of the reference sample for the people assessed.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student keeps a spoken number in mind while checking a simple instruction. What system supports this temporary storage and processing?
options: Only sensory adaptation
A peripheral hormone gland
Working memory
Only a permanent autobiographical archive
questions.answer: Working memory
questions.explanation: Working memory temporarily maintains and manipulates information needed for an ongoing task.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A person recalls a group success as mainly their own achievement despite records showing equal contributions. What bias fits?
options: Proof that the other contributors were absent
A self-enhancing memory bias
Perfectly neutral reconstruction
Random sampling error in the records by definition
questions.answer: A self-enhancing memory bias
questions.explanation: Memory can be reconstructed in ways that favour one's own contribution or self-image.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A learner connects new concepts to examples from their own experiences. Why can this improve later recall?
options: Personal relevance can provide richer encoding and retrieval cues
It guarantees flawless memory for every detail
It removes all need to understand the concepts
Personally relevant material can never be forgotten
questions.answer: Personal relevance can provide richer encoding and retrieval cues
questions.explanation: Self-referential elaboration can make information more meaningfully connected to existing knowledge.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: In a standard attachment observation, a child explores while using the caregiver as a secure base and seeks comfort on reunion. Which pattern is most consistent?
options: A conclusion that the child never experiences distress
Proof that attachment has no role in exploration
A diagnosis based on a single isolated action
Secure attachment
questions.answer: Secure attachment
questions.explanation: The coordinated pattern of exploration and comfort seeking is characteristic of secure attachment in the model.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student attributes a disappointing result entirely to a teacher's dislike and sees no role for their own preparation. What belief is illustrated?
options: Proof that the teacher caused the result
A measure of the student's actual intelligence
An external locus of control for that outcome
Strong perceived control over the outcome
questions.answer: An external locus of control for that outcome
questions.explanation: The attribution locates the outcome's control outside the self, but does not establish whether that explanation is accurate.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A theory is adjusted so that every possible observation counts as support. Why is this a scientific weakness?
options: Its predictions must be numerically precise
No conceivable result could count against it
A theory becomes stronger when no test can challenge it
It has necessarily been replicated in every population
questions.answer: No conceivable result could count against it
questions.explanation: A scientific explanation must expose itself to possible disconfirmation rather than accommodate every outcome automatically.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A result contradicts a theory's prediction, but the study's measurement was unreliable. Why seek a stronger replication before deciding?
options: The contradiction may reflect measurement problems rather than a failure of the theory
A theory can never be challenged by evidence
Repeating a study guarantees that the theory will be confirmed
An unreliable measure necessarily produces the correct result
questions.answer: The contradiction may reflect measurement problems rather than a failure of the theory
questions.explanation: Evaluating a theory requires considering the quality and reproducibility of evidence that appears to support or challenge it.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: An unusual patient shows a pattern that challenges an existing memory theory. What is the strongest use of the case?
options: Assume the patient's pattern represents every person
Discard it solely because it concerns one person
Estimate its population prevalence directly from the single case
Inform or challenge theory while testing how widely the pattern applies
questions.answer: Inform or challenge theory while testing how widely the pattern applies
questions.explanation: A case can be theoretically informative without establishing how common the pattern is across a population.
