questions.answer: Industrial-organizational psychology
questions.explanation: Industrial-organizational psychology examines people and behaviour in work settings.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A psychologist studies one person's unusual memory difficulties in great depth. Which method is illustrated?
options: A census of every adult
A randomised national experiment
A meta-analysis of hundreds of experiments
A case study
questions.answer: A case study
questions.explanation: A case study provides intensive information about a particular individual or small unit.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A researcher records how children share toys during ordinary playground activity without assigning conditions. What method fits?
options: Random allocation to treatments
A test of a drug's biological effects
Naturalistic observation
A laboratory experiment
questions.answer: Naturalistic observation
questions.explanation: The behaviour is observed in its usual setting without an experimental manipulation.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Students who report more television time tend to receive lower exam marks. What relationship is described?
options: Identical marks for all students
A negative correlation
A positive correlation
Proof that television causes lower marks
questions.answer: A negative correlation
questions.explanation: The variables tend to move in opposite directions; the association alone does not establish causation.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student deliberately moves their hand to pick up a pencil. Which system controls the relevant voluntary skeletal-muscle activity?
options: The somatic nervous system
Only the digestive system
Only the endocrine glands
The parasympathetic system alone
questions.answer: The somatic nervous system
questions.explanation: Somatic motor pathways carry commands to skeletal muscles involved in voluntary movement.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A faint tone is detected on about half the presentations under defined conditions. What does its intensity approximate?
options: The maximum tolerable intensity
A difference threshold between two loud tones
The highest frequency a speaker can produce
The absolute threshold
questions.answer: The absolute threshold
questions.explanation: The absolute threshold is conventionally defined by detection on half of presentations.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A room's unchanged smell becomes less noticeable after someone has been inside for a while. What process fits?
options: Proof that the smell has disappeared
A new conditioned fear response
Sensory adaptation
An automatic increase in the smell's concentration
questions.answer: Sensory adaptation
questions.explanation: Responsiveness can decline during continued exposure to a relatively constant stimulus.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Dots placed close together are seen as separate clusters despite sharing the same colour. Which grouping cue is most relevant?
options: A difference in genetic inheritance
Proximity
A change in sound frequency
A reinforcement schedule
questions.answer: Proximity
questions.explanation: Nearby elements tend to be grouped together in visual perception.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A broken outline is perceived as a complete circle. Which principle best explains this?
options: Closure
Negative reinforcement
Retroactive interference
Random sampling
questions.answer: Closure
questions.explanation: Closure describes perceiving a complete form despite gaps in the available visual information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A child learns to fear one furry toy and then responds similarly to other furry toys. What process is illustrated?
options: Complete extinction
Learning with no stimulus association
A fixed-interval reinforcement schedule
Stimulus generalisation
questions.answer: Stimulus generalisation
questions.explanation: A learned response can extend to stimuli resembling the original conditioned stimulus.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: An agreed privilege is removed after a behaviour, and that behaviour subsequently decreases. What is illustrated?
options: Negative reinforcement
Classical extinction alone
Negative punishment
Positive reinforcement
questions.answer: Negative punishment
questions.explanation: Removing a valued consequence to reduce a behaviour is negative punishment; negative refers to removal.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A coach first rewards a rough attempt, then rewards progressively closer versions of a target skill. What is the method?
options: Unconditional stimulus presentation only
Shaping
Random sampling
Sensory adaptation
questions.answer: Shaping
questions.explanation: Shaping reinforces successive approximations toward a desired behaviour.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Asked to picture a leader on a sports team, a student immediately imagines the captain as a typical example. What does the captain serve as?
options: A prototype
A randomised control
A sensory threshold
A conditioned reflex
questions.answer: A prototype
questions.explanation: A prototype is a representative example used to organise a category.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student follows a definite sequence of valid steps guaranteed to solve a particular class of problem. What approach is used?
options: A guess with no rule
A stereotype alone
An unrelated memory cue
An algorithm
questions.answer: An algorithm
questions.explanation: An algorithm specifies a procedure that produces a solution when correctly applied to a suitable problem.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A shopper uses a quick rule of thumb to narrow many choices, accepting that it may occasionally fail. What is used?
options: A randomised experiment
A sensory transduction process
A heuristic
A guaranteed exhaustive algorithm
questions.answer: A heuristic
questions.explanation: A heuristic reduces decision effort but does not guarantee a correct or optimal answer.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student knows a familiar word and can describe its meaning but temporarily cannot produce it. What does this illustrate?
options: Successful recall of the missing word
Retrieval blocking
Proof that the word was never learned
Permanent loss of all language knowledge
questions.answer: Retrieval blocking
questions.explanation: The tip-of-the-tongue experience reflects a temporary difficulty accessing stored information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A learner remembers a sequence using a sentence whose initial letters match the required items. What strategy is used?
options: An acrostic mnemonic
Random guessing
A placebo comparison
A punishment schedule
questions.answer: An acrostic mnemonic
questions.explanation: The sentence provides organised cues for retrieving the ordered information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A child uses precise finger movements to cut out a small paper shape. What type of skill is mainly involved?
options: Only gross locomotion
A purely hormonal reflex
A measure of language comprehension
Fine motor skill
questions.answer: Fine motor skill
questions.explanation: Fine motor skills involve controlled movements of relatively small muscles, particularly in the hands and fingers.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A learner completes a task mainly to receive a promised reward. What kind of motivation is emphasised?
options: An absence of any motive
Sensory adaptation
Extrinsic motivation
Intrinsic enjoyment alone
questions.answer: Extrinsic motivation
questions.explanation: Extrinsic motivation is directed toward an external consequence rather than enjoyment of the activity itself.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A researcher assesses the same children repeatedly over several years. What is a main advantage over comparing different age groups once?
options: It proves every change is caused by age alone
It can track change within the same individuals
It eliminates all effects of participants leaving
It guarantees that historical events have no influence
questions.answer: It can track change within the same individuals
questions.explanation: Longitudinal research follows individuals over time, though attrition and other influences still require consideration.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Participants with the greatest difficulties disproportionately leave a long study. Why can the final results be misleading?
options: The remaining sample may no longer represent the original group
Every remaining measurement becomes mathematically incorrect
Leaving necessarily improves the study's generalisability
A longer study automatically removes selection bias
questions.answer: The remaining sample may no longer represent the original group
questions.explanation: Selective attrition can change who is represented in the analysed outcomes.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Names are randomly selected from a complete school register for a survey. What does this procedure principally support?
options: Proof that any correlation is causal
Random assignment to different treatments
Identical responses from all selected pupils
A less selectively recruited sample of that school
questions.answer: A less selectively recruited sample of that school
questions.explanation: Random sampling concerns selection from a population; it is different from assigning experimental conditions.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A researcher varies study-noise level and measures recall accuracy. Which pairing is correct?
options: Both are necessarily uncontrolled confounders
Neither variable can be measured
Noise is the independent variable; recall is the dependent variable
Recall is the independent variable; noise is the dependent variable
questions.answer: Noise is the independent variable; recall is the dependent variable
questions.explanation: The independent variable is manipulated, and the dependent variable records the outcome of interest.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: An experiment compares an active intervention with an apparently similar inactive one while participants do not know their allocation. What is the purpose of the inactive comparison?
options: Ensure that the inactive treatment contains the active ingredient
Help distinguish intervention effects from participant expectations
Guarantee that every participant has identical expectations
Remove the need to measure outcomes
questions.answer: Help distinguish intervention effects from participant expectations
questions.explanation: A credible placebo comparison can help control expectancy-related influences on reported or observed outcomes.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: In a model synapse, a substance activates receptors normally activated by a neurotransmitter. What effect is most consistent with agonist action?
options: It mimics or facilitates signalling in that system
It necessarily destroys every receptor
It blocks all neurotransmitter activity by definition
It prevents the receptor from having any response
questions.answer: It mimics or facilitates signalling in that system
questions.explanation: An agonist can imitate or enhance activity associated with a neurotransmitter system.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A person distinguishes colour well in bright light but poorly in dim conditions. Which receptor difference helps explain this?
options: Rods provide equally detailed colour vision at every light level
Cones operate only when no light reaches the eye
The retina stops all signalling in dim light
Cone-mediated colour vision works best with sufficient illumination
questions.answer: Cone-mediated colour vision works best with sufficient illumination
questions.explanation: Cones support colour discrimination and function best in brighter conditions; rod-dominated dim-light vision has limited colour information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: After prolonged fixation on a green patch, a reddish afterimage appears on a white surface. Which explanation fits?
options: The eye has created a new external light source
Green and red are identical wavelengths
Adaptation within opposing colour-response systems
The white surface physically turns red
questions.answer: Adaptation within opposing colour-response systems
questions.explanation: Unequal adaptation in opponent colour mechanisms can produce a complementary afterimage.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Two lines cross, yet viewers perceive two smooth continuing paths instead of several sharply turning pieces. What principle is illustrated?
options: An endocrine feedback loop
Good continuation
Extinction of a conditioned response
Negative punishment
questions.answer: Good continuation
questions.explanation: The visual system tends to organise elements into smoothly continuing contours.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A tone previously paired with food is repeatedly presented without food, and salivation to the tone declines. What changed?
options: The learned predictive relationship is no longer reinforced by pairing
The tone was never a conditioned stimulus
Food has become biologically incapable of producing salivation
The animal has lost all learning capacity
questions.answer: The learned predictive relationship is no longer reinforced by pairing
questions.explanation: Repeated presentation without the unconditioned stimulus produces extinction of the conditioned response.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A response is rewarded after an unpredictable number of repetitions. Which schedule describes this?
options: Fixed interval
Fixed ratio
Variable interval
Variable ratio
questions.answer: Variable ratio
questions.explanation: Ratio schedules depend on response counts, and variable means the required count changes unpredictably.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student entering a familiar café expects to queue, order, pay and collect food. What is this organised expectation?
options: A genetic mutation
A difference threshold
An event script
An action potential
questions.answer: An event script
questions.explanation: An event schema or script represents the expected sequence of actions in a familiar situation.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A person judges an applicant solely by resemblance to a familiar occupational stereotype while ignoring the applicant's record. What shortcut is dominating?
options: A guaranteed deductive algorithm
Representativeness-based judgement
Careful use of all relevant individual evidence
Random assignment
questions.answer: Representativeness-based judgement
questions.explanation: Judging category membership by resemblance can overshadow more informative evidence about the individual.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A learner compares explanations against a dataset and evaluates which fits best. Which form of ability is most directly exercised in the triarchic model?
options: Analytical intelligence
Only practical familiarity with daily routines
Only generating novel ideas without evaluation
A fixed measure of physical strength
questions.answer: Analytical intelligence
questions.explanation: Analytical ability concerns examining, comparing and evaluating information or proposed explanations.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A test is normed only on a narrow, unusually selected group. What is a concern when interpreting scores from a broader population?
options: Norming guarantees fairness for every possible group
The test must contain no correct answers
A smaller reference group automatically gives universal validity
The comparison norms may not represent that population
questions.answer: The comparison norms may not represent that population
questions.explanation: Norm-based interpretation depends on the suitability of the reference sample for the people assessed.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student keeps a spoken number in mind while checking a simple instruction. What system supports this temporary storage and processing?
options: Only sensory adaptation
A peripheral hormone gland
Working memory
Only a permanent autobiographical archive
questions.answer: Working memory
questions.explanation: Working memory temporarily maintains and manipulates information needed for an ongoing task.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A person recalls a group success as mainly their own achievement despite records showing equal contributions. What bias fits?
options: Proof that the other contributors were absent
A self-enhancing memory bias
Perfectly neutral reconstruction
Random sampling error in the records by definition
questions.answer: A self-enhancing memory bias
questions.explanation: Memory can be reconstructed in ways that favour one's own contribution or self-image.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A learner connects new concepts to examples from their own experiences. Why can this improve later recall?
options: Personal relevance can provide richer encoding and retrieval cues
It guarantees flawless memory for every detail
It removes all need to understand the concepts
Personally relevant material can never be forgotten
questions.answer: Personal relevance can provide richer encoding and retrieval cues
questions.explanation: Self-referential elaboration can make information more meaningfully connected to existing knowledge.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: In a standard attachment observation, a child explores while using the caregiver as a secure base and seeks comfort on reunion. Which pattern is most consistent?
options: A conclusion that the child never experiences distress
Proof that attachment has no role in exploration
A diagnosis based on a single isolated action
Secure attachment
questions.answer: Secure attachment
questions.explanation: The coordinated pattern of exploration and comfort seeking is characteristic of secure attachment in the model.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A student attributes a disappointing result entirely to a teacher's dislike and sees no role for their own preparation. What belief is illustrated?
options: Proof that the teacher caused the result
A measure of the student's actual intelligence
An external locus of control for that outcome
Strong perceived control over the outcome
questions.answer: An external locus of control for that outcome
questions.explanation: The attribution locates the outcome's control outside the self, but does not establish whether that explanation is accurate.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A theory is adjusted so that every possible observation counts as support. Why is this a scientific weakness?
options: Its predictions must be numerically precise
No conceivable result could count against it
A theory becomes stronger when no test can challenge it
It has necessarily been replicated in every population
questions.answer: No conceivable result could count against it
questions.explanation: A scientific explanation must expose itself to possible disconfirmation rather than accommodate every outcome automatically.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A result contradicts a theory's prediction, but the study's measurement was unreliable. Why seek a stronger replication before deciding?
options: The contradiction may reflect measurement problems rather than a failure of the theory
A theory can never be challenged by evidence
Repeating a study guarantees that the theory will be confirmed
An unreliable measure necessarily produces the correct result
questions.answer: The contradiction may reflect measurement problems rather than a failure of the theory
questions.explanation: Evaluating a theory requires considering the quality and reproducibility of evidence that appears to support or challenge it.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: An unusual patient shows a pattern that challenges an existing memory theory. What is the strongest use of the case?
options: Assume the patient's pattern represents every person
Discard it solely because it concerns one person
Estimate its population prevalence directly from the single case
Inform or challenge theory while testing how widely the pattern applies
questions.answer: Inform or challenge theory while testing how widely the pattern applies
questions.explanation: A case can be theoretically informative without establishing how common the pattern is across a population.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A naturalistic study records genuine settings, but people know they are watched. What limitation remains?
options: Observation becomes a randomised experiment automatically
No behaviour can be recorded outside a laboratory
Awareness of observation can alter behaviour
A natural setting guarantees completely unaffected behaviour
questions.answer: Awareness of observation can alter behaviour
questions.explanation: Realistic settings can improve relevance, but observer awareness and measurement choices still affect validity.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: School records show a change in behaviour after a policy, but recording practices changed at the same time. What must be separated?
options: A causal effect that is already proven by chronology
Change in behaviour from change in how it was recorded
The school's name from its postal address only
The number of archived pages from their paper size
questions.answer: Change in behaviour from change in how it was recorded
questions.explanation: An apparent historical trend can partly reflect changes in measurement rather than the underlying behaviour.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: One study reports a correlation of −0.90 and another +0.40. Which has the stronger linear association?
options: The first, because strength depends on magnitude rather than sign
The second, because positive always means stronger
Both, because every nonzero correlation has equal strength
Neither, because negative correlations are impossible
questions.answer: The first, because strength depends on magnitude rather than sign
questions.explanation: The absolute coefficient is larger in the first study; the sign indicates direction.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A dataset follows a strong curved pattern but has a linear correlation near zero. What follows?
options: The variables must be statistically independent
The curved pattern must be a graphing error
A zero coefficient proves a negative causal effect
Near-zero linear correlation need not mean no relationship
questions.answer: Near-zero linear correlation need not mean no relationship
questions.explanation: A linear correlation measures linear association and can miss systematic nonlinear patterns.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Two studies claim to measure aggression, but one counts interruptions and the other physical acts. Why compare their definitions before combining results?
options: Any count is automatically a complete measure of aggression
Different definitions prove both studies have no value
They may measure different aspects of the broader concept
The same label guarantees identical measurement
questions.answer: They may measure different aspects of the broader concept
questions.explanation: Operational definitions determine what observations represent a construct and therefore affect interpretation and comparability.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A proposed study conceals its purpose to reduce response bias. Why is scientific usefulness alone insufficient to justify the concealment?
options: A useful aim guarantees that all methods are acceptable
Ethical review must consider necessity, harm, consent arrangements and debriefing
Concealment automatically makes every result invalid
Avoiding response bias removes every duty to participants
questions.answer: Ethical review must consider necessity, harm, consent arrangements and debriefing
questions.explanation: Methodological benefits must be weighed alongside participants' rights and protections.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A teacher says a research survey is optional but implies that refusal will damage a student's standing. What ethical issue arises?
options: The pressure undermines genuinely voluntary participation
The word optional removes all coercive influence
Survey length alone determines whether consent is free
Refusal proves that the student lacks research ability
questions.answer: The pressure undermines genuinely voluntary participation
questions.explanation: Consent can be compromised by pressure from someone with authority even when participation is formally described as optional.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Two cells share the same DNA sequence but express different genes after different regulatory signals. What does this show?
options: Every difference in gene expression requires a new mutation
The cells cannot belong to the same organism
Environmental and regulatory influences cannot affect gene activity
Gene activity can differ without a difference in DNA sequence
questions.answer: Gene activity can differ without a difference in DNA sequence
questions.explanation: Regulation, including epigenetic mechanisms, can alter expression without changing the underlying base sequence.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A conditioned response declines during extinction but briefly returns after a rest. Why is extinction not simply erasure of all prior learning?
options: Recovery proves that no extinction occurred
All learned responses must grow continuously without interruption
The earlier association can still influence responding under changed conditions
The original stimulus was never learned
questions.answer: The earlier association can still influence responding under changed conditions
questions.explanation: Spontaneous recovery indicates that reduced responding after extinction does not necessarily mean the original learning has vanished.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: One learner improves through rewards for closer attempts; another copies a demonstration. Why distinguish the methods?
options: Observing a model is the definition of negative punishment
The first emphasises consequences of successive approximations; the second observation of a model
Both require identical experience of direct rewards
Neither can influence a learned skill
questions.answer: The first emphasises consequences of successive approximations; the second observation of a model
questions.explanation: Shaping and observational learning describe different mechanisms that may also operate together.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A familiar shortcut works well in one setting but fails when the underlying conditions change. What is the sound conclusion?
options: Its usefulness depends on how well its assumptions fit the setting
The shortcut is therefore useless in every setting
Success once guarantees success in every later problem
Heuristics always outperform systematic analysis
questions.answer: Its usefulness depends on how well its assumptions fit the setting
questions.explanation: Efficient heuristics can be valuable but are vulnerable when cues no longer predict outcomes reliably.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A test predicts outcomes in its norming group but performs poorly in another group with different experiences. What needs evaluation?
options: Only whether the printed test title is unchanged
Whether identical scoring guarantees identical meaning
Whether the original group can be ignored in every analysis
Validity and fairness for the intended population
questions.answer: Validity and fairness for the intended population
questions.explanation: Evidence of validity is tied to the interpretation, purpose and population, not simply to a test's existence.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Two people with similar inherited predispositions develop differently under different experiences. Which explanation best accommodates this?
options: Experience requires genes to have no influence
Different outcomes prove that neither genes nor environment matters
Development can reflect interactions between inherited factors and environment
Genes determine every outcome independently of experience
questions.answer: Development can reflect interactions between inherited factors and environment
questions.explanation: Biological predispositions and experience can work together in producing individual differences.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: A vivid, confidently reported memory changes in details across repeated accounts. What does this indicate?
options: Vivid memories cannot be reconstructed
Subjective vividness does not guarantee accuracy
Confidence makes every detail objectively correct
Changing an account proves deliberate dishonesty in every case
questions.answer: Subjective vividness does not guarantee accuracy
questions.explanation: Emotional or vivid recollection can still be affected by reconstruction and later information.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Identical twins raised apart show similarities, but their environments were not assigned randomly. What should a careful interpretation avoid?
options: Treating similarity as proof that environment has no influence
Considering inherited influences at all
Comparing similarities with other evidence
Acknowledging that multiple influences may operate
questions.answer: Treating similarity as proof that environment has no influence
questions.explanation: Twin evidence can inform genetic contributions without excluding environmental similarities, selection or gene–environment processes.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: Workers change behaviour after researchers begin observing them, even without the planned treatment. What should the study consider?
options: Proof that the planned treatment caused every change
A guarantee that awareness never affects behaviour
The impossibility of measuring workplace behaviour
Effects of observation and expectations as alternative influences
questions.answer: Effects of observation and expectations as alternative influences
questions.explanation: Participation and attention may affect behaviour, so they must be considered when attributing change to a treatment.

questions.subject: Psychology
questions.q: People in lower-control jobs report more stress-related problems, but their working and living conditions also differ. What conclusion is justified?
options: Job conditions cannot affect stress
The association rules out all environmental explanations
Perceived control is a candidate influence, but the association alone isolates no single cause
Control is proven to be the only cause
questions.answer: Perceived control is a candidate influence, but the association alone isolates no single cause
questions.explanation: Other correlated conditions can contribute to the relationship, so stronger designs are needed to isolate causal effects.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A learner wants to improve distance-running endurance. Which training best matches that aim?
options: Only practising a standing balance pose
Only practising one maximal throw
Only memorising competition rules
Progressive sustained aerobic activity
questions.answer: Progressive sustained aerobic activity
questions.explanation: Endurance training should develop the ability to sustain activity over time.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A comfortable exercise routine no longer challenges a learner. What principle supports a planned, gradual increase in demand?
options: Randomly changing every session
Avoiding all recovery
Progressive overload
Complete inactivity
questions.answer: Progressive overload
questions.explanation: Adaptation requires an appropriate challenge that progresses with capacity.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Why begin a sports session with gradually increasing movement?
options: To produce maximum fatigue immediately
To prepare the body for the activity ahead
To guarantee that no injury can occur
To replace every skill practice
questions.answer: To prepare the body for the activity ahead
questions.explanation: A gradual warm-up prepares movement and physiological responses without guaranteeing injury prevention.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Why include recovery between demanding training sessions?
options: Adaptation and restoration need time
Recovery permanently removes fitness
Every rest period causes immediate complete detraining
Muscles improve only during exhaustion
questions.answer: Adaptation and restoration need time
questions.explanation: Training stress and recovery together support adaptation.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A player changes direction quickly to follow an opponent. Which ability is most directly demonstrated?
options: Maximum static strength alone
Flexibility alone
Resting pulse rate
Agility
questions.answer: Agility
questions.explanation: Agility involves controlled changes of direction in response to the task.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A gymnast widens the base of support while holding a stationary position. What usually happens to stability?
options: It depends only on clothing colour
The centre of mass must leave the body
It increases if other conditions stay the same
It always disappears
questions.answer: It increases if other conditions stay the same
questions.explanation: A wider base provides a larger area within which the centre of mass can remain supported.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: During a controlled lowering of a weight, the active muscle lengthens. What kind of action is this?
options: Only a nerve reflex without muscle activity
Eccentric contraction
Concentric contraction
No muscular force
questions.answer: Eccentric contraction
questions.explanation: An eccentric action produces force while the muscle lengthens.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: During moderate running, breathing and heart rate rise. What is the main functional reason?
options: To support increased gas exchange and delivery to working tissues
To stop blood reaching muscles
To eliminate the need for cellular respiration
To reduce oxygen delivery to zero
questions.answer: To support increased gas exchange and delivery to working tissues
questions.explanation: Working tissues require greater transport of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Two students compare shuttle-run results from different course lengths. What should they do first?
options: Assume the shorter course is always harder
Compare only their shoe brands
Ignore course length
Use the same test protocol before comparing results
questions.answer: Use the same test protocol before comparing results
questions.explanation: A meaningful comparison requires consistent conditions and procedures.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A coach says, Keep your eyes on the target during the pass. Why is this more useful than Do better?
options: It describes the player's personality
It removes the need to practise
It identifies a specific action to adjust
It guarantees immediate mastery
questions.answer: It identifies a specific action to adjust
questions.explanation: Specific feedback gives the learner a clear behaviour to work on.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Two defenders keep moving toward the same attacker, leaving space open. What is a useful response?
options: Both follow the ball regardless of team shape
Agree clear responsibilities and communicate switches
Stop communicating altogether
Blame the quieter player after each play
questions.answer: Agree clear responsibilities and communicate switches
questions.explanation: Coordinated responsibilities reduce duplicated coverage and unattended space.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A player notices damaged equipment before a lesson. What is the appropriate action?
options: Report it and avoid using it until checked
Hide the damage to keep the lesson moving
Test it at maximum force
Give it to a less experienced player
questions.answer: Report it and avoid using it until checked
questions.explanation: Reporting a hazard lets the responsible adult assess it before further use.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Two drinks have different bottle sizes. How can their sugar concentration be compared fairly?
options: Compare only sugar per bottle
Compare the size of their logos
Assume the larger bottle is less concentrated
Compare sugar per equal volume
questions.answer: Compare sugar per equal volume
questions.explanation: A common volume separates concentration from the amount in the container.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Which goal is easiest to evaluate after a month?
options: Always feel perfect
Never make a mistake
Complete the agreed training sessions and compare a standard endurance test
Become the best at everything
questions.answer: Complete the agreed training sessions and compare a standard endurance test
questions.explanation: A defined process and consistent outcome measure allow progress to be checked.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A learner needs a different way to perform a catching task. Which approach preserves the learning aim?
options: Replace feedback with public comparisons
Adapt equipment or rules while practising the same underlying skill
Exclude the learner from all practice
Assume the learner cannot improve
questions.answer: Adapt equipment or rules while practising the same underlying skill
questions.explanation: An appropriate adaptation can enable participation in the intended skill.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A learner performs a new skill well immediately after instruction. Why test it again after a delay?
options: To examine whether improvement is retained
To guarantee the first score was false
To measure only how much praise was given
To eliminate all individual differences
questions.answer: To examine whether improvement is retained
questions.explanation: Learning involves a relatively lasting change, whereas a single performance may reflect temporary support or conditions.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A coach praises a learner's improved technique even when another learner wins. What focus does this promote?
options: Success defined only by defeating others
Avoidance of any feedback
A guarantee of future victory
Personal progress and mastery
questions.answer: Personal progress and mastery
questions.explanation: Recognising improvement directs attention toward skill development rather than only social comparison.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Which goal is most directly under a player's control during practice?
options: Guarantee selection for the national team
Ensure that nobody else improves
Follow the planned movement cue on each attempt
Make every opponent perform poorly
questions.answer: Follow the planned movement cue on each attempt
questions.explanation: A process goal concerns the performer's actions rather than outcomes partly controlled by others.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A performer repeatedly watches irrelevant crowd movement during a precision task. What should attention be redirected toward?
options: Unrelated events from the previous day
Task-relevant cues
Every spectator at once
Only the final league table
questions.answer: Task-relevant cues
questions.explanation: Effective attentional focus prioritises information useful for executing the current task.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A beginner copies a respected teammate's preparation routine after watching its use. What learning process is illustrated?
options: Observational learning
A purely inherited routine requiring no experience
Learning with no model or observation
A reflex triggered only by loud sound
questions.answer: Observational learning
questions.explanation: Behaviour can be acquired by observing and imitating a model, especially one the learner values.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A programme adds demanding sessions every day while performance and motivation decline. Which factor should be reviewed?
options: Whether the equipment has matching colours
Whether recovery can be removed completely
Whether every session must become harder
Whether training demand exceeds recovery
questions.answer: Whether training demand exceeds recovery
questions.explanation: Declining performance with rising load can indicate an imbalance between demand and recovery.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A swimmer improves swimming endurance but shows limited improvement in sprint starts. Why is this plausible?
options: Fitness transfers equally to every task
Sprint starts contain no physical skill
Different tasks require partly different adaptations
Endurance training prevents all skill learning
questions.answer: Different tasks require partly different adaptations
questions.explanation: Sustained swimming and explosive starts place different demands on the body and technique.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Why alternate work and recovery periods in an interval session?
options: To guarantee the same adaptation for every athlete
To manage repeated efforts at a chosen intensity
To make intensity impossible to control
To remove all physiological demand
questions.answer: To manage repeated efforts at a chosen intensity
questions.explanation: Recovery intervals allow planned repetition and control of demanding efforts.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Holding a small weight farther from the elbow makes the same arm position harder to maintain. Why?
options: The weight creates a larger moment about the elbow
The weight's mass has increased
Gravity has stopped acting
The elbow becomes frictionless
questions.answer: The weight creates a larger moment about the elbow
questions.explanation: A greater perpendicular distance increases the moment produced by the same force.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Why can flexing the knees during a controlled landing reduce average impact force for the same momentum change?
options: It removes all momentum before contact
It increases body mass
It prevents gravity from acting
It increases the time over which the body slows
questions.answer: It increases the time over which the body slows
questions.explanation: For the same impulse, extending stopping time reduces average force.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A short maximal sprint and a long steady run emphasise different energy contributions. Which conclusion is sound?
options: Long runs require no ATP
Sprints cannot use stored chemical energy
The relative contribution of energy pathways depends on intensity and duration
Only one pathway ever operates at a time
questions.answer: The relative contribution of energy pathways depends on intensity and duration
questions.explanation: Energy systems overlap, but their relative contributions vary with the task.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A learner's repeated balance-test scores vary greatly under otherwise similar conditions. What is the main concern?
options: The highest score must represent every attempt
The test may have low repeatability
The test must measure aerobic capacity
The learner's height has certainly changed
questions.answer: The test may have low repeatability
questions.explanation: Large unexplained variation weakens confidence in consistent measurement.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A coach uses a spelling test to rank football dribbling skill. What is wrong with the assessment?
options: It does not directly measure the intended skill
It necessarily takes too little time
All written tests are unreliable
Dribbling cannot be assessed
questions.answer: It does not directly measure the intended skill
questions.explanation: Validity concerns whether a measure supports the intended interpretation.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A learner relies on instructions after every movement and struggles alone. What change could support independence?
options: Increase dependence on continuous commands forever
Remove all practice opportunities
Give only unrelated praise
Gradually encourage self-evaluation and reduce constant prompting
questions.answer: Gradually encourage self-evaluation and reduce constant prompting
questions.explanation: Guided self-evaluation can help learners recognise and correct their own performance.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A player can pass accurately in isolation but struggles when opponents move. What practice best addresses the gap?
options: Stop practising passes
Study only the history of the ball
Practise passing in progressively realistic decision situations
Repeat only identical unopposed passes indefinitely
questions.answer: Practise passing in progressively realistic decision situations
questions.explanation: Game-like situations add perception and decision demands absent from isolated practice.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A team leads narrowly near the end of a game. Why might it favour controlled possession over risky long passes?
options: Because scoring is no longer relevant
To reduce unnecessary loss of possession in that situation
Because long passes are always forbidden
Because possession guarantees victory
questions.answer: To reduce unnecessary loss of possession in that situation
questions.explanation: Tactical choices depend on time, score and the risk of turnovers.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Two people have the same BMI but different muscle mass. What does this show?
options: BMI alone does not distinguish fat from muscle
They necessarily have identical body composition
BMI directly measures every tissue
Muscle has no mass
questions.answer: BMI alone does not distinguish fat from muscle
questions.explanation: BMI combines height and weight without separating the sources of body mass.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: After training, the same submaximal task requires a lower heart rate under comparable conditions. What is a plausible interpretation?
options: Proof that no energy is being used
Evidence that the heart has stopped adapting
Proof of superior fitness in every sport
Improved cardiovascular efficiency
questions.answer: Improved cardiovascular efficiency
questions.explanation: A trained cardiovascular system may meet the same demand with fewer beats; the observation has a limited scope.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A supplement advertisement promises instant fitness without exercise. What is the strongest first evaluation step?
options: Judge only the packaging
Treat repeated advertising as a controlled trial
Look for credible evidence and examine the claim's limits
Assume a celebrity endorsement proves it
questions.answer: Look for credible evidence and examine the claim's limits
questions.explanation: Evidence and plausible scope matter more than repetition or endorsement.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A captain gives every skilled player practice time but repeatedly excludes beginners. Which change better supports team development?
options: Stop giving feedback to anyone
Provide meaningful practice opportunities with appropriate support
Keep beginners watching indefinitely
Assign roles only by friendship
questions.answer: Provide meaningful practice opportunities with appropriate support
questions.explanation: Participation and suitable challenge allow less experienced players to develop.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: After a poor performance, an athlete focuses on a changeable preparation strategy rather than declaring permanent lack of ability. Why may this support persistence?
options: The athlete identifies a controllable route to improvement
The athlete has proved ability is irrelevant
Changing an explanation guarantees a win
The poor performance is erased from the record
questions.answer: The athlete identifies a controllable route to improvement
questions.explanation: Attributing difficulty to a modifiable factor can support perceived control and future effort.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A training group rewards only the highest-ranked participant and ignores improvement among others. What risk can this create?
options: Every participant must become intrinsically motivated
Individual skill differences must disappear
Effort becomes impossible to observe
Some learners may interpret success solely through comparison with others
questions.answer: Some learners may interpret success solely through comparison with others
questions.explanation: A strongly performance-oriented climate can make social ranking more salient than mastery or personal progress.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A coach asks a player to describe the likely cause of an error before offering feedback. What can this develop?
options: Proof that the coach has no useful knowledge
Immediate perfection without practice
The player's ability to evaluate their own performance
A requirement to avoid all external feedback
questions.answer: The player's ability to evaluate their own performance
questions.explanation: Guided reflection can help learners connect movement outcomes with their own actions and develop self-monitoring.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: The activation level that helps a simple explosive movement disrupts a complex precision skill for the same performer. What does this suggest?
options: Arousal affects only spectators
Useful arousal levels can depend on task demands
One activation level must be optimal for every task
Precision skills require no attention
questions.answer: Useful arousal levels can depend on task demands
questions.explanation: The relationship between activation and performance can vary with skill complexity and control requirements.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: An athlete mentally rehearses the timing and feel of a movement alongside physical practice. What is the intended role of imagery?
options: Support preparation and representation of the skill
Replace all need for actual physical learning
Guarantee an identical result in every competition
Increase muscle force without any physiological mechanism
questions.answer: Support preparation and representation of the skill
questions.explanation: Imagery can complement practice by rehearsing relevant sensory and movement representations.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A class improves after a new training plan, but also receives more practice time. What can be concluded about the plan alone?
options: The plan caused the entire improvement
Extra practice cannot influence performance
The plan has been proved ineffective
Its separate effect is not isolated
questions.answer: Its separate effect is not isolated
questions.explanation: Both changes could contribute, so the design does not isolate the plan's effect.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: An outdoor endurance test is repeated in much hotter weather. Why interpret the score change cautiously?
options: Fitness cannot change over time
Hot weather guarantees a better score
Environmental conditions can affect performance independently of fitness
Temperature changes the distance printed on the track
questions.answer: Environmental conditions can affect performance independently of fitness
questions.explanation: A change in testing conditions complicates attribution to training or fitness alone.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A player completes a skill faster but makes more errors. How should progress be evaluated?
options: Assume any increase in speed means mastery
Assess both speed and accuracy against the task's demands
Use speed alone in every sport
Ignore errors if movement looks confident
questions.answer: Assess both speed and accuracy against the task's demands
questions.explanation: Skill quality depends on successful execution as well as time taken.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A jump result improves by less than the measuring device's usual variation. What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: The apparent improvement may not exceed measurement noise
The improvement proves a major adaptation
The device must be deliberately misleading
The learner has certainly become less fit
questions.answer: The apparent improvement may not exceed measurement noise
questions.explanation: A change smaller than typical measurement variation is uncertain without stronger evidence.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Two learners follow the same workload, but one recovers well and the other struggles. What follows?
options: Identical schedules guarantee identical adaptation
The struggling learner should always double the load
Recovery differences are irrelevant to planning
The same external workload can create different internal demands
questions.answer: The same external workload can create different internal demands
questions.explanation: Capacity and context differ, so responses should inform individual adjustments.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A skater pulls the arms inward while spinning with little external torque. Why does rotation speed increase?
options: Body mass increases
Gravity supplies a large twisting force
Moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum is approximately conserved
Angular momentum must vanish
questions.answer: Moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum is approximately conserved
questions.explanation: Reducing the distribution of mass away from the axis increases angular speed for the same angular momentum.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A player lowers the centre of mass for stability, but must then jump quickly. What should guide the movement choice?
options: Use one posture for every situation
Balance stability needs with the demands of the next action
Assume the lowest possible position is always best
Ignore the opponent and task
questions.answer: Balance stability needs with the demands of the next action
questions.explanation: A stable posture can involve a trade-off with movement readiness depending on the action required.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A player executes well in drills but chooses poor options in matches. Which assessment would best identify the problem?
options: Observe perception and decisions in representative game situations
Measure only maximum grip strength
Count only training attendance
Repeat a vocabulary test
questions.answer: Observe perception and decisions in representative game situations
questions.explanation: Match decisions require reading the situation and selecting an action, not just executing a rehearsed movement.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: To compare two training methods, what is especially important besides consistent outcome tests?
options: Matching shirt colours
Giving one group much more practice without accounting for it
Selecting only the best result from one group
Comparable starting ability and training exposure
questions.answer: Comparable starting ability and training exposure
questions.explanation: Baseline and exposure differences can otherwise explain the result attributed to training method.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A coach claims one technique suits every athlete because it worked for a champion. What is the weakness?
options: Technique cannot be examined scientifically
All individual differences are irrelevant
One successful example does not establish universal suitability
Champions never use effective techniques
questions.answer: One successful example does not establish universal suitability
questions.explanation: A single case cannot establish that the method fits different bodies, skills and tasks.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Students who train more also report better wellbeing. Which statement is best supported by this observation alone?
options: Every nonparticipant has poor wellbeing
Training and reported wellbeing are associated
Training is the only possible cause
Wellbeing can never influence participation
questions.answer: Training and reported wellbeing are associated
questions.explanation: An association alone does not exclude reverse causation or other influences.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A team increases tactical practice near a tournament while managing physical load. What is the rationale?
options: Training emphasis can change with the phase and competition demands
Physical preparation becomes permanently unnecessary
The same maximal workload is required daily
Tactics and physical demands are unrelated
questions.answer: Training emphasis can change with the phase and competition demands
questions.explanation: Planning can vary emphasis over time while preserving readiness and recovery.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: An adapted task uses a lighter ball to assess the same throwing technique. What makes the comparison defensible?
options: All scores must be identical
Equipment differences must be hidden
The lighter ball automatically earns a higher score
The assessment criteria focus on the shared skill and document the adaptation
questions.answer: The assessment criteria focus on the shared skill and document the adaptation
questions.explanation: Transparent adaptations can maintain the intended learning target while changing access conditions.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A learner meets every attendance goal but shows little skill improvement. What should be reconsidered?
options: Whether feedback should be banned
Whether every session should be cancelled
Whether practice quality and outcome measures match the learning goal
Whether attendance alone proves mastery
questions.answer: Whether practice quality and outcome measures match the learning goal
questions.explanation: Participation is a process measure; improvement also depends on the content and quality of practice.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A team can exploit an opponent's misunderstanding of an agreed safety rule. Which response best combines fairness and responsibility?
options: Treat winning as overriding every agreed safeguard
Clarify the rule before continuing play
Keep the misunderstanding secret to gain advantage
Encourage more confusion
questions.answer: Clarify the rule before continuing play
questions.explanation: Clarification supports informed, fair participation under the shared rules.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: A learner excels in a fixed drill but struggles when distances and opponents vary. What does this reveal about judging learning?
options: Practice success may not establish adaptable performance in changing contexts
The fixed drill proves full transfer to every game situation
Changing contexts cannot affect skilled action
The learner must have forgotten every movement
questions.answer: Practice success may not establish adaptable performance in changing contexts
questions.explanation: Retention and transfer tests provide information beyond performance under the original practice conditions.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Two athletes have similar personality questionnaire profiles but very different performances. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: The questionnaire proves their training histories are identical
One personality profile guarantees one performance level
Context and skills cannot contribute to performance
Personality alone does not determine sporting success
questions.answer: Personality alone does not determine sporting success
questions.explanation: Performance reflects interactions among skills, preparation, context and individual characteristics.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: An athlete attends every session because they fear losing selection, while another attends for enjoyment. Why is attendance alone insufficient to compare motivation quality?
options: Enjoyment and external pressure are the same construct
Motives can be read directly from session counts
The same behaviour can arise from different underlying reasons
Attendance proves identical intrinsic motivation
questions.answer: The same behaviour can arise from different underlying reasons
questions.explanation: Observable participation does not by itself distinguish intrinsic interest from controlled or external motives.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: Two athletes experience the same competitive demand but interpret it differently, one as manageable and one as overwhelming. What does this highlight?
options: Perceived coping resources cannot matter
Appraisal can influence the stress response
Identical demands guarantee identical psychological responses
Only the official competition score determines stress
questions.answer: Appraisal can influence the stress response
questions.explanation: Stress depends partly on how demands are evaluated relative to perceived resources and control.

questions.subject: Sports Exercise & Health Science
questions.q: An athlete follows an improved preparation plan and sets a personal best but loses to a stronger opponent. How should progress be judged?
options: Separate achieved process and performance goals from the competitive outcome
Treat the loss as proof that no progress occurred
Ignore the personal best because it was measured
Assume the preparation plan guarantees future victories
questions.answer: Separate achieved process and performance goals from the competitive outcome
questions.explanation: Outcome depends partly on competitors, so process and performance evidence can show progress despite a loss.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: An owner pays for a personal holiday from the business bank account. How should this normally be treated in the sole trader's accounts?
options: As a reduction in the owner's personal spending outside the accounts
As drawings, not a business operating expense
As additional sales revenue
As a purchase of business inventory
questions.answer: As drawings, not a business operating expense
questions.explanation: The business entity concept separates the owner's private transactions from business expenses.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A sole trader puts personal cash into the business. What is the immediate accounting effect?
options: Business cash and owner's capital increase
Sales revenue and operating profit increase
Business liabilities and drawings increase
Cash decreases while capital increases
questions.answer: Business cash and owner's capital increase
questions.explanation: An owner's contribution increases the business's assets and equity without being trading income.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A business buys equipment on credit. What happens when the purchase is recorded?
options: An asset increases and a liability decreases
Cash increases and revenue increases
Owner's drawings increase
An asset and a liability increase
questions.answer: An asset and a liability increase
questions.explanation: The equipment is acquired while payment remains owed to the supplier.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A business buys equipment using cash. Ignoring other effects, what happens to total assets at purchase?
options: Total assets fall by twice the price
The purchase immediately creates sales revenue
One asset replaces another, so the total is unchanged
Total assets necessarily double
questions.answer: One asset replaces another, so the total is unchanged
questions.explanation: Cash decreases and equipment increases by the same transaction amount.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Services are completed this month, but the customer will pay next month. Under accrual accounting, what is recorded now?
options: An owner's capital contribution
Revenue and a receivable
Cash received and no revenue
A liability to the customer for the whole fee
questions.answer: Revenue and a receivable
questions.explanation: Revenue is recognised when earned, with a receivable representing the amount still due.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A business pays rent covering part of the next accounting period. How is the unused portion treated at the reporting date?
options: As a prepayment asset
As an expense belonging entirely to the current period
As sales revenue
As a payable already settled twice
questions.answer: As a prepayment asset
questions.explanation: The payment relates to a future benefit, so that portion is carried forward rather than charged to the current period.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Electricity has been used by year-end, but the bill has not yet been paid. What adjustment is needed?
options: Ignore the cost until cash is paid
Recognise an asset and sales revenue
Reduce the expense because payment is late
Recognise the expense and a liability
questions.answer: Recognise the expense and a liability
questions.explanation: Accrual accounting includes costs incurred in the period even when payment follows later.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A machine is purchased to be used for several years. Why is its full cost not normally charged as a one-day operating expense?
options: Machines never lose service potential
Only inventory can be an asset
Its benefits extend over several accounting periods
Every cash payment must be recorded as revenue
questions.answer: Its benefits extend over several accounting periods
questions.explanation: The machine is recognised as an asset and its depreciable cost is allocated over its useful life.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Equipment helps earn revenue over several years. What does depreciation allocate?
options: Its owner's personal income
Its depreciable cost over those periods
Cash into a separate replacement fund automatically
Its current selling price each day
questions.answer: Its depreciable cost over those periods
questions.explanation: Depreciation allocates cost; it is not itself a cash saving mechanism or a market valuation process.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Goods bought for resale remain unsold at year-end. Why are they not all included in the current cost of goods sold?
options: They remain an asset until sold or otherwise expensed
Unsold goods are automatically revenue
All purchases must be drawings
Inventory cannot appear in a statement of financial position
questions.answer: They remain an asset until sold or otherwise expensed
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold relates to goods sold, while qualifying unsold inventory is carried forward.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A trial balance totals equally on both sides. What does this establish?
options: Every transaction has been recorded correctly
No transaction has been omitted
Every account is classified correctly
Total recorded debit balances equal total recorded credit balances
questions.answer: Total recorded debit balances equal total recorded credit balances
questions.explanation: Equality is an arithmetic check, but some errors affect both sides equally or omit both entries.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A bank statement shows a charge not yet entered in the cash book. What should the business record?
options: A reduction in the supplier's invoice price
A new capital contribution
A bank expense and a reduction in the bank balance
An increase in sales and cash
questions.answer: A bank expense and a reduction in the bank balance
questions.explanation: The charge reduces the business's bank funds and is recorded as the relevant expense.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A customer's debt is confirmed irrecoverable. What should happen to that receivable?
options: It is transferred to cash without collection
It is written off and the loss recognised
It is retained as fully recoverable indefinitely
It becomes additional sales revenue
questions.answer: It is written off and the loss recognised
questions.explanation: A receivable with no recoverable amount should no longer remain as an asset at its original value.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A partnership agreement specifies unequal profit shares. Should profit automatically be divided equally?
options: No; the agreed sharing arrangement should be applied
Yes; every partnership must divide every profit equally
Yes; profit must match each partner's age
No; all profit belongs to the partner who collected cash
questions.answer: No; the agreed sharing arrangement should be applied
questions.explanation: An agreed profit-sharing arrangement governs allocation in the stated situation.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A partnership charges a partner interest on drawings under its agreement. What is the purpose of the charge?
options: To record interest paid to a bank
To increase cash automatically without settlement
To classify drawings as sales
To account for the partner's use of business funds for personal withdrawal
questions.answer: To account for the partner's use of business funds for personal withdrawal
questions.explanation: The charge adjusts the allocation between the partnership and the withdrawing partner under the agreement.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A new partner joins an established profitable firm. Why might goodwill be considered?
options: Admission makes all existing assets worthless
Goodwill is the same as an unpaid supplier invoice
The incoming partner may gain a share of an existing business advantage
Goodwill always equals the cash in the bank
questions.answer: The incoming partner may gain a share of an existing business advantage
questions.explanation: Goodwill reflects benefits such as reputation and earning capacity that can affect the partners' agreed settlement.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A company raises funds by issuing ordinary shares. How does this differ from taking a conventional loan?
options: The transaction necessarily creates an operating loss
The funds represent ownership capital rather than a repayable loan principal
The company must record every share receipt as sales
Ordinary shareholders become trade payables
questions.answer: The funds represent ownership capital rather than a repayable loan principal
questions.explanation: Share capital is equity funding; borrowing creates a creditor relationship and repayment obligations.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A company owes interest on its issued debentures for the period. How is this generally treated?
options: As a finance cost
As an ordinary shareholder's dividend
As additional share capital
As a customer advance
questions.answer: As a finance cost
questions.explanation: Debenture interest is a cost of borrowing, distinct from a distribution of profit to owners.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A business has valuable buildings but little cash to meet bills due tomorrow. What issue does this illustrate?
options: Owning buildings guarantees that every bill can be paid immediately
Profit and cash are always identical
Long-term assets are the same as cash on demand
Asset wealth does not guarantee immediate liquidity
questions.answer: Asset wealth does not guarantee immediate liquidity
questions.explanation: The ability to meet near-term obligations depends on accessible cash and liquid resources, not only total asset value.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Depreciation reduces reported profit. Does recording the depreciation entry itself pay cash to anyone?
options: Yes; the asset's supplier receives the amount again
No; therefore it can never affect profit
No; the entry is a noncash allocation
Yes; cash is paid to the depreciation account
questions.answer: No; the entry is a noncash allocation
questions.explanation: The cash acquisition and the later allocation of cost are separate accounting events.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A credit sale is omitted completely from the books. Why can the trial balance still agree?
options: Omission changes only the debit total
Both the debit and credit entries are missing
The customer automatically records the sale in the seller's books
Trial balances do not contain any revenue accounts
questions.answer: Both the debit and credit entries are missing
questions.explanation: An equal two-sided omission leaves debit and credit totals equal while understating the relevant accounts.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A cheque issued and recorded by the business has not yet been presented to the bank. Why do the cash book and statement differ?
options: The business has recorded a payment that the bank has not yet processed
The business must record the same expense a second time
The cheque is automatically a bank error
The payment must be treated as sales revenue
questions.answer: The business has recorded a payment that the bank has not yet processed
questions.explanation: An unpresented cheque is a timing difference between the two records.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Closing inventory is overstated while other figures are correct. What happens to cost of goods sold and gross profit?
options: Both are overstated
Cost of goods sold is overstated and gross profit understated
Both remain unchanged
Cost of goods sold is understated and gross profit overstated
questions.answer: Cost of goods sold is understated and gross profit overstated
questions.explanation: Closing inventory is deducted in calculating cost of goods sold, so overstating it lowers that cost and raises profit.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A fixed depreciation rate is applied to a declining carrying amount. Why does the annual charge normally fall?
options: The asset's original cost rises each year
Cash received from customers determines the charge
The rate is applied to a smaller base each year
The rate must increase each year
questions.answer: The rate is applied to a smaller base each year
questions.explanation: Under reducing-balance depreciation, the percentage stays fixed while the carrying amount declines.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: An expense incurred this year is paid next year. What happens if the year-end accrual is omitted?
options: Assets and liabilities both increase correctly
Current profit is overstated and liabilities understated
Current profit is understated and liabilities overstated
Only cash changes
questions.answer: Current profit is overstated and liabilities understated
questions.explanation: Omitting the expense increases reported profit and omitting the payable reduces reported liabilities.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Last year's rent prepayment is used during the current period. What should happen to that portion?
options: The prepayment asset decreases and rent expense is recognised
The prepayment asset increases again without payment
It becomes current-period sales revenue
It remains an asset forever
questions.answer: The prepayment asset decreases and rent expense is recognised
questions.explanation: As the prepaid benefit is consumed, its cost moves from the asset to the relevant period's expense.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Evidence suggests that some receivables may not be collected, but the exact debts are not yet known. What is the purpose of an allowance?
options: To cancel every customer debt automatically
To record cash already collected
To guarantee the remaining customers will pay
To reflect estimated credit losses in the carrying amount
questions.answer: To reflect estimated credit losses in the carrying amount
questions.explanation: An allowance accounts for estimated noncollection without treating every balance as individually confirmed irrecoverable.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A business describes profit as a percentage of selling price. Why is this not the same as markup on cost?
options: Selling price and cost must be equal
Markup excludes the cost of goods sold entirely
The two percentages use different denominators
Gross profit has a different cash value under each name
questions.answer: The two percentages use different denominators
questions.explanation: Margin relates gross profit to revenue; markup relates it to cost.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: When starting from profit in an indirect operating cash-flow calculation, why is depreciation added back?
options: It is always a financing cash inflow
It reduced profit without causing a current operating cash payment
It is a new cash receipt from customers
It increases the original cost of inventory
questions.answer: It reduced profit without causing a current operating cash payment
questions.explanation: The adjustment reverses a noncash expense included in the profit starting figure.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: Revenue is recognised, but trade receivables increase during the period. All else equal, how does this affect cash from customers relative to revenue?
options: Cash collection is lower than recognised revenue
Cash collection must exceed revenue
Revenue must be zero
Every receivable increase is a cash inflow
questions.answer: Cash collection is lower than recognised revenue
questions.explanation: An increase in unpaid customer balances means part of recognised revenue has not yet been collected.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A company receives a new bank loan. Why does this increase cash without increasing profit at receipt?
options: All cash receipts are excluded from accounting
The money becomes a depreciation charge
The bank has purchased the company's inventory
It creates a liability rather than earned revenue
questions.answer: It creates a liability rather than earned revenue
questions.explanation: Borrowed funds must be repaid and are financing, not income earned from operations.

questions.subject: Accounting
questions.q: A company distributes part of its accumulated profit as a dividend. How is this different from paying an operating expense?
options: It is always interest on a loan
It is the purchase of a new productive asset
It is a distribution to owners rather than a cost of earning the period's revenue
It increases sales revenue
questions.answer: It is a distribution to owners rather than a cost of earning the period's revenue
questions.explanation: Dividends distribute equity returns, while operating expenses contribute to determining profit.
