questions.explanation: A shared zero may cancel completely or leave a denominator factor producing unbounded behaviour.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: The domain of f is [2,8]. What is the domain of g(x)=f(2x-2)?
questions.explanation: The input condition 2≤2x-2≤8 gives 2≤x≤5.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: A higher-degree polynomial fits all recorded points exactly but behaves implausibly between them. What concern arises?
options: The data must be wrong because the fit is exact
Exact fit may have come at the expense of a useful model
Interpolation guarantees reliable prediction
Higher degree always removes modelling assumptions
questions.answer: Exact fit may have come at the expense of a useful model
questions.explanation: A model can overfit sampled points and fail to reflect the underlying relationship.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: A solution of a transformed logarithmic equation makes an original logarithm's argument negative. What should happen to it?
options: Reject it as outside the original real domain
Keep it because the transformed equation holds
Replace the logarithm by its absolute value without justification
Accept it only if it is an integer
questions.answer: Reject it as outside the original real domain
questions.explanation: Algebraic transformations do not remove the original domain restrictions.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: f and g are individually defined at x, but f(g(x)) is not. What can explain this?
options: g(x) must equal x
Composition is impossible for all nonidentical functions
g(x) lies outside the domain of f
Both functions must be discontinuous at x
questions.answer: g(x) lies outside the domain of f
questions.explanation: A composition requires both the inner evaluation and the outer evaluation at its result to be valid.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: A positive exponential model with base greater than 1 is compared with a positive-leading-coefficient polynomial. What eventually happens for large positive inputs?
options: The exponential becomes linear
The exponential exceeds the polynomial
The polynomial must always remain larger
They must become identical
questions.answer: The exponential exceeds the polynomial
questions.explanation: Exponential growth eventually dominates any fixed-degree polynomial, though the crossover may occur far out.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.topic: Unit 2: growth parameter and time units
questions.q: An exponential model is rewritten from years to months without changing the phenomenon. What must happen to its monthly growth factor?
options: It must equal twelve times the yearly factor
It must equal the yearly factor divided by twelve
It must remain numerically unchanged
Its twelfth power must equal the yearly growth factor
questions.answer: Its twelfth power must equal the yearly growth factor
questions.explanation: Twelve successive monthly multiplications must reproduce one yearly multiplication.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: A semi-log plot is nearly linear. What does this establish most directly?
options: A guarantee of exact future predictions
Proof that measurement errors are absent
Evidence for an exponential-shaped association, not its cause
Proof that one variable causes the other
questions.answer: Evidence for an exponential-shaped association, not its cause
questions.explanation: A transformed pattern helps select a relationship's form without establishing causal explanation.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: A model is written A times b^(t+c), with fixed known b>0, b≠1. Why cannot data on the curve alone generally identify A and c separately?
options: Only their combined factor A b^c determines the vertical scale
The model contains no output information
Every choice of b gives the same curve
The model is necessarily periodic
questions.answer: Only their combined factor A b^c determines the vertical scale
questions.explanation: Different pairs of A and c can produce the same combined multiplier and therefore the same function.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: Why is arcsin(sin(3π/4)) equal to π/4 rather than 3π/4?
options: Sine has period π
Both angles lie in the principal arcsine interval
Arcsine always halves positive angles
The inverse returns the angle in its principal interval with that sine
questions.answer: The inverse returns the angle in its principal interval with that sine
questions.explanation: The two angles share a sine value, but only π/4 lies in the conventional principal interval.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: Why can different-looking sine and cosine formulas describe the same periodic graph?
options: Changing function names removes the need to match phase
A phase shift can convert sine to cosine
Sine and cosine have different ranges
Every sinusoidal formula is unique as written
questions.answer: A phase shift can convert sine to cosine
questions.explanation: Trigonometric identities allow equivalent representations with adjusted phase parameters.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: A sinusoidal model has a negative coefficient multiplying sine. Why is its amplitude still positive?
options: Amplitude is the magnitude of the vertical displacement from the midline
A negative coefficient makes every value positive
The coefficient's sign changes only the period
Amplitude equals the signed maximum value
questions.answer: Amplitude is the magnitude of the vertical displacement from the midline
questions.explanation: The sign can reflect the cycle, while the size of oscillation is measured by an absolute magnitude.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.topic: Unit 3: radius change and Cartesian motion
questions.q: On a polar curve, r increases while θ changes. Why does this not guarantee x increases?
options: An increasing radius forces a constant angle
Cosine is positive at every angle
x=r cos θ depends on both changing quantities
x always equals r
questions.answer: x=r cos θ depends on both changing quantities
questions.explanation: The changing direction can offset or reverse the horizontal effect of increasing radius.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: A student uses arccos(1.2) while solving a real trigonometric equation. What does this reveal?
options: Cosine can exceed 1 only for negative angles
The proposed cosine value is outside the real range of cosine
The angle must exceed 2π
The inverse gives two real angles
questions.answer: The proposed cosine value is outside the real range of cosine
questions.explanation: A unit-circle horizontal coordinate stays between -1 and 1, so no real angle has cosine 1.2.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.q: Dividing an equation by sin x makes it simpler. What must be checked separately?
options: Only solutions where cos x=0
Every positive x must be rejected
The equation's period must be doubled
Solutions where sin x=0
questions.answer: Solutions where sin x=0
questions.explanation: Division excludes zeros of the divisor, which may have satisfied the original equation.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.topic: Unit 4 optional, not AP-exam assessed: determinant and geometry
questions.q: A plane linear transformation has determinant -2. What does this imply about area and orientation?
options: Areas are negative
Every vector reverses direction with unchanged length
Areas double and orientation reverses
Areas halve and orientation is preserved
questions.answer: Areas double and orientation reverses
questions.explanation: Absolute determinant gives area scaling, while a negative sign indicates orientation reversal.

questions.subject: AP Precalculus
questions.topic: Unit 4 optional, not AP-exam assessed: parametrisation and motion
questions.q: Two parametrisations trace the same line segment in the same direction but take different times. What can differ?
options: Their rates of motion
The geometric endpoints of that same segment
The segment's slope
The set of points making up the segment
questions.answer: Their rates of motion
questions.explanation: A geometric path does not uniquely specify how quickly its points are traversed.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A researcher links changes in hippocampal cells to memory formation. Which perspective is most directly used?
options: Biological
Humanistic
Sociocultural
Psychodynamic
questions.answer: Biological
questions.explanation: The explanation connects mental functioning with processes in the nervous system.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A researcher studies how job demands match workers' abilities. Which application of psychology fits?
options: Clinical psychology
Sport psychology
School counselling
Industrial-organizational psychology
questions.answer: Industrial-organizational psychology
questions.explanation: Industrial-organizational psychology examines people and behaviour in work settings.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A psychologist studies one person's unusual memory difficulties in great depth. Which method is illustrated?
options: A randomised national experiment
A meta-analysis of hundreds of experiments
A case study
A census of every adult
questions.answer: A case study
questions.explanation: A case study provides intensive information about a particular individual or small unit.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A researcher records how children share toys during ordinary playground activity without assigning conditions. What method fits?
options: A test of a drug's biological effects
Naturalistic observation
A laboratory experiment
Random allocation to treatments
questions.answer: Naturalistic observation
questions.explanation: The behaviour is observed in its usual setting without an experimental manipulation.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Students who report more television time tend to receive lower exam marks. What relationship is described?
options: A negative correlation
A positive correlation
Proof that television causes lower marks
Identical marks for all students
questions.answer: A negative correlation
questions.explanation: The variables tend to move in opposite directions; the association alone does not establish causation.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A student deliberately moves their hand to pick up a pencil. Which system controls the relevant voluntary skeletal-muscle activity?
options: Only the digestive system
Only the endocrine glands
The parasympathetic system alone
The somatic nervous system
questions.answer: The somatic nervous system
questions.explanation: Somatic motor pathways carry commands to skeletal muscles involved in voluntary movement.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A faint tone is detected on about half the presentations under defined conditions. What does its intensity approximate?
options: A difference threshold between two loud tones
The highest frequency a speaker can produce
The absolute threshold
The maximum tolerable intensity
questions.answer: The absolute threshold
questions.explanation: The absolute threshold is conventionally defined by detection on half of presentations.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A room's unchanged smell becomes less noticeable after someone has been inside for a while. What process fits?
options: A new conditioned fear response
Sensory adaptation
An automatic increase in the smell's concentration
Proof that the smell has disappeared
questions.answer: Sensory adaptation
questions.explanation: Responsiveness can decline during continued exposure to a relatively constant stimulus.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Dots placed close together are seen as separate clusters despite sharing the same colour. Which grouping cue is most relevant?
options: Proximity
A change in sound frequency
A reinforcement schedule
A difference in genetic inheritance
questions.answer: Proximity
questions.explanation: Nearby elements tend to be grouped together in visual perception.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A broken outline is perceived as a complete circle. Which principle best explains this?
options: Negative reinforcement
Retroactive interference
Random sampling
Closure
questions.answer: Closure
questions.explanation: Closure describes perceiving a complete form despite gaps in the available visual information.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A child learns to fear one furry toy and then responds similarly to other furry toys. What process is illustrated?
options: Learning with no stimulus association
A fixed-interval reinforcement schedule
Stimulus generalisation
Complete extinction
questions.answer: Stimulus generalisation
questions.explanation: A learned response can extend to stimuli resembling the original conditioned stimulus.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: An agreed privilege is removed after a behaviour, and that behaviour subsequently decreases. What is illustrated?
options: Classical extinction alone
Negative punishment
Positive reinforcement
Negative reinforcement
questions.answer: Negative punishment
questions.explanation: Removing a valued consequence to reduce a behaviour is negative punishment; negative refers to removal.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A coach first rewards a rough attempt, then rewards progressively closer versions of a target skill. What is the method?
options: Shaping
Random sampling
Sensory adaptation
Unconditional stimulus presentation only
questions.answer: Shaping
questions.explanation: Shaping reinforces successive approximations toward a desired behaviour.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Asked to picture a leader on a sports team, a student immediately imagines the captain as a typical example. What does the captain serve as?
options: A randomised control
A sensory threshold
A conditioned reflex
A prototype
questions.answer: A prototype
questions.explanation: A prototype is a representative example used to organise a category.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A student follows a definite sequence of valid steps guaranteed to solve a particular class of problem. What approach is used?
options: A stereotype alone
An unrelated memory cue
An algorithm
A guess with no rule
questions.answer: An algorithm
questions.explanation: An algorithm specifies a procedure that produces a solution when correctly applied to a suitable problem.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A shopper uses a quick rule of thumb to narrow many choices, accepting that it may occasionally fail. What is used?
options: A sensory transduction process
A heuristic
A guaranteed exhaustive algorithm
A randomised experiment
questions.answer: A heuristic
questions.explanation: A heuristic reduces decision effort but does not guarantee a correct or optimal answer.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A student knows a familiar word and can describe its meaning but temporarily cannot produce it. What does this illustrate?
options: Retrieval blocking
Proof that the word was never learned
Permanent loss of all language knowledge
Successful recall of the missing word
questions.answer: Retrieval blocking
questions.explanation: The tip-of-the-tongue experience reflects a temporary difficulty accessing stored information.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A learner remembers a sequence using a sentence whose initial letters match the required items. What strategy is used?
options: Random guessing
A placebo comparison
A punishment schedule
An acrostic mnemonic
questions.answer: An acrostic mnemonic
questions.explanation: The sentence provides organised cues for retrieving the ordered information.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A child uses precise finger movements to cut out a small paper shape. What type of skill is mainly involved?
options: A purely hormonal reflex
A measure of language comprehension
Fine motor skill
Only gross locomotion
questions.answer: Fine motor skill
questions.explanation: Fine motor skills involve controlled movements of relatively small muscles, particularly in the hands and fingers.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A learner completes a task mainly to receive a promised reward. What kind of motivation is emphasised?
options: Sensory adaptation
Extrinsic motivation
Intrinsic enjoyment alone
An absence of any motive
questions.answer: Extrinsic motivation
questions.explanation: Extrinsic motivation is directed toward an external consequence rather than enjoyment of the activity itself.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A researcher assesses the same children repeatedly over several years. What is a main advantage over comparing different age groups once?
options: It can track change within the same individuals
It eliminates all effects of participants leaving
It guarantees that historical events have no influence
It proves every change is caused by age alone
questions.answer: It can track change within the same individuals
questions.explanation: Longitudinal research follows individuals over time, though attrition and other influences still require consideration.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Participants with the greatest difficulties disproportionately leave a long study. Why can the final results be misleading?
options: Every remaining measurement becomes mathematically incorrect
Leaving necessarily improves the study's generalisability
A longer study automatically removes selection bias
The remaining sample may no longer represent the original group
questions.answer: The remaining sample may no longer represent the original group
questions.explanation: Selective attrition can change who is represented in the analysed outcomes.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Names are randomly selected from a complete school register for a survey. What does this procedure principally support?
options: Random assignment to different treatments
Identical responses from all selected pupils
A less selectively recruited sample of that school
Proof that any correlation is causal
questions.answer: A less selectively recruited sample of that school
questions.explanation: Random sampling concerns selection from a population; it is different from assigning experimental conditions.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A researcher varies study-noise level and measures recall accuracy. Which pairing is correct?
options: Neither variable can be measured
Noise is the independent variable; recall is the dependent variable
Recall is the independent variable; noise is the dependent variable
Both are necessarily uncontrolled confounders
questions.answer: Noise is the independent variable; recall is the dependent variable
questions.explanation: The independent variable is manipulated, and the dependent variable records the outcome of interest.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: An experiment compares an active intervention with an apparently similar inactive one while participants do not know their allocation. What is the purpose of the inactive comparison?
options: Help distinguish intervention effects from participant expectations
Guarantee that every participant has identical expectations
Remove the need to measure outcomes
Ensure that the inactive treatment contains the active ingredient
questions.answer: Help distinguish intervention effects from participant expectations
questions.explanation: A credible placebo comparison can help control expectancy-related influences on reported or observed outcomes.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: In a model synapse, a substance activates receptors normally activated by a neurotransmitter. What effect is most consistent with agonist action?
options: It necessarily destroys every receptor
It blocks all neurotransmitter activity by definition
It prevents the receptor from having any response
It mimics or facilitates signalling in that system
questions.answer: It mimics or facilitates signalling in that system
questions.explanation: An agonist can imitate or enhance activity associated with a neurotransmitter system.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A person distinguishes colour well in bright light but poorly in dim conditions. Which receptor difference helps explain this?
options: Cones operate only when no light reaches the eye
The retina stops all signalling in dim light
Cone-mediated colour vision works best with sufficient illumination
Rods provide equally detailed colour vision at every light level
questions.answer: Cone-mediated colour vision works best with sufficient illumination
questions.explanation: Cones support colour discrimination and function best in brighter conditions; rod-dominated dim-light vision has limited colour information.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: After prolonged fixation on a green patch, a reddish afterimage appears on a white surface. Which explanation fits?
options: Green and red are identical wavelengths
Adaptation within opposing colour-response systems
The white surface physically turns red
The eye has created a new external light source
questions.answer: Adaptation within opposing colour-response systems
questions.explanation: Unequal adaptation in opponent colour mechanisms can produce a complementary afterimage.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Two lines cross, yet viewers perceive two smooth continuing paths instead of several sharply turning pieces. What principle is illustrated?
options: Good continuation
Extinction of a conditioned response
Negative punishment
An endocrine feedback loop
questions.answer: Good continuation
questions.explanation: The visual system tends to organise elements into smoothly continuing contours.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A tone previously paired with food is repeatedly presented without food, and salivation to the tone declines. What changed?
options: The tone was never a conditioned stimulus
Food has become biologically incapable of producing salivation
The animal has lost all learning capacity
The learned predictive relationship is no longer reinforced by pairing
questions.answer: The learned predictive relationship is no longer reinforced by pairing
questions.explanation: Repeated presentation without the unconditioned stimulus produces extinction of the conditioned response.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A response is rewarded after an unpredictable number of repetitions. Which schedule describes this?
options: Fixed ratio
Variable interval
Variable ratio
Fixed interval
questions.answer: Variable ratio
questions.explanation: Ratio schedules depend on response counts, and variable means the required count changes unpredictably.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A student entering a familiar café expects to queue, order, pay and collect food. What is this organised expectation?
options: A difference threshold
An event script
An action potential
A genetic mutation
questions.answer: An event script
questions.explanation: An event schema or script represents the expected sequence of actions in a familiar situation.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A person judges an applicant solely by resemblance to a familiar occupational stereotype while ignoring the applicant's record. What shortcut is dominating?
options: Representativeness-based judgement
Careful use of all relevant individual evidence
Random assignment
A guaranteed deductive algorithm
questions.answer: Representativeness-based judgement
questions.explanation: Judging category membership by resemblance can overshadow more informative evidence about the individual.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A learner compares explanations against a dataset and evaluates which fits best. Which form of ability is most directly exercised in the triarchic model?
options: Only practical familiarity with daily routines
Only generating novel ideas without evaluation
A fixed measure of physical strength
Analytical intelligence
questions.answer: Analytical intelligence
questions.explanation: Analytical ability concerns examining, comparing and evaluating information or proposed explanations.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A test is normed only on a narrow, unusually selected group. What is a concern when interpreting scores from a broader population?
options: The test must contain no correct answers
A smaller reference group automatically gives universal validity
The comparison norms may not represent that population
Norming guarantees fairness for every possible group
questions.answer: The comparison norms may not represent that population
questions.explanation: Norm-based interpretation depends on the suitability of the reference sample for the people assessed.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A student keeps a spoken number in mind while checking a simple instruction. What system supports this temporary storage and processing?
options: A peripheral hormone gland
Working memory
Only a permanent autobiographical archive
Only sensory adaptation
questions.answer: Working memory
questions.explanation: Working memory temporarily maintains and manipulates information needed for an ongoing task.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A person recalls a group success as mainly their own achievement despite records showing equal contributions. What bias fits?
options: A self-enhancing memory bias
Perfectly neutral reconstruction
Random sampling error in the records by definition
Proof that the other contributors were absent
questions.answer: A self-enhancing memory bias
questions.explanation: Memory can be reconstructed in ways that favour one's own contribution or self-image.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A learner connects new concepts to examples from their own experiences. Why can this improve later recall?
options: It guarantees flawless memory for every detail
It removes all need to understand the concepts
Personally relevant material can never be forgotten
Personal relevance can provide richer encoding and retrieval cues
questions.answer: Personal relevance can provide richer encoding and retrieval cues
questions.explanation: Self-referential elaboration can make information more meaningfully connected to existing knowledge.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: In a standard attachment observation, a child explores while using the caregiver as a secure base and seeks comfort on reunion. Which pattern is most consistent?
options: Proof that attachment has no role in exploration
A diagnosis based on a single isolated action
Secure attachment
A conclusion that the child never experiences distress
questions.answer: Secure attachment
questions.explanation: The coordinated pattern of exploration and comfort seeking is characteristic of secure attachment in the model.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A student attributes a disappointing result entirely to a teacher's dislike and sees no role for their own preparation. What belief is illustrated?
options: A measure of the student's actual intelligence
An external locus of control for that outcome
Strong perceived control over the outcome
Proof that the teacher caused the result
questions.answer: An external locus of control for that outcome
questions.explanation: The attribution locates the outcome's control outside the self, but does not establish whether that explanation is accurate.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A theory is adjusted so that every possible observation counts as support. Why is this a scientific weakness?
options: No conceivable result could count against it
A theory becomes stronger when no test can challenge it
It has necessarily been replicated in every population
Its predictions must be numerically precise
questions.answer: No conceivable result could count against it
questions.explanation: A scientific explanation must expose itself to possible disconfirmation rather than accommodate every outcome automatically.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A result contradicts a theory's prediction, but the study's measurement was unreliable. Why seek a stronger replication before deciding?
options: A theory can never be challenged by evidence
Repeating a study guarantees that the theory will be confirmed
An unreliable measure necessarily produces the correct result
The contradiction may reflect measurement problems rather than a failure of the theory
questions.answer: The contradiction may reflect measurement problems rather than a failure of the theory
questions.explanation: Evaluating a theory requires considering the quality and reproducibility of evidence that appears to support or challenge it.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: An unusual patient shows a pattern that challenges an existing memory theory. What is the strongest use of the case?
options: Discard it solely because it concerns one person
Estimate its population prevalence directly from the single case
Inform or challenge theory while testing how widely the pattern applies
Assume the patient's pattern represents every person
questions.answer: Inform or challenge theory while testing how widely the pattern applies
questions.explanation: A case can be theoretically informative without establishing how common the pattern is across a population.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A naturalistic study records genuine settings, but people know they are watched. What limitation remains?
options: No behaviour can be recorded outside a laboratory
Awareness of observation can alter behaviour
A natural setting guarantees completely unaffected behaviour
Observation becomes a randomised experiment automatically
questions.answer: Awareness of observation can alter behaviour
questions.explanation: Realistic settings can improve relevance, but observer awareness and measurement choices still affect validity.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: School records show a change in behaviour after a policy, but recording practices changed at the same time. What must be separated?
options: Change in behaviour from change in how it was recorded
The school's name from its postal address only
The number of archived pages from their paper size
A causal effect that is already proven by chronology
questions.answer: Change in behaviour from change in how it was recorded
questions.explanation: An apparent historical trend can partly reflect changes in measurement rather than the underlying behaviour.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: One study reports a correlation of −0.90 and another +0.40. Which has the stronger linear association?
options: The second, because positive always means stronger
Both, because every nonzero correlation has equal strength
Neither, because negative correlations are impossible
The first, because strength depends on magnitude rather than sign
questions.answer: The first, because strength depends on magnitude rather than sign
questions.explanation: The absolute coefficient is larger in the first study; the sign indicates direction.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A dataset follows a strong curved pattern but has a linear correlation near zero. What follows?
options: The curved pattern must be a graphing error
A zero coefficient proves a negative causal effect
Near-zero linear correlation need not mean no relationship
The variables must be statistically independent
questions.answer: Near-zero linear correlation need not mean no relationship
questions.explanation: A linear correlation measures linear association and can miss systematic nonlinear patterns.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Two studies claim to measure aggression, but one counts interruptions and the other physical acts. Why compare their definitions before combining results?
options: Different definitions prove both studies have no value
They may measure different aspects of the broader concept
The same label guarantees identical measurement
Any count is automatically a complete measure of aggression
questions.answer: They may measure different aspects of the broader concept
questions.explanation: Operational definitions determine what observations represent a construct and therefore affect interpretation and comparability.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A proposed study conceals its purpose to reduce response bias. Why is scientific usefulness alone insufficient to justify the concealment?
options: Ethical review must consider necessity, harm, consent arrangements and debriefing
Concealment automatically makes every result invalid
Avoiding response bias removes every duty to participants
A useful aim guarantees that all methods are acceptable
questions.answer: Ethical review must consider necessity, harm, consent arrangements and debriefing
questions.explanation: Methodological benefits must be weighed alongside participants' rights and protections.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A teacher says a research survey is optional but implies that refusal will damage a student's standing. What ethical issue arises?
options: The word optional removes all coercive influence
Survey length alone determines whether consent is free
Refusal proves that the student lacks research ability
The pressure undermines genuinely voluntary participation
questions.answer: The pressure undermines genuinely voluntary participation
questions.explanation: Consent can be compromised by pressure from someone with authority even when participation is formally described as optional.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Two cells share the same DNA sequence but express different genes after different regulatory signals. What does this show?
options: The cells cannot belong to the same organism
Environmental and regulatory influences cannot affect gene activity
Gene activity can differ without a difference in DNA sequence
Every difference in gene expression requires a new mutation
questions.answer: Gene activity can differ without a difference in DNA sequence
questions.explanation: Regulation, including epigenetic mechanisms, can alter expression without changing the underlying base sequence.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A conditioned response declines during extinction but briefly returns after a rest. Why is extinction not simply erasure of all prior learning?
options: All learned responses must grow continuously without interruption
The earlier association can still influence responding under changed conditions
The original stimulus was never learned
Recovery proves that no extinction occurred
questions.answer: The earlier association can still influence responding under changed conditions
questions.explanation: Spontaneous recovery indicates that reduced responding after extinction does not necessarily mean the original learning has vanished.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: One learner improves through rewards for closer attempts; another copies a demonstration. Why distinguish the methods?
options: The first emphasises consequences of successive approximations; the second observation of a model
Both require identical experience of direct rewards
Neither can influence a learned skill
Observing a model is the definition of negative punishment
questions.answer: The first emphasises consequences of successive approximations; the second observation of a model
questions.explanation: Shaping and observational learning describe different mechanisms that may also operate together.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A familiar shortcut works well in one setting but fails when the underlying conditions change. What is the sound conclusion?
options: The shortcut is therefore useless in every setting
Success once guarantees success in every later problem
Heuristics always outperform systematic analysis
Its usefulness depends on how well its assumptions fit the setting
questions.answer: Its usefulness depends on how well its assumptions fit the setting
questions.explanation: Efficient heuristics can be valuable but are vulnerable when cues no longer predict outcomes reliably.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A test predicts outcomes in its norming group but performs poorly in another group with different experiences. What needs evaluation?
options: Whether identical scoring guarantees identical meaning
Whether the original group can be ignored in every analysis
Validity and fairness for the intended population
Only whether the printed test title is unchanged
questions.answer: Validity and fairness for the intended population
questions.explanation: Evidence of validity is tied to the interpretation, purpose and population, not simply to a test's existence.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Two people with similar inherited predispositions develop differently under different experiences. Which explanation best accommodates this?
options: Different outcomes prove that neither genes nor environment matters
Development can reflect interactions between inherited factors and environment
Genes determine every outcome independently of experience
Experience requires genes to have no influence
questions.answer: Development can reflect interactions between inherited factors and environment
questions.explanation: Biological predispositions and experience can work together in producing individual differences.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: A vivid, confidently reported memory changes in details across repeated accounts. What does this indicate?
options: Subjective vividness does not guarantee accuracy
Confidence makes every detail objectively correct
Changing an account proves deliberate dishonesty in every case
Vivid memories cannot be reconstructed
questions.answer: Subjective vividness does not guarantee accuracy
questions.explanation: Emotional or vivid recollection can still be affected by reconstruction and later information.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Identical twins raised apart show similarities, but their environments were not assigned randomly. What should a careful interpretation avoid?
options: Considering inherited influences at all
Comparing similarities with other evidence
Acknowledging that multiple influences may operate
Treating similarity as proof that environment has no influence
questions.answer: Treating similarity as proof that environment has no influence
questions.explanation: Twin evidence can inform genetic contributions without excluding environmental similarities, selection or gene–environment processes.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: Workers change behaviour after researchers begin observing them, even without the planned treatment. What should the study consider?
options: A guarantee that awareness never affects behaviour
The impossibility of measuring workplace behaviour
Effects of observation and expectations as alternative influences
Proof that the planned treatment caused every change
questions.answer: Effects of observation and expectations as alternative influences
questions.explanation: Participation and attention may affect behaviour, so they must be considered when attributing change to a treatment.

questions.subject: AP Psychology
questions.q: People in lower-control jobs report more stress-related problems, but their working and living conditions also differ. What conclusion is justified?
options: The association rules out all environmental explanations
Perceived control is a candidate influence, but the association alone isolates no single cause
Control is proven to be the only cause
Job conditions cannot affect stress
questions.answer: Perceived control is a candidate influence, but the association alone isolates no single cause
questions.explanation: Other correlated conditions can contribute to the relationship, so stronger designs are needed to isolate causal effects.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A student wants to investigate travel to school statistically. Which question anticipates variation across students?
options: What is the school's postal address?
What time does the school officially open?
What is the name of the nearest bus stop?
How do journey times vary among students at this school?
questions.answer: How do journey times vary among students at this school?
questions.explanation: Journey times are variable measurements that can be collected and compared across students.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: One unusually long delivery delay is added to an otherwise tightly grouped set of delivery times. Which centre is usually less affected?
options: The sum divided by the number of observations
The median
The mean
The midpoint of the minimum and maximum
questions.answer: The median
questions.explanation: The median depends on ordered position and is less sensitive to a single extreme value than the mean or midrange.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Two classes have the same median test score, but one has a much larger interquartile range. What follows?
options: Its middle half of scores is more spread out
Its mean must be higher
Its highest score must be lower
Its scores must all be above the shared median
questions.answer: Its middle half of scores is more spread out
questions.explanation: The interquartile range describes the spread between the first and third quartiles, not the location of the centre.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A survey about library access is offered only through an app that some students cannot use. What is the main sampling concern?
options: The sample is automatically a census
Every included answer is necessarily inaccurate
Students without app access are excluded
The response options contain too many categories
questions.answer: Students without app access are excluded
questions.explanation: The sampling process misses a relevant part of the student population.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Volunteers are randomly assigned to two study methods. What does the assignment help achieve?
options: Proof that both methods have equal effects
Comparable groups on other characteristics in the long run
A random sample of all students in the country
Exactly equal prior knowledge in every realised group
questions.answer: Comparable groups on other characteristics in the long run
questions.explanation: Random assignment reduces systematic differences between treatment groups and supports causal comparisons.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A reliable probability model gives a 0.3 chance that a randomly selected delivery is late. What is the chance it is not late?
questions.explanation: Late and not late are complementary outcomes, so their probabilities sum to one.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A table shows club membership by year group. To find the proportion of Year 12 students in the club, which denominator is needed?
options: The total number of students in all years
The number of Year 12 club members only
The total number of Year 12 students
The total number of club members
questions.answer: The total number of Year 12 students
questions.explanation: Conditioning on Year 12 restricts the reference group to all Year 12 students.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: One card is drawn. The events it is a heart and it is a spade cannot both occur. What is the probability of both?
options: Zero
The sum of their individual probabilities
The product of their individual probabilities
One minus the probability of a heart
questions.answer: Zero
questions.explanation: A single card cannot belong to both suits, so the intersection is empty.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A game has a 20% win chance per independent play. Which simulation correctly represents one play using equally likely digits 0–9?
options: Treat five digits as wins and five as losses
Treat one digit as a win and nine as losses
Treat every second generated digit as a win regardless of its value
Treat two digits as wins and eight as losses
questions.answer: Treat two digits as wins and eight as losses
questions.explanation: Two of ten equally likely digits give the required probability of 0.2.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: In a normal distribution, a measurement lies above the mean. What can be concluded about its standardised z-score?
options: It equals the measurement's percentile
It is positive
It is zero
It must exceed 2
questions.answer: It is positive
questions.explanation: Subtracting the mean gives a positive difference; dividing by a positive standard deviation preserves its sign.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A random sample finds that 60% of students prefer an earlier lunch. How should this percentage be used?
options: As an estimate of the population preference proportion
As proof that exactly 60% of all students agree
As the chance that the sample was random
As the proportion who would agree under every possible sampling method
questions.answer: As an estimate of the population preference proportion
questions.explanation: A sample proportion estimates a population proportion and can vary from sample to sample.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A valid confidence interval for a population support proportion is entirely above 0.5. What does this support?
options: Support from exactly half the population
A guarantee that every random sample has a majority
A population majority in favour at that confidence level
Unanimous population support
questions.answer: A population majority in favour at that confidence level
questions.explanation: Values compatible with the interval all exceed one half, supporting a majority claim without implying unanimity.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A manufacturer claims its defect proportion is 0.02. A researcher suspects it is higher. Which alternative matches that suspicion?
options: The population defect proportion equals 0.02
The population defect proportion exceeds 0.02
The sample defect proportion equals 0.02
The population defect proportion is below 0.02
questions.answer: The population defect proportion exceeds 0.02
questions.explanation: The directional suspicion concerns a population parameter greater than the claimed value.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Under independence, 40% of students choose art. In a year group of 50 students, what expected art count follows?
questions.explanation: Independence applies the same 40% art proportion within that year group, giving 0.4 times 50.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A school records each sampled student's journey time in minutes. Which population quantity would a one-sample mean interval estimate?
options: Every student's exact journey time
The largest journey time in the school
The population average journey time
The population proportion who travel by bus
questions.answer: The population average journey time
questions.explanation: A mean procedure estimates the centre of a quantitative variable such as elapsed time.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 4: uncertainty in the standard deviation
questions.q: A mean is estimated from a random sample, and the population standard deviation is unknown. Why use a t procedure when its conditions hold?
options: It accounts for estimating variability from the sample
It assumes that the population standard deviation is zero
It estimates a categorical proportion instead of a mean
It guarantees that the sample data are normal
questions.answer: It accounts for estimating variability from the sample
questions.explanation: The t procedure incorporates uncertainty from estimating the population standard deviation using the sample.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A valid confidence interval for mean time with method A minus mean time with method B is entirely negative. What does it suggest?
options: Method A has a higher population mean time
Every individual using A is faster than every individual using B
The two population means are exactly equal
Method A has a lower population mean time
questions.answer: Method A has a lower population mean time
questions.explanation: The sign of the whole interval supports a lower mean for A, not a claim about every individual.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A scatterplot of practice time and test score tends upward. What association does it show?
options: The variables have no relationship unless all points lie on a line
Higher practice times tend to occur with higher scores
Every extra minute guarantees the same score increase
Practice time has been proved to cause the score difference
questions.answer: Higher practice times tend to occur with higher scores
questions.explanation: An upward pattern indicates positive association, but does not by itself establish causation or a deterministic rule.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A fitted line predicts 4 extra books read for each additional library visit. What does its slope describe?
options: The predicted change in books for a one-visit increase
The predicted books read when visits equal zero
The correlation between visits and books
The actual change for every individual student
questions.answer: The predicted change in books for a one-visit increase
questions.explanation: A regression slope describes a change in predicted response for a unit increase in the explanatory variable.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A height model was fitted using children aged 8–12. Why question its prediction for age 40?
options: The intercept must be zero for adult predictions
A positive childhood association guarantees continuing adult growth
Age 40 lies far beyond the data used to fit the relationship
Regression can never predict an unobserved value
questions.answer: Age 40 lies far beyond the data used to fit the relationship
questions.explanation: Relationships observed within one age range may not continue far outside it.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A team asks whether students with longer commutes report less sleep. What data would directly address the question?
options: Total enrolment and the number of bus routes
Commute time and sleep duration recorded for each sampled student
The school's average commute and a different school's average sleep
Only the longest commute at the school
questions.answer: Commute time and sleep duration recorded for each sampled student
questions.explanation: Paired measurements on the same individuals allow the relationship between the two variables to be investigated.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A miscalibrated scale added 2 grams to every recorded mass. After subtracting 2 from all readings, what happens to the standard deviation?
options: It decreases by 2 grams
It is divided by 2
It becomes zero if the mean is corrected
It stays unchanged
questions.answer: It stays unchanged
questions.explanation: Subtracting the same constant moves the centre but preserves every deviation from the mean.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A school samples students randomly within each year group instead of selecting only one year. What advantage does this provide?
options: Equal opinions within each sampled year
Automatic selection of every student in the school
Planned representation from every year group
Elimination of all nonresponse
questions.answer: Planned representation from every year group
questions.explanation: Stratification ensures that each specified subgroup contributes observations to the sample.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Students choosing an optional study app already have stronger prior grades. Why is their later higher score insufficient to establish an app effect?
options: Prior attainment and app use are mixed in the comparison
Any observed difference proves the app caused improvement
The score difference is invalid only if the groups have equal sizes
Self-selection supplies the same protection as random assignment
questions.answer: Prior attainment and app use are mixed in the comparison
questions.explanation: The groups differ in a factor that can affect the outcome independently of using the app.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: An experiment assigns each of two fertilisers randomly within both sunny and shaded areas. Why block by light conditions?
options: To give one fertiliser only sunny plots
To remove the need for replication
To ensure the two fertilisers have equal effects
To compare fertilisers under similar light while accounting for light-related variation
questions.answer: To compare fertilisers under similar light while accounting for light-related variation
questions.explanation: Randomising within blocks separates treatment comparisons from predictable differences between light conditions.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Two year groups have different sizes. Why compare club membership percentages within each year rather than raw member counts?
options: Equal percentages require equal membership counts
Percentages account for the different group totals
Raw counts always reverse the true association
Percentages remove every sampling bias
questions.answer: Percentages account for the different group totals
questions.explanation: Group-specific proportions put the comparisons on a common relative scale.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: For events A and B with P(B)>0, P(A given B) equals P(A). What does this imply?
options: Knowing B occurred does not change A's probability
A and B cannot occur together
A must have probability one half
A and B must be the same event
questions.answer: Knowing B occurred does not change A's probability
questions.explanation: This equality is the probability condition for independence of the two events.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Two valid simulations estimate the same probability, one using 100 repetitions and one using 10,000. What is generally expected of the larger simulation?
options: A different probability model solely because it runs longer
A larger probability for the event being simulated
Less random fluctuation in the estimated proportion
A guarantee that its estimate equals the exact probability
questions.answer: Less random fluctuation in the estimated proportion
questions.explanation: More independent repetitions generally stabilise the relative frequency without changing the underlying model.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A game's expected payout is 2.40 tokens, although each play pays either 0 or 6 tokens. How is 2.40 interpreted?
options: The smallest possible payout
The long-run average payout per play
The payout that must occur most often
A payout guaranteed on the next play
questions.answer: The long-run average payout per play
questions.explanation: An expected value is a probability-weighted average and need not be an attainable outcome of one trial.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Two normal populations have the same mean but different standard deviations. For the same value above the mean, which population gives the larger z-score?
options: The population with the larger standard deviation
Both always give the same z-score
The population with the larger sample size, regardless of spread
The population with the smaller standard deviation
questions.answer: The population with the smaller standard deviation
questions.explanation: The same positive distance from the mean represents more standard deviations when the standard deviation is smaller.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: For the same sample, why is a 99% confidence interval generally wider than a 95% interval using the same method?
options: The population becomes more variable when confidence increases
The 99% method uses fewer observed successes
Higher coverage requires a larger margin of error
The sample proportion changes when confidence increases
questions.answer: Higher coverage requires a larger margin of error
questions.explanation: Increasing confidence increases the critical value while the observed data remain unchanged.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 3: Type I error in context
questions.q: A test concludes that a defect proportion has increased when the true proportion has not increased from its null value. What happened?
options: A Type I error
A Type II error
A correct rejection
A sampling method with no possible random variation
questions.answer: A Type I error
questions.explanation: A Type I error rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 3: pooling in a two-proportion test
questions.q: Why does a test of equal population proportions commonly pool the sample successes when estimating its null standard error?
options: The alternative assumes both proportions are zero
Pooling makes the observed proportions equal
Pooling removes the need for independent samples
The null assumes one common population proportion
questions.answer: The null assumes one common population proportion
questions.explanation: Under the equality null, the combined data estimate the common proportion used in the null sampling model.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A valid interval for pA-pB is from 0.04 to 0.10. Which interpretation is appropriate?
options: Every future sample difference must lie in this interval
A's population proportion is estimated to exceed B's by 4–10 percentage points
A's proportion is 4–10 times B's proportion
Between 4% and 10% of individuals belong to both groups
questions.answer: A's population proportion is estimated to exceed B's by 4–10 percentage points
questions.explanation: A difference between proportions is an absolute percentage-point difference, not a relative multiplier or a guarantee for future samples.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 4: standard error and sample size
questions.q: For independent observations from the same population, what happens to the sample mean's standard error when sample size is quadrupled?
options: It is halved
It is quartered
It doubles
It stays the same
questions.answer: It is halved
questions.explanation: The standard error is proportional to one divided by the square root of the sample size.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Twelve students provide before-and-after scores. When checking a paired t procedure's normality condition, which distribution matters?
options: Only the after scores
The pooled scores treated as 24 independent observations
The distribution of within-student score differences
Only the before scores
questions.answer: The distribution of within-student score differences
questions.explanation: A paired analysis is a one-sample analysis of the differences, so its distributional checks concern those differences.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A school tests whether a new schedule reduces average waiting time below 10 minutes. Which parameter statement fits the alternative?
options: The population mean waiting time differs from 10 in either direction
The population mean waiting time is below 10 minutes
The observed sample mean equals 10 minutes
The population standard deviation is below 10 minutes
questions.answer: The population mean waiting time is below 10 minutes
questions.explanation: The question specifies a decrease in a population mean, so the alternative is directional.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: All heights are converted from centimetres to metres before calculating correlation with arm span. What happens to correlation?
options: It is divided by 100
It changes sign
It becomes closer to zero automatically
It stays the same
questions.answer: It stays the same
questions.explanation: Correlation is unchanged by a positive linear change of measurement units.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A fitted line has R²=0.64. What does this describe?
options: The response increases by 64 units per unit of predictor
There is a 64% probability that the predictor causes the response
64% of the observed response variation is accounted for by the fitted linear model
64% of the observations lie exactly on the fitted line
questions.answer: 64% of the observed response variation is accounted for by the fitted linear model
questions.explanation: R² compares variation accounted for by the model with total variation of the observed response around its mean.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A model predicts travel time from distance using data only for journeys of 5–20 km. Why might its intercept lack a useful practical interpretation?
options: It predicts time at zero distance, outside the observed range
An intercept always measures correlation
The intercept must equal the shortest observed journey
A positive slope forces the intercept to be zero
questions.answer: It predicts time at zero distance, outside the observed range
questions.explanation: The intercept's input value can lie outside the context and range where the relationship was observed.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A huge voluntary online poll gives a very narrow conventional confidence interval. People with strong opinions were especially likely to respond. What is the strongest criticism?
options: A large sample necessarily removes self-selection bias
The narrow interval proves that all population groups were represented
The estimated proportion must be unbiased because its standard error is small
The narrow interval does not account for self-selection bias
questions.answer: The narrow interval does not account for self-selection bias
questions.explanation: A calculation of random sampling uncertainty cannot correct a systematically unrepresentative recruitment process.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 1: order effects in paired designs
questions.q: Every participant tries interface A first and B second on the same task. Scores improve on B. What design change best separates interface effects from practice?
options: Give interface B a longer practice session for every participant
Randomise or counterbalance the interface order across participants
Increase the sample size while keeping A first for everyone
Compare only the two overall sample means and ignore pairing
questions.answer: Randomise or counterbalance the interface order across participants
questions.explanation: Varying order prevents practice from being systematically attached to one interface.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Two histograms of the same data look different because their bin widths differ. What should a reviewer infer?
options: Apparent detail can depend on grouping, so inspect the bin choices and underlying data
One graph necessarily uses fabricated observations
The sample means must differ between the histograms
Narrower bins always provide the only correct summary
questions.answer: Apparent detail can depend on grouping, so inspect the bin choices and underlying data
questions.explanation: A histogram groups observations into intervals; changing those intervals can reveal or obscure features without changing the data.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A survey samples a few whole classrooms, and classmates tend to give similar answers. Why can treating all answers as independent understate uncertainty?
options: Cluster sampling necessarily changes the population's true proportion
The uncertainty depends only on the total number of answers
Many answers within a classroom provide less independent information than the same number spread across classrooms
Every additional classmate provides an entirely new independent group
questions.answer: Many answers within a classroom provide less independent information than the same number spread across classrooms
questions.explanation: Similarity within clusters reduces the effective independent information relative to a simple random sample of the same size.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Treatments are randomly assigned, but assessors know the assignment and use a partly subjective rating. Why might blinding assessors still help?
options: Blinding removes all natural variation in participant outcomes
It can reduce treatment-related differences in how outcomes are rated
Random assignment guarantees that assessors have identical expectations
Blinding changes the treatment received into a random sample of the population
questions.answer: It can reduce treatment-related differences in how outcomes are rated
questions.explanation: Random assignment addresses group comparability, whereas blinding can protect outcome measurement from assessor expectations.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Method A has a higher success rate in each of two difficulty groups, but a lower overall success rate than B. How can this occur?
options: Conditional comparisons must have been calculated incorrectly
The overall rates must equal the unweighted mean of the two group rates
A higher rate in each group guarantees a higher rate after any pooling
A is used much more often for the harder cases
questions.answer: A is used much more often for the harder cases
questions.explanation: Overall rates weight groups by their sizes; different mixtures of easier and harder cases can reverse the combined comparison.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Two mutually exclusive events each have positive probability. Why are they not independent?
options: Mutually exclusive events always have equal probabilities
Their probabilities must sum to more than one
If one occurs, the other's probability becomes zero rather than staying at its positive value
Independent events must always occur together
questions.answer: If one occurs, the other's probability becomes zero rather than staying at its positive value
questions.explanation: Exclusivity makes the intersection zero, whereas independence would require the positive product of the two probabilities.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 2: simulation and sampling without replacement
questions.q: A box has three red and two blue tokens. To simulate drawing two without replacement, why is independently generating each colour with probabilities 3/5 and 2/5 unsuitable?
options: The second draw's colour probabilities depend on the first token removed
The first draw cannot be represented probabilistically
Independent generation would give a correct model for every box size
The colour probabilities must both be one half on the second draw
questions.answer: The second draw's colour probabilities depend on the first token removed
questions.explanation: Removal changes the box composition, and independent draws fail to reproduce that dependence.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Ten components share a power supply; a supply failure can disable several together. Why question a binomial model for the failure count?
options: A fixed number of components rules out a binomial count
Failure and nonfailure provide too few possible trial outcomes
A binomial model requires every component to fail eventually
Component failures may not be independent
questions.answer: Component failures may not be independent
questions.explanation: A common cause can link outcomes across components, violating the independent-trials condition.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 2: sampling distributions versus raw data
questions.q: Larger independent samples produce less variable sample means. Does this imply that individual values in the population become less variable?
options: No; sample means must always have the same spread as individuals
No; averaging reduces sampling variability without changing population spread
Yes; the population standard deviation shrinks as samples grow
Yes; large samples force all individual values toward the mean
questions.answer: No; averaging reduces sampling variability without changing population spread
questions.explanation: The population distribution and the sampling distribution of an average are different objects.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A small study fails to reject equal population proportions, but its interval includes substantial positive and negative differences. What is justified?
options: The evidence is inconclusive; important differences remain compatible with the data
The population proportions have been proved identical
There is strong evidence that both proportions are zero
A nonsignificant result establishes that the study had high power
questions.answer: The evidence is inconclusive; important differences remain compatible with the data
questions.explanation: A wide interval can leave meaningful effects unresolved; nonrejection does not establish equivalence.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: Twenty independent true null hypotheses are each tested at 5%, and only significant results are reported. Why can this be misleading?
options: Independence guarantees that no false rejection occurs
Testing more true nulls makes the family-wide false-rejection chance smaller
The chance of at least one false rejection exceeds 5%
Every individual test now has a 100% false-rejection probability
questions.answer: The chance of at least one false rejection exceeds 5%
questions.explanation: Repeated opportunities for a Type I error increase the probability of at least one such error across the set.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A valid chi-square test rejects independence between year group and elective choice. What does the test alone establish?
options: That the largest observed cell must be the cause of rejection
Evidence of an association somewhere in the table
That every pair of year groups differs significantly
That year group causally determines each student's choice
questions.answer: Evidence of an association somewhere in the table
questions.explanation: The overall test detects a departure from independence; it does not identify every specific difference or establish causation.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 3: expected counts and test validity
questions.q: A large contingency table has a large total sample but several very small expected cell counts. Why still check the chi-square approximation?
options: A large grand total automatically guarantees adequate expected counts in every cell
Observed counts can replace expected counts in every approximation condition
More categories always improve the approximation without additional data
Its adequacy depends on expected cell counts, not just the grand total
questions.answer: Its adequacy depends on expected cell counts, not just the grand total
questions.explanation: A large sample can still be thinly spread across categories, leaving the chi-square approximation unreliable in sparse cells.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A paired t analysis defines change as after minus before. If all differences are instead before minus after, what happens to the two-sided p-value?
options: It becomes one minus the original p-value
It becomes zero whenever the original mean change was positive
It stays the same while the test statistic changes sign
It doubles because the direction was reversed
questions.answer: It stays the same while the test statistic changes sign
questions.explanation: Reversing differences negates their mean and t statistic but preserves the statistic's magnitude and the two-sided tail area.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A researcher repeatedly draws random samples and constructs valid 95% mean intervals. What does the 95% describe?
options: About 95% of intervals from the procedure would contain the fixed population mean
About 95% of individual observations fall inside each mean interval
The population mean changes until it falls inside 95% of intervals
Each realised interval contains exactly 95% of all possible population means
questions.answer: About 95% of intervals from the procedure would contain the fixed population mean
questions.explanation: The confidence level describes the long-run coverage of the method across repeated samples.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.topic: Unit 4: uncertainty in independent mean differences
questions.q: Two independent groups have equally variable sample means. Why does subtracting the means not cancel their sampling uncertainty?
options: Equal variability means both sample means fluctuate identically together
Subtraction always subtracts standard errors directly
A difference of means has uncertainty only when population means differ
Independent fluctuations can go in opposite directions, so their variances add
questions.answer: Independent fluctuations can go in opposite directions, so their variances add
questions.explanation: Independent sampling errors do not track one another; the variance of their difference includes both sources of uncertainty.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: One observation has an x-value far from all the others. Why compare the fitted regression line with and without it?
options: Removing any observation must improve the population model
It may strongly influence the slope even if its fitted residual is small
Every extreme x-value is necessarily a data-entry error
A small residual guarantees an observation has no influence
questions.answer: It may strongly influence the slope even if its fitted residual is small
questions.explanation: An unusual predictor value can pull the fitted line toward itself, so residual size alone does not measure its influence.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A regression predicts y from x with imperfect correlation. Why should its equation not simply be inverted to obtain the least-squares prediction of x from y?
options: The two fits minimise squared errors in different response directions
The correlation changes sign when x and y are exchanged
Both regressions must have the same slope regardless of units
The inverted line always has zero residuals
questions.answer: The two fits minimise squared errors in different response directions
questions.explanation: Least squares depends on which variable is treated as the response; algebraic inversion generally does not produce the reverse fit.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.q: A fitted least-squares line with an intercept has residuals summing to zero. Why does this not prove perfect predictions?
options: Least squares forces all observed responses to be equal
A zero sum implies the response has no variability
Positive and negative errors can cancel while individual errors remain large
Zero total residual requires every residual to equal zero
questions.answer: Positive and negative errors can cancel while individual errors remain large
questions.explanation: The signed sum can cancel; assessing error magnitude requires squared residuals or another measure that does not cancel signs.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A flood-warning system benefits residents even when individual users cannot easily be charged. Why might collective provision be considered?
options: Only its operator can benefit
Individual charges may not capture the shared benefit
Every resident must value it identically
It has no production cost
questions.answer: Individual charges may not capture the shared benefit
questions.explanation: Some services have shared benefits and are difficult to provide solely through individual purchase.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Two groups accept parts of each other's proposals to reach an agreement. What does this illustrate?
options: A negotiated compromise
Complete agreement on every original demand
The absence of conflicting interests
A decision made without participation
questions.answer: A negotiated compromise
questions.explanation: Compromise can reconcile competing aims through concessions rather than identical preferences.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A constitution allocates authority to national and regional governments. What feature does this illustrate?
options: All authority belonging to one local official
The absence of national institutions
A requirement that every policy be identical everywhere
A constitutional division of governing powers
questions.answer: A constitutional division of governing powers
questions.explanation: Federal arrangements divide authority between levels of government under constitutional rules.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A constitution protects expression even when officials dislike criticism. What purpose does the protection serve?
options: Making all political disagreement disappear
Giving officials unlimited control over opinions
Limiting how public power may be used against individuals
Guaranteeing that every statement is accurate
questions.answer: Limiting how public power may be used against individuals
questions.explanation: Rights protections can constrain government action and preserve space for criticism and participation.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A campaign uses petitions, public meetings and lobbying to seek a reform. What do these activities show?
options: Every campaign automatically achieves its goals
Participation can extend beyond voting
Elections are the only means of expressing political demands
Public opinion cannot influence representatives
questions.answer: Participation can extend beyond voting
questions.explanation: Citizens and organised groups can pursue political change through several forms of engagement.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: An article openly states the political position from which it argues. What can readers do with that disclosure?
options: Consider how the stated perspective shapes its selection and interpretation of evidence
Assume every statement is false
Treat disclosure as proof of complete neutrality
Stop checking factual claims
questions.answer: Consider how the stated perspective shapes its selection and interpretation of evidence
questions.explanation: Identifying a perspective helps readers evaluate framing while still examining the evidence.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A poll asks whether respondents support a proposal described as obviously sensible. What is the concern?
options: The wording guarantees a representative sample
The phrase makes every answer more accurate
A leading phrase affects only the survey's length
The wording may lead respondents toward a preferred answer
questions.answer: The wording may lead respondents toward a preferred answer
questions.explanation: Evaluative wording can introduce response bias rather than neutrally measuring opinions.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Voters are asked to approve or reject a specific policy proposition directly. What distinguishes this from electing a representative?
options: It means every voter agrees on the proposal's meaning
It guarantees that the proposal protects all rights
The vote concerns a policy decision rather than selecting a person to decide
It removes every role for public institutions
questions.answer: The vote concerns a policy decision rather than selecting a person to decide
questions.explanation: A referendum puts a proposition to voters, whereas representative elections choose officeholders.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
