questions.q: Several apparently separate news outlets have the same parent owner. What should an analysis of media diversity consider?
options: Ownership makes the content impossible to examine
Common ownership may affect how independent their editorial choices are
Different outlet names prove complete independence
One owner guarantees identical reporting on every issue
questions.answer: Common ownership may affect how independent their editorial choices are
questions.explanation: Ownership structure is relevant to potential influence and diversity, though actual editorial practice also matters.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Reporters examine documents to investigate the misuse of public funds. What democratic function can this support?
options: Public scrutiny of those exercising power
Automatic proof of every accusation
Replacement of all courts by newspapers
Removal of the need for evidence
questions.answer: Public scrutiny of those exercising power
questions.explanation: Investigative reporting can reveal information that helps people hold public authorities accountable.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: In a party-list proportional system, seats are distributed broadly according to parties' vote shares. What is the intended relationship?
options: Every party must receive the same seats
The largest party must win every seat
Votes are irrelevant once parties submit lists
Representation should reflect the distribution of votes more proportionately
questions.answer: Representation should reflect the distribution of votes more proportionately
questions.explanation: Proportional allocation aims to connect the share of seats to electoral support, subject to the system's rules.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: An organisation presents evidence to lawmakers in support of its members' interests. What activity is illustrated?
options: A constitutional amendment by itself
A referendum of all citizens
Lobbying
A judicial verdict
questions.answer: Lobbying
questions.explanation: Lobbying seeks to influence public decisions through communication with decision-makers.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A volunteer joins a campaign because they care about its cause, without expecting personal material reward. What motivates participation here?
options: A requirement to obtain public office
Commitment to the policy aim
A guaranteed financial payment
An absence of political preferences
questions.answer: Commitment to the policy aim
questions.explanation: People can participate because they value a collective or policy objective.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: District boundaries are deliberately drawn to favour one party's chances. What is the main representational concern?
options: Boundary choices can distort how votes translate into seats
Boundaries automatically reveal every voter's preference
Every district must then have identical turnout
Population geography has no connection to representation
questions.answer: Boundary choices can distort how votes translate into seats
questions.explanation: Partisan boundary design can give one side an advantage beyond its overall vote share.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A representative prioritises an area's transport problems after hearing from residents. What relationship is illustrated?
options: A guarantee that every resident has identical priorities
Complete independence from constituent interests
A transfer of all legislative power to one resident
Responsiveness to constituency concerns
questions.answer: Responsiveness to constituency concerns
questions.explanation: Constituency representation involves responding to the interests and concerns of the people represented.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A legislature increasingly includes people from backgrounds previously excluded. Which change is directly described?
options: The end of all political disagreement
A necessary change to every constitutional rule
Greater descriptive representation
Proof that every group's policy aims are achieved
questions.answer: Greater descriptive representation
questions.explanation: Descriptive representation concerns who representatives are, which differs from what policies they pursue.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: In a system authorising judicial review, a court examines whether a law conflicts with the constitution. What role is it exercising?
options: Choosing the next election's winner
Checking legislation against higher constitutional rules
Writing every future law on its own
Conducting a public opinion poll
questions.answer: Checking legislation against higher constitutional rules
questions.explanation: Judicial review assesses the compatibility of public acts with constitutional requirements in systems that provide it.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: One institution makes laws while another implements them under the constitutional arrangement. What distinction is illustrated?
options: Legislative and executive functions
Public and private speech only
National and foreign currency
Two identical tasks with different names
questions.answer: Legislative and executive functions
questions.explanation: Making general rules and administering or enforcing them are distinct governing functions.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A policy is described as successful. Which evidence is most relevant to evaluating that claim?
options: Only the popularity of its name
The size of the report's cover image
The number of times officials repeat the claim
Reliable outcomes compared with the policy's stated objectives
questions.answer: Reliable outcomes compared with the policy's stated objectives
questions.explanation: Evaluation requires evidence about whether intended results were achieved and what other effects occurred.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A government's spending exceeds its revenue in a particular year. What does this describe?
options: A budget surplus
A guarantee that every public service has expanded
A budget deficit for that period
The entire accumulated public debt
questions.answer: A budget deficit for that period
questions.explanation: The annual deficit is a flow, distinct from the stock of debt accumulated over time.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Many groups are allowed to participate, but a small wealthy group has consistently greater access to decision-makers. What should political analysis distinguish?
options: The number of group names from all actual outcomes
Formal opportunities to participate from unequal practical influence
Legal participation from the complete absence of power
Wealth from influence as necessarily unrelated
questions.answer: Formal opportunities to participate from unequal practical influence
questions.explanation: Equal formal access does not establish equal resources, attention or influence in practice.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A respondent gives an immediate answer about an unfamiliar issue, then changes it after learning more. What should a poll analyst consider?
options: Some expressed preferences may be weakly formed or sensitive to information
Every changed answer is deliberate dishonesty
The first answer must be the only genuine preference
All opinions are fixed before people encounter information
questions.answer: Some expressed preferences may be weakly formed or sensitive to information
questions.explanation: Opinions vary in strength and familiarity, so a response need not represent a settled position.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: One chamber represents population while another gives regions equal representation. What tension can this design address?
options: The need to give every region the same population
The elimination of every legislative disagreement
A requirement that both chambers always have identical members
Representation of people alongside representation of constituent regions
questions.answer: Representation of people alongside representation of constituent regions
questions.explanation: Different representation rules can balance population-based and territorial interests.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A higher government requires a new regional service but supplies no additional funding. What issue arises?
options: Regional budgets automatically rise by the required amount
The requirement guarantees uniform local capacity
Responsibility can increase without matching financial resources
The service is necessarily cost-free
questions.answer: Responsibility can increase without matching financial resources
questions.explanation: A mandate can impose costs that the implementing authority must find resources to meet.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Regional governments choose different policies and have unequal revenue bases. What consequence is possible?
options: A constitution makes all implementation differences impossible
Service provision may vary across regions
Every resident must receive identical provision
Regional choice guarantees equal economic resources
questions.answer: Service provision may vary across regions
questions.explanation: Decentralised choices and unequal capacity can produce variation in public services.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A right binds national authorities but is not effectively protected against equivalent regional action. What gap remains?
options: Protection depends on which level exercises the power
The right is necessarily protected equally everywhere
Regional authority can have no effect on individuals
Written national rights automatically resolve every enforcement issue
questions.answer: Protection depends on which level exercises the power
questions.explanation: Effective rights protection requires attention to the authorities bound by the rules and the means of enforcement.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A rule is written identically for everyone but creates severe barriers for one group. What must an equality analysis examine?
options: Only whether the same font is used
Whether every rule must have identical effects in all circumstances
Whether unequal effects make evidence unnecessary
Its practical effects as well as its formally equal wording
questions.answer: Its practical effects as well as its formally equal wording
questions.explanation: Formal uniformity does not settle whether a policy creates unjustified or discriminatory disadvantages.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A policy protects one group's interests while restricting another group's liberty. What should a reasoned assessment consider?
options: A rule that every restriction is justified by popularity
An assumption that interests can never conflict
The justification, effects and proportionality of the competing claims
Only which group is larger
questions.answer: The justification, effects and proportionality of the competing claims
questions.explanation: Political judgement often requires weighing rights and interests rather than treating one benefit as decisive by itself.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A popular top-level candidate attracts voters who also support other candidates from the same party. What effect is illustrated?
options: An absence of party influence
A coattail effect across linked contests
Proof that every candidate has identical personal popularity
A change in the legal voting age
questions.answer: A coattail effect across linked contests
questions.explanation: Support for one prominent candidate can benefit other candidates sharing the party label.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: An officeholder has greater name recognition and a record of constituency service than a new challenger. Why can this matter electorally?
options: Existing office can provide advantages separate from the merits of a new proposal
Holding office guarantees re-election
Challengers cannot communicate with voters
Voters are legally required to support incumbents
questions.answer: Existing office can provide advantages separate from the merits of a new proposal
questions.explanation: Visibility, established networks and service records can contribute to incumbency advantages.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Two reports use the same statistics, but one foregrounds individual stories and the other institutions and long-term trends. What differs?
options: Necessarily the arithmetic of every statistic
The existence of the event being reported
The legal status of both publishers
The framing of the issue
questions.answer: The framing of the issue
questions.explanation: Framing selects which aspects and explanations receive attention, even when some underlying facts are shared.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A small party has substantial national support spread thinly across many single-member plurality districts. Why might it win few seats?
options: Every district must reserve it a seat
The system counts only the opinions of party leaders
It may rarely finish first in any district
National vote share automatically guarantees equal seat share
questions.answer: It may rarely finish first in any district
questions.explanation: Geographically dispersed support can translate poorly into seats where winning each district is decisive.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A campaign's success would benefit supporters and non-contributors alike. Why may it struggle to recruit contributions?
options: A shared aim guarantees equal contributions
People may hope to benefit from others' effort without contributing
The benefit cannot be shared by definition
Non-contributors must receive no benefit
questions.answer: People may hope to benefit from others' effort without contributing
questions.explanation: Free-rider incentives can make collective organisation difficult even when the outcome has broad value.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A system requires both chambers to approve the same bill, but they pass different versions. What must happen before enactment under that rule?
options: The disagreement must be resolved so both approve a common text
Either version automatically becomes law without further action
The larger chamber's version always prevails regardless of the rule
The two texts can be treated as identical because their titles match
questions.answer: The disagreement must be resolved so both approve a common text
questions.explanation: Requiring concurrence gives both chambers a role in agreeing the legislation's actual content.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A proposed constitution makes the executive entirely dependent on a single legislature for appointment and removal. What concern might critics raise?
options: A guarantee that the executive cannot be influenced
The disappearance of all legislative authority
A necessary increase in judicial power in every case
Insufficient institutional independence to check that legislature
questions.answer: Insufficient institutional independence to check that legislature
questions.explanation: The arrangement may concentrate effective control unless other checks and accountability mechanisms operate.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: An executive appeals directly to the public to build support for a policy that legislators resist. What resource is being used?
options: A guarantee of automatic legislative approval
The right to cancel every future election
The visibility and persuasive platform of executive office
A judicial power to invalidate legislation
questions.answer: The visibility and persuasive platform of executive office
questions.explanation: Public communication can create political pressure even when it does not supply a formal power to legislate.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: An executive nominates an official, but another institution must approve the appointment. What is the intended check?
options: The public has no possible interest in appointments
More than one institution participates in selecting the official
The nominee automatically chooses all approvers
Approval is unnecessary once a nomination exists
questions.answer: More than one institution participates in selecting the official
questions.explanation: Shared appointment powers can limit unilateral control, while also creating opportunities for disagreement or delay.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A judge gives weight to the choices of elected institutions when the legal framework permits discretion. What approach does this illustrate?
options: Judicial restraint
A claim that courts never interpret law
A power to replace every elected decision automatically
The abolition of constitutional rules
questions.answer: Judicial restraint
questions.explanation: Judicial restraint emphasises limits on judicial intervention and respect for other institutions' legitimate roles.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A national grant is available only if a regional government adopts specified practices. How can it influence regional policy?
options: The region receives the funds regardless of every condition
Funding conditions have no influence on incentives
The grant removes all need for regional administration
Financial conditions can encourage choices beyond an unconditional transfer
questions.answer: Financial conditions can encourage choices beyond an unconditional transfer
questions.explanation: Conditional grants can shape decisions by linking resources to compliance with policy requirements.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Public employees are selected through job-related qualifications rather than personal party connections. What principle is emphasised?
options: Inheritance of every public position
Selection by the largest private donation
Merit-based recruitment
Political patronage as the only criterion
questions.answer: Merit-based recruitment
questions.explanation: Merit systems aim to connect recruitment with competence rather than personal or partisan favour.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Everyone values a shared benefit, yet voluntary contributions remain low because people expect others to pay. What explains the gap?
options: The outcome cannot have any public-good characteristics
Individual incentives can obstruct a collectively desired outcome
Low contributions prove nobody values the outcome
Shared benefits automatically produce full cooperation
questions.answer: Individual incentives can obstruct a collectively desired outcome
questions.explanation: Collective value does not remove incentives to free ride when benefits cannot easily be withheld from non-contributors.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Two powerful groups reach a compromise that imposes substantial costs on people excluded from negotiation. What remains to assess?
options: Whether the agreement fairly considers affected non-participants
Only whether the negotiating groups are satisfied
Whether compromise automatically guarantees justice
Whether excluded people can have legitimate interests
questions.answer: Whether the agreement fairly considers affected non-participants
questions.explanation: Agreement among participants does not establish legitimacy or fairness for everyone affected.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A constitution makes amendment much harder than ordinary lawmaking. What trade-off does this create?
options: A guarantee that all existing provisions are just
The ability to change every rule without consent
An absence of any future constitutional dispute
Stability and protection against sudden change versus adaptability
questions.answer: Stability and protection against sudden change versus adaptability
questions.explanation: Entrenchment can protect foundational rules but can also make needed reform more difficult.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Two states give regions similar practical powers, but only one constitution protects those powers against ordinary national revocation. Why is the distinction important?
options: A written guarantee proves that no disputes will occur
The number of regions alone determines their legal security
Similar current arrangements can rest on different guarantees of regional autonomy
Practical delegation is always constitutionally identical to federalism
questions.answer: Similar current arrangements can rest on different guarantees of regional autonomy
questions.explanation: The source and protection of regional authority matter alongside the powers currently exercised.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Regional policy experiments reveal useful results, but some effects cross regional borders. What must an evaluation include?
options: A rule that variation prevents any useful comparison
Learning benefits alongside spillovers affecting other jurisdictions
Only outcomes inside the experimenting region
An assumption that regional boundaries stop all effects
questions.answer: Learning benefits alongside spillovers affecting other jurisdictions
questions.explanation: Decentralised experimentation can generate information while creating external effects requiring coordination.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A large voluntary poll has many responses but attracts mainly highly motivated supporters. Why is size alone insufficient?
options: Selection bias can persist despite a large sample
A large poll must represent every group equally
More responses necessarily remove every wording effect
A narrow numerical margin proves random recruitment
questions.answer: Selection bias can persist despite a large sample
questions.explanation: Precision from many observations does not repair systematic differences between respondents and the target population.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A clear majority supports a measure restricting a minority's protected rights. Why does the vote alone not settle legitimacy?
options: A majority can never make any legitimate decision
Minority rights require unanimous agreement on every policy
Popularity automatically eliminates constitutional limits
Democratic decisions must also be assessed against rights and constitutional constraints
questions.answer: Democratic decisions must also be assessed against rights and constitutional constraints
questions.explanation: Majority rule is one democratic principle and operates alongside protections against misuse of public power.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Incumbents win often, but stronger candidates also tend to become incumbents. Why is the win rate alone not the causal effect of holding office?
options: All incumbents and challengers must be equally strong
A causal conclusion requires no comparison
Candidate selection and office advantages may both contribute
The win rate proves office has no possible effect
questions.answer: Candidate selection and office advantages may both contribute
questions.explanation: Separating incumbency's effect requires considering differences that existed before the office was held.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A market has many outlet brands but concentrated ownership and similar source dependence. What would best assess viewpoint diversity?
options: Treat audience size as the only measure of diversity
Examine ownership, editorial practice and the actual range of coverage
Count brand names and assume each is independent
Assume one owner forces identical coverage in every article
questions.answer: Examine ownership, editorial practice and the actual range of coverage
questions.explanation: The number of labels alone does not reveal independence or variation in the information supplied.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Readers see the same event framed either as individual failure or as a result of institutional conditions. Why might their preferred responses differ?
options: Different causal emphases can make different remedies seem appropriate
Framing must change every underlying fact
Readers' preferences cannot respond to interpretation
Only the article's publication date can matter
questions.answer: Different causal emphases can make different remedies seem appropriate
questions.explanation: Explanations of why a problem occurs influence which policy responses appear relevant or justified.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: Two electoral systems produce different seat shares from the same distribution of votes. What follows?
options: The voters must secretly have cast different ballots
One numerical outcome proves every other system undemocratic
Electoral rules have no substantive political consequences
Rules translating votes into seats affect representation
questions.answer: Rules translating votes into seats affect representation
questions.explanation: District structures, thresholds and allocation rules can produce different representative outcomes from similar support.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: An oddly shaped district benefits one party, but settlement patterns are also geographically uneven. What is needed before attributing the result solely to manipulation?
options: An assumption that population geography explains every boundary
Only the colour used to draw the map
Evidence about boundary choices and plausible alternatives given population geography
A rule that every unusual shape proves partisan intent
questions.answer: Evidence about boundary choices and plausible alternatives given population geography
questions.explanation: Assessing gerrymandering requires more than shape alone and should consider the design process and relevant alternatives.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A legislature becomes more socially diverse, but policy outcomes for excluded groups barely change. What distinction matters?
options: Policy outcomes can be inferred from appearance alone
Who holds office and whose interests policy serves are related but distinct
Social diversity has no possible political relevance
Diverse membership guarantees every desired policy
questions.answer: Who holds office and whose interests policy serves are related but distinct
questions.explanation: Descriptive representation does not automatically establish substantive representation in decisions and outcomes.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A proposal has broad support but must pass several independent approval stages. Why can it still fail?
options: Each stage can create a veto point or bargaining obstacle
Popular support automatically overrides all procedures
Multiple stages guarantee faster agreement
Only the proposal's title determines its passage
questions.answer: Each stage can create a veto point or bargaining obstacle
questions.explanation: Institutional procedures shape which preferences become policy and can block measures despite substantial support.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A court can invalidate an elected legislature's law under constitutional rules. What tension must an analysis consider?
options: A choice between having any law and having no law
Proof that elections have no value
A guarantee that courts never make contested interpretations
Protecting constitutional limits while respecting democratic accountability
questions.answer: Protecting constitutional limits while respecting democratic accountability
questions.explanation: Constitutional review can constrain majorities, raising questions about both rights protection and the legitimate scope of judicial power.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A commentator praises judicial restraint only when it helps their preferred policy and demands intervention otherwise. What weakens the argument?
options: No judicial decision can be evaluated
A preferred outcome makes consistency irrelevant
The stated institutional principle is being applied selectively
Every change of opinion is necessarily dishonest
questions.answer: The stated institutional principle is being applied selectively
questions.explanation: A principled institutional argument needs reasons for different treatment beyond whether the outcome is personally favoured.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: An agency is judged only by the number of cases processed and begins prioritising easy cases over urgent complex ones. What problem is illustrated?
options: Complex cases must be outside the agency's responsibility
A performance measure can redirect effort away from the underlying public purpose
Higher counts prove better service for every group
Measurement removes every need for judgement
questions.answer: A performance measure can redirect effort away from the underlying public purpose
questions.explanation: Narrow targets can create incentives that improve the metric while weakening the outcome it was meant to represent.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A public service is contracted to a private provider, but government remains responsible for access and standards. What follows?
options: Contracting changes delivery without removing the need for public oversight
Private delivery automatically ends all public responsibility
A contract guarantees quality without monitoring
Ownership alone resolves every access concern
questions.answer: Contracting changes delivery without removing the need for public oversight
questions.explanation: Accountability requires arrangements for standards, monitoring and remedy even when a different organisation delivers the service.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: An outcome improves after a reform while several other relevant conditions change. What is the strongest evaluation approach?
options: Assign the full improvement to the reform because it came first
Reject all evidence because circumstances are complex
Use only supporters' descriptions of success
Compare credible alternatives and account for the other changes before attributing the effect
questions.answer: Compare credible alternatives and account for the other changes before attributing the effect
questions.explanation: Temporal sequence alone cannot isolate a reform's causal contribution when other influences are changing.

questions.subject: AP US Government & Politics
questions.q: A deficit grows during a downturn even though tax rules and spending programmes are unchanged. Why not assume a new discretionary stimulus?
options: Every deficit increase proves a new law was passed
The public budget is independent of economic conditions
Automatic changes in receipts and some payments can widen the deficit
An unchanged programme guarantees an unchanged budget balance
questions.answer: Automatic changes in receipts and some payments can widen the deficit
questions.explanation: The fiscal balance can respond to the cycle without a deliberate change in policy settings.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two organisms share many inherited structural features. What does this most reasonably suggest?
options: They must be the same species
They cannot differ in DNA
A relatively close evolutionary relationship
Identical habitats are required
questions.answer: A relatively close evolutionary relationship
questions.explanation: Shared inherited features can indicate common ancestry, although convergent features must be distinguished.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A cell is placed in a solution with lower water potential than its cytoplasm. What tends to happen?
options: Water leaves the cell
Water enters the cell only
The cell instantly makes more water
Solute movement must stop
questions.answer: Water leaves the cell
questions.explanation: Water moves by osmosis toward the lower water potential across a selectively permeable membrane.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A cell grows much larger without changing shape. Why can exchange become less efficient relative to its needs?
options: Surface area disappears
Its membrane becomes nonselective automatically
Its enzymes stop existing
Volume increases faster than surface area
questions.answer: Volume increases faster than surface area
questions.explanation: A decreasing surface-area-to-volume ratio makes exchange less sufficient for the larger internal volume.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A tissue repairs a small wound by mitosis. What should daughter cells normally retain?
options: No DNA
The parent cell's chromosome number
Half the parent cell's chromosomes
A completely new genetic code
questions.answer: The parent cell's chromosome number
questions.explanation: Mitosis normally preserves chromosome number in genetically similar daughter cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Why does meiosis reduce chromosome number before fertilisation?
options: It prevents chromosome number doubling each generation
It makes gametes have no genes
It prevents all genetic variation
It makes every offspring identical
questions.answer: It prevents chromosome number doubling each generation
questions.explanation: Fusion of two haploid gametes restores diploidy without continually increasing chromosome number.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A leaf receives light but very little carbon dioxide. Why may increasing light fail to raise photosynthesis?
options: Light never affects photosynthesis
Oxygen replaces carbon dioxide in sugar synthesis
Carbon dioxide is limiting
Chlorophyll must be absent
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide is limiting
questions.explanation: Increasing a nonlimiting factor has little effect when another required factor restricts the rate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A working muscle's ATP demand rises. Why must ATP be continually regenerated?
options: ATP contains no transferable energy
Cells hold only a limited immediately available ATP supply
ATP cannot be broken down
All ATP is stored permanently in DNA
questions.answer: Cells hold only a limited immediately available ATP supply
questions.explanation: ATP is rapidly used and resynthesized to support continuing cellular work.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A shoot bends toward light. Why does unequal growth produce bending?
options: All cells shorten equally
The root changes into a leaf
The light physically pushes the shoot
Cells on one side elongate more
questions.answer: Cells on one side elongate more
questions.explanation: Differential elongation across the shoot causes curvature toward the light.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Alveoli have thin walls and a large total surface area. What does this arrangement improve?
options: Filtration of red blood cells
Production of bone tissue
Diffusion of respiratory gases
Storage of undigested food
questions.answer: Diffusion of respiratory gases
questions.explanation: A short diffusion distance and large surface support rapid oxygen and carbon-dioxide exchange.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A person produces a smaller volume of concentrated urine when conserving water. What kidney change contributes?
options: More water is reabsorbed from the filtrate
All filtration stops permanently
More water is secreted into the tubule
Blood cells pass freely into urine
questions.answer: More water is reabsorbed from the filtrate
questions.explanation: Greater tubular water reabsorption reduces urine volume and concentrates remaining solutes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A reflex withdraws a hand from a painful stimulus before deliberate action. What advantage does this offer?
options: Permanent loss of brain function
A response without any neurons
Proof that muscles detect every stimulus alone
A rapid protective response
questions.answer: A rapid protective response
questions.explanation: Reflex pathways allow quick responses without waiting for conscious planning.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A plant loses water from its leaves while roots have water available. What helps draw replacement water up the xylem?
options: Photosynthesis converting sugar directly into xylem water
Tension generated by transpiration
A separate heart pumping in every leaf
Active transport of each water molecule along the entire stem
questions.answer: Tension generated by transpiration
questions.explanation: Evaporation creates tension in a continuous cohesive water column, drawing water upward from the roots.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A flower receives pollen from another plant of the same species. What may this increase compared with self-pollination?
options: Genetic variation in offspring
The number of chromosomes in every gamete
The certainty that all seeds are identical
The elimination of fertilisation
questions.answer: Genetic variation in offspring
questions.explanation: Cross-pollination can combine alleles from different individuals.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A recessive trait appears in a child of two unaffected parents in a simple autosomal model. What is a possible explanation?
options: The allele must be dominant
The child has no chromosomes
Both parents carry the recessive allele
Neither parent has the allele
questions.answer: Both parents carry the recessive allele
questions.explanation: Two heterozygous parents can each transmit the recessive allele.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Before cell division, DNA is copied. Why is accurate copying important?
options: Proteins cannot exist near DNA
Each daughter cell needs inherited genetic information
DNA supplies all the cell's oxygen
Copying removes every mutation from the species
questions.answer: Each daughter cell needs inherited genetic information
questions.explanation: Replication preserves genetic instructions for transmission to daughter cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Antibiotic treatment leaves a few resistant bacteria alive. Why can resistance become more common afterward?
options: Every bacterium deliberately chooses a mutation
The antibiotic teaches all bacteria to resist
Sensitive bacteria become mammals
Resistant survivors reproduce
questions.answer: Resistant survivors reproduce
questions.explanation: Selection favours resistant variants already present or arising through mutation and gene transfer.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A population grows rapidly, then slows as food becomes scarce. What explains the slowdown?
options: The disappearance of reproduction in all species
A lack of any environmental effect
Density-dependent competition
An unlimited carrying capacity
questions.answer: Density-dependent competition
questions.explanation: Competition intensifies as population density approaches resource limits.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A mosquito-control programme lowers transmission of a mosquito-borne pathogen. Which link has been disrupted?
options: Movement of the pathogen between hosts
Inheritance of every human gene
The production of antibodies by all hosts
The pathogen's need for genetic material
questions.answer: Movement of the pathogen between hosts
questions.explanation: Reducing vectors can reduce transfer between hosts even without treating every infected person.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A reserve protects several connected habitats instead of one tiny isolated patch. What advantage can connections provide?
options: Guaranteed extinction of predators
Elimination of all competition
Identical conditions everywhere
Movement and gene flow between populations
questions.answer: Movement and gene flow between populations
questions.explanation: Habitat connections can reduce isolation and support dispersal and genetic exchange.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A useful gene is introduced into a bacterial plasmid. Why can this help produce its protein?
options: The gene has to become a virus first
The plasmid can carry the gene into a suitable host
The plasmid directly becomes the protein
Bacteria do not require gene expression
questions.answer: The plasmid can carry the gene into a suitable host
questions.explanation: A vector can transfer a gene for expression in a compatible host system.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two species look alike but their similarities evolved independently in similar environments. What should a classification study do?
options: Use additional inherited and molecular evidence
Assume identical appearance proves recent ancestry
Ignore DNA because appearance is always decisive
Treat similar environments as identical genomes
questions.answer: Use additional inherited and molecular evidence
questions.explanation: Convergence can imitate relatedness, so multiple lines of evidence are needed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A membrane protein moves ions against their concentration gradient. What additional requirement is likely?
options: Identical ion concentrations on both sides
Destruction of all membrane proteins
An energy source
A completely impermeable cell wall
questions.answer: An energy source
questions.explanation: Moving against an electrochemical gradient requires energy, directly or through coupling.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Adding more substrate reduces the effect of a reversible competitive inhibitor. Why?
options: The reaction no longer needs enzymes
Substrate competes more successfully for the active site
The inhibitor is converted into substrate
The enzyme is permanently denatured
questions.answer: Substrate competes more successfully for the active site
questions.explanation: Higher substrate concentration increases the likelihood of substrate occupying the shared binding site.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments during meiosis. What can result?
options: A doubling of chromosome number in every gamete
Loss of all genes from both chromosomes
Identical copies of one parental chromosome only
New combinations of alleles on a chromosome
questions.answer: New combinations of alleles on a chromosome
questions.explanation: Crossing over recombines linked alleles between homologous chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Light reactions stop supplying ATP and NADPH. Why does carbon fixation soon slow?
options: Carbon dioxide instantly disappears from the atmosphere
The chloroplast loses all membranes immediately
Carbon reduction needs their energy and reducing power
The Calvin cycle directly absorbs all required photons
questions.answer: Carbon reduction needs their energy and reducing power
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle depends on ATP and NADPH generated by light-dependent reactions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Oxygen becomes unavailable to aerobic cells. Why does the mitochondrial electron-transport chain stall?
options: Its final electron acceptor is missing
Glucose cannot contain carbon anymore
All glycolysis enzymes require oxygen directly
The Krebs cycle becomes a photosynthetic cycle
questions.answer: Its final electron acceptor is missing
questions.explanation: Without oxygen accepting electrons, electron carriers cannot be efficiently reoxidised.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Why can fermentation sustain glycolysis when oxygen is absent?
options: It produces oxygen for mitochondria
It makes ATP without any substrate
It eliminates the need for enzymes
It regenerates NAD+
questions.answer: It regenerates NAD+
questions.explanation: Regeneration of NAD+ allows the oxidation step in glycolysis to continue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two plants receive equal total light but different uninterrupted night lengths and flower differently. What does this suggest?
options: Photosynthesis stops in all long nights permanently
Night duration can regulate flowering
Only total light energy matters
Flowers never respond to timing
questions.answer: Night duration can regulate flowering
questions.explanation: Photoperiodic responses often depend on the duration of uninterrupted darkness.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Exercising tissue releases more carbon dioxide and becomes more acidic. How can this assist oxygen delivery?
options: Haemoglobin's oxygen affinity decreases locally
Haemoglobin binds oxygen irreversibly
Blood stops flowing to that tissue
Carbon dioxide replaces iron in every haem group
questions.answer: Haemoglobin's oxygen affinity decreases locally
questions.explanation: The Bohr effect promotes oxygen unloading where metabolic activity is high.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: ADH secretion rises when blood becomes more concentrated. What combined response is expected?
options: Complete cessation of filtration in all nephrons
Increased loss of water with no feedback
More collecting-duct water reabsorption and less urine
Less water reabsorption and more dilute urine
questions.answer: More collecting-duct water reabsorption and less urine
questions.explanation: ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability, helping conserve water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A chemical synapse normally transmits in one direction. Why?
options: The neurotransmitter destroys the receiving neuron
Vesicle release and postsynaptic receptors are arranged asymmetrically
Electrical charge can move only one way through all materials
Both neurons have identical release machinery at the same contact
questions.answer: Vesicle release and postsynaptic receptors are arranged asymmetrically
questions.explanation: The presynaptic terminal releases transmitter onto receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Sucrose is loaded into phloem at a source. How can this promote bulk flow toward a sink?
options: Sucrose evaporates and pulls sap as a gas
The sieve tube becomes impermeable to all water
Every sucrose molecule is individually pumped along the full tube
Water enters osmotically, raising pressure near the source
questions.answer: Water enters osmotically, raising pressure near the source
questions.explanation: Solute loading draws in water and can establish a pressure difference that drives bulk flow.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A solute's uptake rate levels off as external concentration rises, despite an increasing gradient. What can explain the plateau?
options: The solute must be converted into water
The membrane has acquired unlimited carriers
A limited number of transport proteins are saturated
Diffusion gradients have become irrelevant to all membranes
questions.answer: A limited number of transport proteins are saturated
questions.explanation: Carrier-mediated transport has a finite capacity when the available proteins are fully occupied.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Red and white flowers produce pink heterozygotes in a simple inheritance model. What does this demonstrate?
options: The heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype
The parental alleles are permanently blended and lost
The trait has no genetic basis
Every allele is recessive
questions.answer: The heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype
questions.explanation: Incomplete dominance changes the heterozygote phenotype without erasing the separate alleles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A son inherits an X-linked allele from which parent in the usual XY model?
options: His father
Both parents through the same X chromosome
Neither parent
His mother
questions.answer: His mother
questions.explanation: A son normally receives his X chromosome from his mother and Y chromosome from his father.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A gene's mRNA is present but no protein is produced after ribosome function is blocked. Which stage is directly affected?
options: Chromosome segregation
Translation
DNA replication
Transcription initiation only
questions.answer: Translation
questions.explanation: Ribosomes read mRNA and assemble amino acids during translation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A population's allele frequencies shift sharply after a random disaster leaves few survivors. What process can explain this?
options: Genetic drift through a bottleneck
Directed mutation to help every survivor
Guaranteed stabilising selection
Inheritance of acquired injuries
questions.answer: Genetic drift through a bottleneck
questions.explanation: Chance sampling during a bottleneck can change allele frequencies independently of adaptive value.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A flowering plant gains pollination while an insect gains nectar. What makes this mutualism?
options: Neither species gains anything
Both must be the same species
Both species benefit
Only the insect benefits and the plant is harmed
questions.answer: Both species benefit
questions.explanation: Mutualism describes interactions with a benefit to each participating species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A pond can have less producer biomass than consumer biomass at one instant. How is this possible?
options: Biomass and productivity are identical measures
Producers reproduce and are consumed rapidly
Energy increases at every trophic transfer
Consumers perform all photosynthesis
questions.answer: Producers reproduce and are consumed rapidly
questions.explanation: Rapid producer turnover can sustain consumers despite low standing producer biomass.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A DNA sample is repeatedly heated, cooled with primers, and extended by polymerase. Why are primers needed?
options: They replace all template DNA
They cut every target molecule into amino acids
They convert RNA directly into protein
They provide starting points for DNA synthesis
questions.answer: They provide starting points for DNA synthesis
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase extends from an existing primer with a free 3-prime end.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two populations look different but interbreed and produce fertile offspring naturally. Under a biological species concept, what is strongest evidence they belong to one species?
options: Different local food sources alone
The fact that both have cells
Reproductive compatibility and gene flow
Different body colour alone
questions.answer: Reproductive compatibility and gene flow
questions.explanation: The biological species concept emphasizes reproductive connection rather than appearance alone.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Plant and animal cells are placed in sufficiently dilute solutions. Why can the plant cell become turgid while the animal cell may burst?
options: The plant wall resists expansion and builds opposing pressure
Plant membranes are completely impermeable to water
Animal cells contain no solute
The plant cell has no osmotic gradient
questions.answer: The plant wall resists expansion and builds opposing pressure
questions.explanation: The rigid cell wall limits expansion, allowing pressure potential to oppose further water entry.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A reversible inhibitor binds only away from the active site and reduces active enzyme function; adding substrate does not restore maximum rate. What is supported?
options: Simple competition only for the same active site
A substrate shortage as the sole cause
An increase in enzyme concentration
Noncompetitive inhibition in the ideal model
questions.answer: Noncompetitive inhibition in the ideal model
questions.explanation: An ideal noncompetitive inhibitor lowers functional catalytic capacity that extra substrate cannot restore.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A mitochondrial membrane becomes freely permeable to protons while electron transfer can continue. What happens to ATP synthesis by ATP synthase?
options: It moves into the nucleus
It decreases as the proton gradient dissipates
It increases without limit
It becomes independent of the gradient
questions.answer: It decreases as the proton gradient dissipates
questions.explanation: ATP synthase relies on the proton-motive force; a proton leak uncouples it from electron transport.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A leaf's photosynthesis increases with added CO2 at one light level but barely responds in dim light. What explains the contrast?
options: The limiting factor differs between conditions
CO2 is never a photosynthetic substrate
Dim light destroys every chloroplast instantly
Light and CO2 act independently at all levels
questions.answer: The limiting factor differs between conditions
questions.explanation: CO2 may limit at adequate light, whereas insufficient light limits the response in dim conditions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A stronger stimulus causes more frequent action potentials rather than proportionately taller action potentials in one axon. Why?
options: Stimulus strength changes the genetic code each time
Stronger stimuli eliminate refractory periods
Individual action potentials are all-or-none events
Axons cannot transmit repeated signals
questions.answer: Individual action potentials are all-or-none events
questions.explanation: Stimulus intensity can be encoded by firing frequency while action-potential amplitude remains broadly fixed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A plant cell is turgid at equilibrium with an external solution. Why can water movement balance even though solute concentrations differ?
options: The wall actively pumps each water molecule outward
Pressure inside the cell offsets the solute contribution to water potential
Water cannot cross the membrane in either direction
Solutes no longer contribute to water potential in plants
questions.answer: Pressure inside the cell offsets the solute contribution to water potential
questions.explanation: Water potential includes pressure and solute effects; equal total potentials need not mean equal solute concentrations.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Developing fruits are removed from a plant while healthy leaves remain. Why may carbohydrate distribution change even if leaf photosynthesis initially stays similar?
options: Phloem can transport only toward fruits in every species
All leaf sucrose must instantly become starch in roots
Removing fruits removes every source of water
Removing sinks changes demand and translocation patterns
questions.answer: Removing sinks changes demand and translocation patterns
questions.explanation: Assimilate flow depends on source-sink relationships; changing demand can redirect transport.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two genes yield parental allele combinations much more frequently than recombinants. What is most consistent with this?
options: They have no alleles
Every meiosis produces only recombinant chromosomes
They are linked on the same chromosome
They must be on different chromosomes
questions.answer: They are linked on the same chromosome
questions.explanation: Linked genes tend to be inherited together, with crossing over producing fewer recombinants when loci are close.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A human coding sequence is placed in bacteria, but no protein appears because the promoter is unsuitable. What does this illustrate?
options: A shared genetic code does not guarantee compatible expression signals
Bacteria cannot use any human coding sequence
Promoters are translated into all proteins
DNA bases have completely different chemical identities in bacteria
questions.answer: A shared genetic code does not guarantee compatible expression signals
questions.explanation: Transcription also requires host-recognised regulatory sequences, beyond codon compatibility.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A trait is heritable and improves survival but reduces reproduction enough to lower total offspring contribution. What determines its evolutionary success?
options: Survival duration alone
The organism's desire to pass it on
Body size alone
Its net contribution to reproductive fitness
questions.answer: Its net contribution to reproductive fitness
questions.explanation: Selection depends on genetic contribution to future generations, integrating survival and reproduction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A food chain lengthens while primary production is unchanged. Why does adding a top consumer limit the biomass it can support?
options: Longer chains create energy
Repeated trophic transfers reduce available energy
Energy is fully recycled at each feeding step
All producers stop photosynthesising
questions.answer: Repeated trophic transfers reduce available energy
questions.explanation: Energy transfer is inefficient, leaving progressively less available to additional consumer levels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two equal-sized reserves differ: one contains varied habitats and one is uniform. Why might the varied reserve support more species?
options: It offers more kinds of ecological niches
Area alone determines every species count
Every habitat supports identical communities
Variation eliminates resource limits
questions.answer: It offers more kinds of ecological niches
questions.explanation: Habitat heterogeneity can provide different resources and conditions supporting more species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A PCR negative control with no added template produces the target-sized band. What should be suspected first?
options: A perfectly valid negative control
A need to report every sample as negative
Contamination or another control failure
Proof that the target sequence arose by natural selection during PCR
questions.answer: Contamination or another control failure
questions.explanation: A target-like product in a no-template control undermines confidence that sample products reflect only their original DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A DNA insert and vector have compatible sticky ends but are not ligated. What is missing for stable recombinant DNA formation?
options: Removal of the vector's origin of replication
Covalent sealing of the sugar-phosphate backbone
Conversion of DNA into protein
Destruction of all complementary bases
questions.answer: Covalent sealing of the sugar-phosphate backbone
questions.explanation: Base pairing can align fragments, while ligase seals backbone nicks to stabilize the construct.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two DNA samples produce bands at the same position in a standard size-separating gel. What does this establish most directly?
options: Their complete base sequences must be identical
They came from the same organism
They code for the same protein
The detected fragments have similar lengths
questions.answer: The detected fragments have similar lengths
questions.explanation: Migration in this gel primarily reflects fragment length; different sequences can share the same length.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A small isolated population grows numerically from only a few founders. Why can genetic vulnerability persist despite the larger headcount?
options: Larger population size instantly eliminates inbreeding history
Mutation recreates all lost alleles in one generation
Growth need not restore alleles lost at founding
Every new individual adds an entirely new set of alleles
questions.answer: Growth need not restore alleles lost at founding
questions.explanation: Population expansion can multiply existing genomes without restoring the original diversity lost in a bottleneck.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: At the same oxygen partial pressure, a right-shifted oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve indicates what?
options: Less oxygen bound and easier unloading
More oxygen bound and less unloading
No haemoglobin remains in the blood
Oxygen partial pressure has become zero
questions.answer: Less oxygen bound and easier unloading
questions.explanation: A right shift represents reduced haemoglobin affinity at a given oxygen partial pressure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The medullary osmotic gradient is disrupted while ADH is present. What ability is especially impaired?
options: Filtering any blood plasma at the glomerulus necessarily
Reabsorbing any glucose anywhere
Making erythrocytes inside the collecting duct
Producing highly concentrated urine
questions.answer: Producing highly concentrated urine
questions.explanation: ADH increases water permeability, but water reabsorption still requires an appropriate osmotic gradient.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Species richness stays constant after disturbance, but several species are replaced and energy pathways change. Why is unchanged richness insufficient to show full recovery?
options: Recovery can be measured only by total rainfall
Richness does not capture species identity or ecosystem functioning
Equal richness guarantees identical food webs
Every species performs exactly the same ecological role
questions.answer: Richness does not capture species identity or ecosystem functioning
questions.explanation: A single count of species can hide changes in composition, interactions and function.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Hydrogen and oxygen react in a sealed vessel. Why is total mass unchanged despite new water forming?
options: The vessel creates replacement atoms
Atoms are rearranged rather than created or destroyed
Water has no mass
Gases lose mass when they react
questions.answer: Atoms are rearranged rather than created or destroyed
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions conserve atoms, so a closed system conserves mass.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two atoms have the same proton number but different neutron numbers. Why do they have similar chemical behaviour?
options: Their nuclear masses are identical
Neutrons determine all bonding
They must have different element names
They have the same electronic arrangement when neutral
questions.answer: They have the same electronic arrangement when neutral
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number and normally similar electron configurations.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An atom loses its outermost electron. What happens to its net charge?
options: It remains neutral
Its proton number decreases
It becomes more positive
It becomes more negative
questions.answer: It becomes more positive
questions.explanation: Removing negative charge makes the remaining particle more positive.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but the melt does. Why?
options: Melting allows ions to move
Melting changes ions into free protons
The solid contains no charged particles
Only molten salt contains atoms
questions.answer: Melting allows ions to move
questions.explanation: The solid's ions are fixed in a lattice; mobile ions carry charge in the liquid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why can a covalent molecule contain shared electrons without having a net charge?
options: Sharing removes the electrons' charge
Covalent bonds contain only neutrons
The molecule has no nucleus
The total proton and electron charges can balance
questions.answer: The total proton and electron charges can balance
questions.explanation: Bonding rearranges electrons, while a neutral molecule still has balanced positive and negative charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Ethanol mixes readily with water. Which interaction helps explain this?
options: Breaking every carbon-carbon bond
Hydrogen bonding between their molecules
Metallic bonding between all atoms
Formation of an ionic lattice
questions.answer: Hydrogen bonding between their molecules
questions.explanation: Ethanol's hydroxyl group can form hydrogen bonds with water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A sealed gas sample is compressed slowly at constant temperature. Why does its pressure rise?
options: Molecules strike the walls more frequently per unit area
Its molecules become heavier
Its average kinetic energy must rise
Its amount of gas doubles
questions.answer: Molecules strike the walls more frequently per unit area
questions.explanation: Reduced volume increases wall-collision frequency while mean kinetic energy remains temperature-dependent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why does breaking a covalent bond require energy?
options: Bond electrons have no energy
Breaking bonds always releases heat
Attractive interactions must be overcome
The atoms must always become new elements
questions.answer: Attractive interactions must be overcome
questions.explanation: Energy is required to separate atoms held together by an attractive bond.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Reactants and products remain at constant concentrations in a closed reacting system. What can still be happening?
options: No molecular collisions
Forward and reverse reactions at equal rates
Only the forward reaction
Only the reverse reaction
questions.answer: Forward and reverse reactions at equal rates
questions.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium has continuing reactions whose equal rates leave concentrations unchanged.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An acid is diluted with pure water. What usually happens to hydrogen-ion concentration?
options: It increases
It stays fixed at every dilution
It becomes negative
It decreases
questions.answer: It decreases
questions.explanation: Dilution spreads the acid over more solvent, reducing hydrogen-ion concentration in ordinary acidic solutions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Hydrochloric acid is mixed with just enough sodium hydroxide to neutralise it. What happens to H+ and OH-?
options: They both become electrons
They remain unchanged in equal large concentrations
They form water
They form sodium metal
questions.answer: They form water
questions.explanation: The net ionic neutralisation reaction combines hydrogen and hydroxide ions into water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A galvanic cell powers a lamp. What overall energy conversion occurs?
options: Chemical energy to electrical energy
Electrical energy to nuclear energy
Light energy to chemical energy only
Thermal energy to mass
questions.answer: Chemical energy to electrical energy
questions.explanation: A spontaneous redox reaction drives electron flow through the external circuit.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An electrolytic cell deposits metal at its cathode. What happens to the metal ions there?
options: They lose protons
They gain oxygen in every case
They become more positively charged
They gain electrons
questions.answer: They gain electrons
questions.explanation: Cathodic reduction supplies electrons to metal cations to form neutral metal.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An element's spectrum has two isotope peaks, one much larger than the other. What does the larger peak indicate?
options: That isotope has more electron shells
That isotope is more abundant in the sample
That isotope has twice as many protons
That isotope must be more radioactive
questions.answer: That isotope is more abundant in the sample
questions.explanation: Peak intensity measures relative abundance, while peak position gives mass-to-charge information.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A solid reactant is powdered before reacting with a solution. Why can reaction become faster?
options: More surface is available for collisions
The solid's atoms become smaller
The reaction enthalpy must change
The powder is necessarily a catalyst
questions.answer: More surface is available for collisions
questions.explanation: Increasing surface area exposes more reacting particles to the solution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two compounds have the same molecular formula but different atom connections. What does this imply?
options: Their molecular masses must differ
One cannot contain covalent bonds
They can have different properties
They must be the same substance
questions.answer: They can have different properties
questions.explanation: Structural isomers differ in connectivity, which can change physical and chemical behaviour.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Ethene reacts by adding atoms across its double bond. Why is addition possible?
options: Its carbon-carbon sigma bond must always vanish
The pi bond can be replaced by new sigma bonds
Carbon must gain a fifth bond
The carbon nuclei split
questions.answer: The pi bond can be replaced by new sigma bonds
questions.explanation: The pi component of the double bond can open while new sigma bonds form.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An aldehyde is oxidised under suitable conditions. Which functional group is commonly formed?
options: An alkene group
An ether group only
An amine group
A carboxylic acid group
questions.answer: A carboxylic acid group
questions.explanation: Oxidation of an aldehyde normally produces the corresponding carboxylic acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate and releases gas. What does this show?
options: Every carbon atom becomes gas
It is necessarily a strong mineral acid
Its acidic proton can react with carbonate
It contains no covalent bonds
questions.answer: Its acidic proton can react with carbonate
questions.explanation: Acid-carbonate reactions release carbon dioxide; a weak carboxylic acid can still produce this reaction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Heating disrupts a protein's shape without necessarily breaking its peptide bonds. What may be lost?
options: Its biological function
Its entire elemental composition
Every amino acid residue
All covalent bonds
questions.answer: Its biological function
questions.explanation: Protein function often depends on a specific folded structure that denaturation disrupts.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Equal numbers of nitrogen and hydrogen molecules react to make ammonia. Which is left over if reaction goes to the stoichiometric limit?
options: Hydrogen
Both are fully consumed
Ammonia cannot form
Nitrogen
questions.answer: Nitrogen
questions.explanation: The reaction needs three hydrogen molecules per nitrogen molecule, so hydrogen is limiting in an equal-number mixture.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why is Na+ smaller than a neutral sodium atom?
options: Its nucleus has fewer neutrons necessarily
It has lost its outer electron shell
It has gained a proton
Its remaining electrons repel more strongly than before
questions.answer: It has lost its outer electron shell
questions.explanation: Losing the outermost electron removes the occupied third shell and strengthens attraction per remaining electron.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An element shows a large jump after its second ionisation energy. What does this suggest?
options: It has two relatively accessible valence electrons
It has two neutrons
It must be a noble gas
Its third electron is easier to remove
questions.answer: It has two relatively accessible valence electrons
questions.explanation: A large jump suggests that further removal enters a more strongly bound inner shell.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two comparable bonds differ mainly in bond order. Which trend is generally expected for the higher-order bond?
options: Longer and stronger in all cases
Identical length and energy
Shorter and stronger
Longer and weaker
questions.answer: Shorter and stronger
questions.explanation: More shared bonding electron density generally strengthens a bond and shortens its equilibrium length.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why does water have an unusually high boiling point compared with H2S?
options: Water's O-H covalent bonds must break on boiling
Water forms a stronger extended hydrogen-bond network
Water has greater molecular mass
H2S has no electrons
questions.answer: Water forms a stronger extended hydrogen-bond network
questions.explanation: Boiling separates molecules; strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding raises the energy required.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A liquid evaporates into a much larger available gas volume. What usually happens to the substance's entropy?
options: It decreases necessarily
It is unchanged because mass is conserved
It becomes zero
It increases
questions.answer: It increases
questions.explanation: The gaseous state allows many more accessible arrangements and molecular positions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, increased pressure at fixed temperature favours which side?
options: Neither side because gases cannot equilibrate
Whichever side contains a catalyst
Ammonia
Nitrogen and hydrogen
questions.answer: Ammonia
questions.explanation: Compression favours the side with fewer gas molecules, which is the ammonia side.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Equal-concentration strong and weak monoprotic acids are compared. Why does the weak acid usually have higher pH?
options: A smaller fraction of its molecules ionises
Each molecule releases more protons
Its concentration must be zero
Its conjugate base is absent
questions.answer: A smaller fraction of its molecules ionises
questions.explanation: Partial ionisation gives a lower hydrogen-ion concentration than a fully dissociated acid of equal concentration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A little acid is added to a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base. Why does pH change only slightly?
options: The solvent loses all polarity
The weak acid becomes a strong acid
The added acid is not conserved
The conjugate base consumes much of the added H+
questions.answer: The conjugate base consumes much of the added H+
questions.explanation: The buffer's base component reacts with added hydrogen ions, limiting the concentration change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A species oxidises another reactant. What happens to that species itself?
options: It cannot change oxidation state
It is reduced
It is also oxidised necessarily
Its electrons vanish
questions.answer: It is reduced
questions.explanation: The oxidising agent accepts electrons and undergoes reduction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why is a salt bridge useful in a galvanic cell?
options: It allows ionic movement that prevents charge buildup
It sends electrons through the solution between electrodes
It replaces both electrodes
It makes the redox reaction nonspontaneous
questions.answer: It allows ionic movement that prevents charge buildup
questions.explanation: Ion migration maintains electrical neutrality as oxidation and reduction proceed in separate compartments.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A molecule has several hydrogen atoms but only one proton NMR signal under suitable conditions. What does this suggest?
options: All carbon atoms must be absent
The sample must be ionic
The hydrogens occupy equivalent chemical environments
The molecule contains exactly one hydrogen atom
questions.answer: The hydrogens occupy equivalent chemical environments
questions.explanation: Equivalent proton environments share a chemical shift; signal count need not equal total hydrogen count.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A molecular-ion region has two peaks two mass units apart in approximately a three-to-one ratio. What evidence would this pattern support?
options: A molecule containing only hydrogen
One chlorine atom in the molecular ion
One fluorine atom with two equally common isotopes
Two carbon atoms being removed successively
questions.answer: One chlorine atom in the molecular ion
questions.explanation: The common chlorine isotopes differ by two mass units and occur in an approximately three-to-one abundance ratio.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Doubling a reactant concentration doubles the initial rate while other conditions are fixed. What does this support?
options: Second-order dependence on that reactant
Zero-order dependence on that reactant
A negative reaction order necessarily
First-order dependence on that reactant
questions.answer: First-order dependence on that reactant
questions.explanation: A proportional rate change is consistent with a first-power concentration dependence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why can a small temperature increase greatly accelerate a reaction?
options: The activation energy must rise
The equilibrium constant always becomes one
The fraction of collisions above activation energy increases
Every collision becomes successful
questions.answer: The fraction of collisions above activation energy increases
questions.explanation: The high-energy tail of the molecular energy distribution grows with temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A haloalkane forms an alkene by losing a hydrogen and a halogen from adjacent carbons. Which change distinguishes this process?
options: A carbon-carbon double bond forms
The carbon chain necessarily lengthens
An oxygen atom replaces the halogen
The molecule must become an ionic solid
questions.answer: A carbon-carbon double bond forms
questions.explanation: Elimination removes groups from neighbouring atoms and forms a pi bond.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Under controlled oxidation, a primary alcohol forms an aldehyde. Why is further oxidation often prevented by removing the aldehyde promptly?
options: Aldehydes cannot evaporate
The alcohol changes into a ketone when distilled
Removing product stops all molecular collisions
Aldehydes can oxidise further to acids
questions.answer: Aldehydes can oxidise further to acids
questions.explanation: Separating the aldehyde limits its continued exposure to the oxidising agent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A carbonyl carbon is attacked by a nucleophile. Why?
options: The carbonyl group is nonpolar
The C=O bond makes carbon partially positive
Carbon always carries a full positive charge
Oxygen donates all its electrons permanently
questions.answer: The C=O bond makes carbon partially positive
questions.explanation: Oxygen draws electron density toward itself, making carbon electrophilic.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An ester is hydrolysed under acidic conditions. Which products are expected?
options: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol
Two alkenes
An amine and an alkane
Only carbon dioxide and water
questions.answer: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis reverses ester formation by restoring an acid and alcohol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A polyester chain is hydrolysed under suitable conditions. What structural feature allows the chain to break?
options: A complete absence of oxygen atoms
A requirement that every monomer be an alkene
Hydrolysable ester links in the backbone
Only the presence of carbon-carbon single bonds
questions.answer: Hydrolysable ester links in the backbone
questions.explanation: Water can cleave ester links, dividing the chain into smaller molecules with acid and alcohol groups.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A product yield is lower than the stoichiometric maximum although the limiting reactant is consumed. Which explanation is possible?
options: The balanced equation must contain fractional atoms
Some reactant formed a side product
Mass conservation failed
The limiting reactant was unlimited
questions.answer: Some reactant formed a side product
