Relate expressive choices to phrasing, structure and effect
Assume the louder performance is always more faithful
Count only the performers' followers
questions.answer: Relate expressive choices to phrasing, structure and effect
questions.explanation: Interpretive choices can be assessed through musical evidence and coherence with the work.

questions.subject: Arts
questions.q: An accompaniment consistently masks the intended melody. What adjustment most directly addresses the problem?
options: Rebalance dynamics or register so the melody can be heard
Speed up every part equally
Add more accompaniment at the same level
Change the programme title
questions.answer: Rebalance dynamics or register so the melody can be heard
questions.explanation: The relative prominence of layers affects whether the intended musical focus is audible.

questions.subject: Arts
questions.q: A composer delays an expected harmonic arrival while maintaining the phrase's direction. What effect may result?
options: A necessary loss of all structure
A guaranteed change to a different instrument
The removal of every tonal relationship
Sustained expectation before resolution
questions.answer: Sustained expectation before resolution
questions.explanation: Delaying an anticipated arrival can extend musical tension within a coherent progression.

questions.subject: Arts
questions.q: An arrangement keeps a traditional melody but changes instrumentation and rhythm. What is the strongest analytical approach?
options: Call it unrelated because any detail changed
Judge it only by recording length
Identify what is retained, what changes and how those choices affect the result
Call it identical because one melody remains
questions.answer: Identify what is retained, what changes and how those choices affect the result
questions.explanation: Analysis can distinguish continuity from transformation without assuming either complete sameness or total separation.

questions.subject: Arts
questions.topic: Visual arts: formal and contextual evidence
questions.q: Two artworks share a colour scheme but were made for different audiences and purposes. Why is similarity of colour insufficient to establish identical meaning?
options: Every shared colour indicates direct copying
Meaning also depends on imagery, context and use
Colour never contributes to meaning
Different audiences make formal analysis impossible
questions.answer: Meaning also depends on imagery, context and use
questions.explanation: Formal resemblance is one part of interpretation and does not erase contextual differences.

questions.subject: Arts
questions.topic: Visual arts: scale and viewing experience
questions.q: A small sketch is enlarged into a mural without changing its proportions. Why might the viewer's experience still change?
options: Physical scale changes bodily relation, viewing distance and impact
Proportion alone fixes every possible response
An enlarged image necessarily changes its subject
Scale affects only the artist's signature
questions.answer: Physical scale changes bodily relation, viewing distance and impact
questions.explanation: Keeping relative dimensions does not preserve the work's physical presence or the conditions under which it is seen.

questions.subject: Arts
questions.q: One production plays a character's silence as resistance and another as fear. How should the choices be evaluated?
options: By assuming the louder production is automatically correct
By requiring silence to have one universal meaning
By ignoring all preceding action
Against textual cues and their coherence within each production
questions.answer: Against textual cues and their coherence within each production
questions.explanation: Performance choices can support different interpretations when they are coherent with the text and production context.

questions.subject: Arts
questions.q: An arranger moves an accompaniment into the melody's register and the lines become difficult to distinguish. What trade-off should be evaluated?
options: Whether two parts can ever sound together
Whether all accompaniments must be removed
The desired blended texture against clarity of the melodic line
Whether register changes the written tempo automatically
questions.answer: The desired blended texture against clarity of the melodic line
questions.explanation: Overlapping registers can promote blending but can reduce perceptual separation, depending on timbre and balance.

questions.subject: Arts
questions.q: A reviewer dislikes an installation's unsettling atmosphere, although the brief aimed to provoke unease. Which assessment is strongest?
options: Avoid examining any formal choices
Distinguish personal preference from evidence that the intended effect was achieved
Treat dislike alone as proof of technical failure
Assume intention guarantees success without audience evidence
questions.answer: Distinguish personal preference from evidence that the intended effect was achieved
questions.explanation: A reasoned evaluation can recognise effective artistic choices while separately stating a personal response.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two organisms share many inherited structural features. What does this most reasonably suggest?
options: Identical chromosome numbers in both organisms
An inability to interbreed with any related organism
A relatively close evolutionary relationship
A recent common habitat regardless of ancestry
questions.answer: A relatively close evolutionary relationship
questions.explanation: Shared inherited features can indicate common ancestry, although convergent features must be distinguished.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A cell is placed in a solution with lower water potential than its cytoplasm. What tends to happen?
options: Water leaves the cell
Water enters the cell down its water-potential gradient
Equal water movement in both directions gives no net change
Water leaves only if the cell spends ATP on osmosis
questions.answer: Water leaves the cell
questions.explanation: Water moves by osmosis toward the lower water potential across a selectively permeable membrane.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A cell grows much larger without changing shape. Why can exchange become less efficient relative to its needs?
options: Surface area increases faster than volume
Diffusion distances inside the cell become shorter
The membrane's permeability must decrease as the cell grows
Volume increases faster than surface area
questions.answer: Volume increases faster than surface area
questions.explanation: A decreasing surface-area-to-volume ratio makes exchange less sufficient for the larger internal volume.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A tissue repairs a small wound by mitosis. What should daughter cells normally retain?
options: A chromosome number determined by the wound's size
The parent cell's chromosome number
Half the parent cell's chromosome number
Twice the parent cell's chromosome number
questions.answer: The parent cell's chromosome number
questions.explanation: Mitosis normally preserves chromosome number in genetically similar daughter cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Why does meiosis reduce chromosome number before fertilisation?
options: It prevents chromosome number doubling each generation
It ensures that fertilisation produces haploid body cells
It doubles the number of chromosome sets in each gamete
It removes all recessive alleles before fertilisation
questions.answer: It prevents chromosome number doubling each generation
questions.explanation: Fusion of two haploid gametes restores diploidy without continually increasing chromosome number.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A leaf receives light but very little carbon dioxide. Why may increasing light fail to raise photosynthesis?
options: Oxygen can replace carbon dioxide as the carbon source
The rate must rise in direct proportion to light at all intensities
Carbon dioxide is limiting
Extra light provides the carbon needed for sugar synthesis
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide is limiting
questions.explanation: Increasing a nonlimiting factor has little effect when another required factor restricts the rate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A working muscle's ATP demand rises. Why must ATP be continually regenerated?
options: ATP stores increase automatically when the muscle contracts
Cells hold only a limited immediately available ATP supply
ATP is consumed only during resting periods
ATP regeneration occurs only after the muscle stops working
questions.answer: Cells hold only a limited immediately available ATP supply
questions.explanation: ATP is rapidly used and resynthesized to support continuing cellular work.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A shoot bends toward light. Why does unequal growth produce bending?
options: Cells on the illuminated side always elongate faster
Equal elongation on both sides changes the shoot's direction
Water loss from both sides makes the shoot extend symmetrically
Cells on one side elongate more
questions.answer: Cells on one side elongate more
questions.explanation: Differential elongation across the shoot causes curvature toward the light.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Alveoli have thin walls and a large total surface area. What does this arrangement improve?
options: Maintaining equal oxygen concentrations in air and blood
Increasing the distance gases travel between air and blood
Diffusion of respiratory gases
Active pumping of oxygen across a thick barrier
questions.answer: Diffusion of respiratory gases
questions.explanation: A short diffusion distance and large surface support rapid oxygen and carbon-dioxide exchange.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A person produces a smaller volume of concentrated urine when conserving water. What kidney change contributes?
options: More water is reabsorbed from the filtrate
Less water is reabsorbed from the collecting ducts
More water is secreted into the filtrate
Water reabsorption stays fixed while filtration must increase
questions.answer: More water is reabsorbed from the filtrate
questions.explanation: Greater tubular water reabsorption reduces urine volume and concentrates remaining solutes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A reflex withdraws a hand from a painful stimulus before deliberate action. What advantage does this offer?
options: It waits for conscious pain assessment before activating muscles
It prevents sensory information from ever reaching the brain
It produces a learned response that requires prior practice
A rapid protective response
questions.answer: A rapid protective response
questions.explanation: Reflex pathways allow quick responses without waiting for conscious planning.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A muscle pulls on a bone across a joint. Why is another muscle needed for the opposite movement?
options: The same muscle reverses its line of pull without changing attachment
Muscles actively pull rather than push
A contracting muscle can actively push the bone back when it relaxes
Tendons contract independently to reverse the first muscle's pull
questions.answer: Muscles actively pull rather than push
questions.explanation: Antagonistic muscles create opposing joint movements by pulling in different directions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A flower receives pollen from another plant of the same species. What may this increase compared with self-pollination?
options: Genetic variation in offspring
The frequency of identical allele combinations in every offspring
The chromosome number in each resulting embryo
The probability that every recessive allele is eliminated
questions.answer: Genetic variation in offspring
questions.explanation: Cross-pollination can combine alleles from different individuals.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A recessive trait appears in a child of two unaffected parents in a simple autosomal model. What is a possible explanation?
options: Both parents have two dominant alleles at that locus
An autosomal recessive allele is passed only through the mother
Both parents carry the recessive allele
Only one parent carries the allele and the other has two dominant alleles
questions.answer: Both parents carry the recessive allele
questions.explanation: Two heterozygous parents can each transmit the recessive allele.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Before cell division, DNA is copied. Why is accurate copying important?
options: DNA copying converts all inactive genes into active genes
Each daughter cell needs inherited genetic information
DNA replication creates the spindle that separates the cells
DNA replication gives each daughter cell half the usual chromosome number
questions.answer: Each daughter cell needs inherited genetic information
questions.explanation: Replication preserves genetic instructions for transmission to daughter cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Antibiotic treatment leaves a few resistant bacteria alive. Why can resistance become more common afterward?
options: Individual sensitive bacteria develop resistance because they need it
The antibiotic directs a useful mutation in each surviving cell
Resistant survivors lose their resistance as soon as treatment ends
Resistant survivors reproduce
questions.answer: Resistant survivors reproduce
questions.explanation: Selection favours resistant variants already present or arising through mutation and gene transfer.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A population grows rapidly, then slows as food becomes scarce. What explains the slowdown?
options: An increase in carrying capacity caused by food scarcity
A constant per-capita growth rate despite resource limitation
Density-dependent competition
Density-independent mortality caused solely by a storm
questions.answer: Density-dependent competition
questions.explanation: Competition intensifies as population density approaches resource limits.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Magnifying an image makes two nearby structures larger but still blurred together. What limitation remains?
options: Insufficient resolution
Insufficient enlargement despite the already larger image
Low contrast as the necessary cause of every unresolved image
An incorrect scale-bar label as the cause of overlapping detail
questions.answer: Insufficient resolution
questions.explanation: Magnification enlarges an image, while resolution determines whether close details can be distinguished.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A reserve protects several connected habitats instead of one tiny isolated patch. What advantage can connections provide?
options: Preventing all dispersal between breeding groups
Making the populations genetically identical immediately
Removing the need to maintain habitat quality within each patch
Movement and gene flow between populations
questions.answer: Movement and gene flow between populations
questions.explanation: Habitat connections can reduce isolation and support dispersal and genetic exchange.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A useful gene is introduced into a bacterial plasmid. Why can this help produce its protein?
options: The DNA sequence becomes the amino-acid sequence without transcription
The plasmid can carry the gene into a suitable host
The plasmid translates the gene without host ribosomes
Insertion alone guarantees expression in every bacterial species
questions.answer: The plasmid can carry the gene into a suitable host
questions.explanation: A vector can transfer a gene for expression in a compatible host system.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two species look alike but their similarities evolved independently in similar environments. What should a classification study do?
options: Use additional inherited and molecular evidence
Assume identical appearance proves recent ancestry
Ignore DNA because appearance is always decisive
Treat similar environments as identical genomes
questions.answer: Use additional inherited and molecular evidence
questions.explanation: Convergence can imitate relatedness, so multiple lines of evidence are needed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A membrane protein moves ions against their concentration gradient. What additional requirement is likely?
options: Identical ion concentrations on both sides
Destruction of all membrane proteins
An energy source
A completely impermeable cell wall
questions.answer: An energy source
questions.explanation: Moving against an electrochemical gradient requires energy, directly or through coupling.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Adding more substrate reduces the effect of a reversible competitive inhibitor. Why?
options: The reaction no longer needs enzymes
Substrate competes more successfully for the active site
The inhibitor is converted into substrate
The enzyme is permanently denatured
questions.answer: Substrate competes more successfully for the active site
questions.explanation: Higher substrate concentration increases the likelihood of substrate occupying the shared binding site.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments during meiosis. What can result?
options: A doubling of chromosome number in every gamete
Loss of all genes from both chromosomes
Identical copies of one parental chromosome only
New combinations of alleles on a chromosome
questions.answer: New combinations of alleles on a chromosome
questions.explanation: Crossing over recombines linked alleles between homologous chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Light reactions stop supplying ATP and NADPH. Why does carbon fixation soon slow?
options: Carbon dioxide instantly disappears from the atmosphere
The chloroplast loses all membranes immediately
Carbon reduction needs their energy and reducing power
The Calvin cycle directly absorbs all required photons
questions.answer: Carbon reduction needs their energy and reducing power
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle depends on ATP and NADPH generated by light-dependent reactions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Oxygen becomes unavailable to aerobic cells. Why does the mitochondrial electron-transport chain stall?
options: Its final electron acceptor is missing
Glucose cannot contain carbon anymore
All glycolysis enzymes require oxygen directly
The Krebs cycle becomes a photosynthetic cycle
questions.answer: Its final electron acceptor is missing
questions.explanation: Without oxygen accepting electrons, electron carriers cannot be efficiently reoxidised.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Why can fermentation sustain glycolysis when oxygen is absent?
options: It produces oxygen for mitochondria
It makes ATP without any substrate
It eliminates the need for enzymes
It regenerates NAD+
questions.answer: It regenerates NAD+
questions.explanation: Regeneration of NAD+ allows the oxidation step in glycolysis to continue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Sucrose is loaded into phloem at a source. How can this promote bulk flow toward a sink?
options: Every sucrose molecule is individually pumped along the full tube
Water enters osmotically, raising pressure near the source
Sucrose evaporates and pulls sap as a gas
The sieve tube becomes impermeable to all water
questions.answer: Water enters osmotically, raising pressure near the source
questions.explanation: Solute loading draws in water and can establish a pressure difference that drives bulk flow.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Exercising tissue releases more carbon dioxide and becomes more acidic. How can this assist oxygen delivery?
options: Haemoglobin's oxygen affinity decreases locally
Haemoglobin binds oxygen irreversibly
Blood stops flowing to that tissue
Carbon dioxide replaces iron in every haem group
questions.answer: Haemoglobin's oxygen affinity decreases locally
questions.explanation: The Bohr effect promotes oxygen unloading where metabolic activity is high.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: ADH secretion rises when blood becomes more concentrated. What combined response is expected?
options: Complete cessation of filtration in all nephrons
Increased loss of water with no feedback
More collecting-duct water reabsorption and less urine
Less water reabsorption and more dilute urine
questions.answer: More collecting-duct water reabsorption and less urine
questions.explanation: ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability, helping conserve water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A chemical synapse normally transmits in one direction. Why?
options: The neurotransmitter destroys the receiving neuron
Vesicle release and postsynaptic receptors are arranged asymmetrically
Electrical charge can move only one way through all materials
Both neurons have identical release machinery at the same contact
questions.answer: Vesicle release and postsynaptic receptors are arranged asymmetrically
questions.explanation: The presynaptic terminal releases transmitter onto receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A skeletal muscle sarcomere shortens while actin and myosin filament lengths stay constant. How?
options: Both filaments are chemically dissolved
Actin converts completely into myosin
The muscle loses all ATP
The filaments slide past each other
questions.answer: The filaments slide past each other
questions.explanation: Cross-bridge cycling increases filament overlap without shortening individual filaments.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: An edit alters a gene's regulatory sequence without changing its protein-coding sequence. What can still change?
options: The amino-acid sequence must always change
The number of protons in each DNA atom
When or how much of the protein is made
The genetic code used by every ribosome
questions.answer: When or how much of the protein is made
questions.explanation: Regulatory DNA influences expression, so protein abundance or timing can change without altering its amino-acid sequence.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Red and white flowers produce pink heterozygotes in a simple inheritance model. What does this demonstrate?
options: The heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype
The parental alleles are permanently blended and lost
The trait has no genetic basis
Every allele is recessive
questions.answer: The heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype
questions.explanation: Incomplete dominance changes the heterozygote phenotype without erasing the separate alleles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A son inherits an X-linked allele from which parent in the usual XY model?
options: His father
Both parents through the same X chromosome
Neither parent
His mother
questions.answer: His mother
questions.explanation: A son normally receives his X chromosome from his mother and Y chromosome from his father.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A gene's mRNA is present but no protein is produced after ribosome function is blocked. Which stage is directly affected?
options: Chromosome segregation
Translation
DNA replication
Transcription initiation only
questions.answer: Translation
questions.explanation: Ribosomes read mRNA and assemble amino acids during translation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A population's allele frequencies shift sharply after a random disaster leaves few survivors. What process can explain this?
options: Genetic drift through a bottleneck
Directed mutation to help every survivor
Guaranteed stabilising selection
Inheritance of acquired injuries
questions.answer: Genetic drift through a bottleneck
questions.explanation: Chance sampling during a bottleneck can change allele frequencies independently of adaptive value.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A flowering plant gains pollination while an insect gains nectar. What makes this mutualism?
options: Neither species gains anything
Both must be the same species
Both species benefit
Only the insect benefits and the plant is harmed
questions.answer: Both species benefit
questions.explanation: Mutualism describes interactions with a benefit to each participating species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A pond can have less producer biomass than consumer biomass at one instant. How is this possible?
options: Biomass and productivity are identical measures
Producers reproduce and are consumed rapidly
Energy increases at every trophic transfer
Consumers perform all photosynthesis
questions.answer: Producers reproduce and are consumed rapidly
questions.explanation: Rapid producer turnover can sustain consumers despite low standing producer biomass.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A DNA sample is repeatedly heated, cooled with primers, and extended by polymerase. Why are primers needed?
options: They replace all template DNA
They cut every target molecule into amino acids
They convert RNA directly into protein
They provide starting points for DNA synthesis
questions.answer: They provide starting points for DNA synthesis
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase extends from an existing primer with a free 3-prime end.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two populations look different but interbreed and produce fertile offspring naturally. Under a biological species concept, what is strongest evidence they belong to one species?
options: Different local food sources alone
The fact that both have cells
Reproductive compatibility and gene flow
Different body colour alone
questions.answer: Reproductive compatibility and gene flow
questions.explanation: The biological species concept emphasizes reproductive connection rather than appearance alone.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Plant and animal cells are placed in sufficiently dilute solutions. Why can the plant cell become turgid while the animal cell may burst?
options: The plant wall resists expansion and builds opposing pressure
Plant membranes are completely impermeable to water
Animal cells contain no solute
The plant cell has no osmotic gradient
questions.answer: The plant wall resists expansion and builds opposing pressure
questions.explanation: The rigid cell wall limits expansion, allowing pressure potential to oppose further water entry.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A reversible inhibitor binds only away from the active site and reduces active enzyme function; adding substrate does not restore maximum rate. What is supported?
options: Simple competition only for the same active site
A substrate shortage as the sole cause
An increase in enzyme concentration
Noncompetitive inhibition in the ideal model
questions.answer: Noncompetitive inhibition in the ideal model
questions.explanation: An ideal noncompetitive inhibitor lowers functional catalytic capacity that extra substrate cannot restore.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A mitochondrial membrane becomes freely permeable to protons while electron transfer can continue. What happens to ATP synthesis by ATP synthase?
options: It moves into the nucleus
It decreases as the proton gradient dissipates
It increases without limit
It becomes independent of the gradient
questions.answer: It decreases as the proton gradient dissipates
questions.explanation: ATP synthase relies on the proton-motive force; a proton leak uncouples it from electron transport.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A leaf's photosynthesis increases with added CO2 at one light level but barely responds in dim light. What explains the contrast?
options: The limiting factor differs between conditions
CO2 is never a photosynthetic substrate
Dim light destroys every chloroplast instantly
Light and CO2 act independently at all levels
questions.answer: The limiting factor differs between conditions
questions.explanation: CO2 may limit at adequate light, whereas insufficient light limits the response in dim conditions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A stronger stimulus causes more frequent action potentials rather than proportionately taller action potentials in one axon. Why?
options: Stimulus strength changes the genetic code each time
Stronger stimuli eliminate refractory periods
Individual action potentials are all-or-none events
Axons cannot transmit repeated signals
questions.answer: Individual action potentials are all-or-none events
questions.explanation: Stimulus intensity can be encoded by firing frequency while action-potential amplitude remains broadly fixed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: ATP becomes unavailable in a contracted muscle fibre. Why can cross-bridges remain attached?
options: Calcium immediately removes every cross-bridge
ATP binding is needed to detach myosin from actin
ATP destroys all actin filaments
Myosin is never attached during contraction
questions.answer: ATP binding is needed to detach myosin from actin
questions.explanation: ATP binding releases the myosin head from actin; depletion prevents normal detachment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A trait follows mitochondrial inheritance in the usual human model. Why can affected mothers pass it on while affected fathers generally do not?
options: Fathers have no mitochondria
Mitochondrial DNA is carried on the Y chromosome
Only sons receive egg cytoplasm
Most embryonic mitochondria come from the egg
questions.answer: Most embryonic mitochondria come from the egg
questions.explanation: The egg supplies nearly all zygotic cytoplasm and mitochondria in typical human inheritance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two genes yield parental allele combinations much more frequently than recombinants. What is most consistent with this?
options: They have no alleles
Every meiosis produces only recombinant chromosomes
They are linked on the same chromosome
They must be on different chromosomes
questions.answer: They are linked on the same chromosome
questions.explanation: Linked genes tend to be inherited together, with crossing over producing fewer recombinants when loci are close.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A human coding sequence is placed in bacteria, but no protein appears because the promoter is unsuitable. What does this illustrate?
options: A shared genetic code does not guarantee compatible expression signals
Bacteria cannot use any human coding sequence
Promoters are translated into all proteins
DNA bases have completely different chemical identities in bacteria
questions.answer: A shared genetic code does not guarantee compatible expression signals
questions.explanation: Transcription also requires host-recognised regulatory sequences, beyond codon compatibility.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A trait is heritable and improves survival but reduces reproduction enough to lower total offspring contribution. What determines its evolutionary success?
options: Survival duration alone
The organism's desire to pass it on
Body size alone
Its net contribution to reproductive fitness
questions.answer: Its net contribution to reproductive fitness
questions.explanation: Selection depends on genetic contribution to future generations, integrating survival and reproduction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A food chain lengthens while primary production is unchanged. Why does adding a top consumer limit the biomass it can support?
options: Longer chains create energy
Repeated trophic transfers reduce available energy
Energy is fully recycled at each feeding step
All producers stop photosynthesising
questions.answer: Repeated trophic transfers reduce available energy
questions.explanation: Energy transfer is inefficient, leaving progressively less available to additional consumer levels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two equal-sized reserves differ: one contains varied habitats and one is uniform. Why might the varied reserve support more species?
options: It offers more kinds of ecological niches
Area alone determines every species count
Every habitat supports identical communities
Variation eliminates resource limits
questions.answer: It offers more kinds of ecological niches
questions.explanation: Habitat heterogeneity can provide different resources and conditions supporting more species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A PCR negative control with no added template produces the target-sized band. What should be suspected first?
options: A perfectly valid negative control
A need to report every sample as negative
Contamination or another control failure
Proof that the target sequence arose by natural selection during PCR
questions.answer: Contamination or another control failure
questions.explanation: A target-like product in a no-template control undermines confidence that sample products reflect only their original DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A DNA insert and vector have compatible sticky ends but are not ligated. What is missing for stable recombinant DNA formation?
options: Removal of the vector's origin of replication
Covalent sealing of the sugar-phosphate backbone
Conversion of DNA into protein
Destruction of all complementary bases
questions.answer: Covalent sealing of the sugar-phosphate backbone
questions.explanation: Base pairing can align fragments, while ligase seals backbone nicks to stabilize the construct.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: Two DNA samples produce bands at the same position in a standard size-separating gel. What does this establish most directly?
options: Their complete base sequences must be identical
They came from the same organism
They code for the same protein
The detected fragments have similar lengths
questions.answer: The detected fragments have similar lengths
questions.explanation: Migration in this gel primarily reflects fragment length; different sequences can share the same length.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: A small isolated population grows numerically from only a few founders. Why can genetic vulnerability persist despite the larger headcount?
options: Larger population size instantly eliminates inbreeding history
Mutation recreates all lost alleles in one generation
Growth need not restore alleles lost at founding
Every new individual adds an entirely new set of alleles
questions.answer: Growth need not restore alleles lost at founding
questions.explanation: Population expansion can multiply existing genomes without restoring the original diversity lost in a bottleneck.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: At the same oxygen partial pressure, a right-shifted oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve indicates what?
options: Less oxygen bound and easier unloading
More oxygen bound and less unloading
No haemoglobin remains in the blood
Oxygen partial pressure has become zero
questions.answer: Less oxygen bound and easier unloading
questions.explanation: A right shift represents reduced haemoglobin affinity at a given oxygen partial pressure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: The medullary osmotic gradient is disrupted while ADH is present. What ability is especially impaired?
options: Filtering any blood plasma at the glomerulus necessarily
Reabsorbing any glucose anywhere
Making erythrocytes inside the collecting duct
Producing highly concentrated urine
questions.answer: Producing highly concentrated urine
questions.explanation: ADH increases water permeability, but water reabsorption still requires an appropriate osmotic gradient.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.q: During succession on bare rock, early colonisers help later plants establish. Which mechanism explains this facilitation?
options: All nutrients disappear permanently
Weathering and organic-matter accumulation improve substrate
Early colonisers create mature soil instantly
The rock already contains a complete forest root system
questions.answer: Weathering and organic-matter accumulation improve substrate
questions.explanation: Pioneer organisms can modify the substrate and add organic matter, supporting subsequent communities.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Hydrogen and oxygen react in a sealed vessel. Why is total mass unchanged despite new water forming?
options: The vessel creates replacement atoms
Atoms are rearranged rather than created or destroyed
Water has no mass
Gases lose mass when they react
questions.answer: Atoms are rearranged rather than created or destroyed
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions conserve atoms, so a closed system conserves mass.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two atoms have the same proton number but different neutron numbers. Why do they have similar chemical behaviour?
options: Their nuclear masses are identical
Neutrons determine all bonding
They must have different element names
They have the same electronic arrangement when neutral
questions.answer: They have the same electronic arrangement when neutral
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number and normally similar electron configurations.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An atom loses its outermost electron. What happens to its net charge?
options: It remains neutral
Its proton number decreases
It becomes more positive
It becomes more negative
questions.answer: It becomes more positive
questions.explanation: Removing negative charge makes the remaining particle more positive.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but the melt does. Why?
options: Melting allows ions to move
Melting changes ions into free protons
The solid contains no charged particles
Only molten salt contains atoms
questions.answer: Melting allows ions to move
questions.explanation: The solid's ions are fixed in a lattice; mobile ions carry charge in the liquid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why can a covalent molecule contain shared electrons without having a net charge?
options: Sharing removes the electrons' charge
Covalent bonds contain only neutrons
The molecule has no nucleus
The total proton and electron charges can balance
questions.answer: The total proton and electron charges can balance
questions.explanation: Bonding rearranges electrons, while a neutral molecule still has balanced positive and negative charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Ethanol mixes readily with water. Which interaction helps explain this?
options: Breaking every carbon-carbon bond
Hydrogen bonding between their molecules
Metallic bonding between all atoms
Formation of an ionic lattice
questions.answer: Hydrogen bonding between their molecules
questions.explanation: Ethanol's hydroxyl group can form hydrogen bonds with water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A sealed gas sample is compressed slowly at constant temperature. Why does its pressure rise?
options: Molecules strike the walls more frequently per unit area
Its molecules become heavier
Its average kinetic energy must rise
Its amount of gas doubles
questions.answer: Molecules strike the walls more frequently per unit area
questions.explanation: Reduced volume increases wall-collision frequency while mean kinetic energy remains temperature-dependent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why does breaking a covalent bond require energy?
options: Bond electrons have no energy
Breaking bonds always releases heat
Attractive interactions must be overcome
The atoms must always become new elements
questions.answer: Attractive interactions must be overcome
questions.explanation: Energy is required to separate atoms held together by an attractive bond.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Reactants and products remain at constant concentrations in a closed reacting system. What can still be happening?
options: No molecular collisions
Forward and reverse reactions at equal rates
Only the forward reaction
Only the reverse reaction
questions.answer: Forward and reverse reactions at equal rates
questions.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium has continuing reactions whose equal rates leave concentrations unchanged.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An acid is diluted with pure water. What usually happens to hydrogen-ion concentration?
options: It increases
It stays fixed at every dilution
It becomes negative
It decreases
questions.answer: It decreases
questions.explanation: Dilution spreads the acid over more solvent, reducing hydrogen-ion concentration in ordinary acidic solutions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Hydrochloric acid is mixed with just enough sodium hydroxide to neutralise it. What happens to H+ and OH-?
options: They both become electrons
They remain unchanged in equal large concentrations
They form water
They form sodium metal
questions.answer: They form water
questions.explanation: The net ionic neutralisation reaction combines hydrogen and hydroxide ions into water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A galvanic cell powers a lamp. What overall energy conversion occurs?
options: Chemical energy to electrical energy
Electrical energy to nuclear energy
Light energy to chemical energy only
Thermal energy to mass
questions.answer: Chemical energy to electrical energy
questions.explanation: A spontaneous redox reaction drives electron flow through the external circuit.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An electrolytic cell deposits metal at its cathode. What happens to the metal ions there?
options: They lose protons
They gain oxygen in every case
They become more positively charged
They gain electrons
questions.answer: They gain electrons
questions.explanation: Cathodic reduction supplies electrons to metal cations to form neutral metal.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two substances move different distances on the same chromatogram. What helps explain the separation?
options: Both substances necessarily have different colours
They interact differently with the mobile and stationary phases
One substance has ceased to contain atoms
The stationary phase must travel with one substance
questions.answer: They interact differently with the mobile and stationary phases
questions.explanation: Different relative affinities lead to different migration speeds through a chromatographic system.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A solid reactant is powdered before reacting with a solution. Why can reaction become faster?
options: More surface is available for collisions
The solid's atoms become smaller
The reaction enthalpy must change
The powder is necessarily a catalyst
questions.answer: More surface is available for collisions
questions.explanation: Increasing surface area exposes more reacting particles to the solution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two compounds have the same molecular formula but different atom connections. What does this imply?
options: Their molecular masses must differ
One cannot contain covalent bonds
They can have different properties
They must be the same substance
questions.answer: They can have different properties
questions.explanation: Structural isomers differ in connectivity, which can change physical and chemical behaviour.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Ethene reacts by adding atoms across its double bond. Why is addition possible?
options: Its carbon-carbon sigma bond must always vanish
The pi bond can be replaced by new sigma bonds
Carbon must gain a fifth bond
The carbon nuclei split
questions.answer: The pi bond can be replaced by new sigma bonds
questions.explanation: The pi component of the double bond can open while new sigma bonds form.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An aldehyde is oxidised under suitable conditions. Which functional group is commonly formed?
options: An alkene group
An ether group only
An amine group
A carboxylic acid group
questions.answer: A carboxylic acid group
questions.explanation: Oxidation of an aldehyde normally produces the corresponding carboxylic acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate and releases gas. What does this show?
options: Every carbon atom becomes gas
It is necessarily a strong mineral acid
Its acidic proton can react with carbonate
It contains no covalent bonds
questions.answer: Its acidic proton can react with carbonate
questions.explanation: Acid-carbonate reactions release carbon dioxide; a weak carboxylic acid can still produce this reaction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Many ethene molecules join to form a long chain. What happens to their carbon-carbon double bonds?
options: Their pi bonds are replaced as new links join monomers
Every carbon-carbon bond breaks completely
Each monomer releases water
The carbon atoms all become ions
questions.answer: Their pi bonds are replaced as new links join monomers
questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation opens the double bonds to form a saturated backbone without eliminating a small molecule.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Equal numbers of nitrogen and hydrogen molecules react to make ammonia. Which is left over if reaction goes to the stoichiometric limit?
options: Hydrogen
Both are fully consumed
Ammonia cannot form
Nitrogen
questions.answer: Nitrogen
questions.explanation: The reaction needs three hydrogen molecules per nitrogen molecule, so hydrogen is limiting in an equal-number mixture.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why is Na+ smaller than a neutral sodium atom?
options: Its nucleus has fewer neutrons necessarily
It has lost its outer electron shell
It has gained a proton
Its remaining electrons repel more strongly than before
questions.answer: It has lost its outer electron shell
questions.explanation: Losing the outermost electron removes the occupied third shell and strengthens attraction per remaining electron.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An element shows a large jump after its second ionisation energy. What does this suggest?
options: It has two relatively accessible valence electrons
It has two neutrons
It must be a noble gas
Its third electron is easier to remove
questions.answer: It has two relatively accessible valence electrons
questions.explanation: A large jump suggests that further removal enters a more strongly bound inner shell.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A molecule has several hydrogen atoms but only one proton NMR signal under suitable conditions. What does this suggest?
options: All carbon atoms must be absent
The sample must be ionic
The hydrogens occupy equivalent chemical environments
The molecule contains exactly one hydrogen atom
questions.answer: The hydrogens occupy equivalent chemical environments
questions.explanation: Equivalent proton environments share a chemical shift; signal count need not equal total hydrogen count.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why does water have an unusually high boiling point compared with H2S?
options: Water's O-H covalent bonds must break on boiling
Water forms a stronger extended hydrogen-bond network
Water has greater molecular mass
H2S has no electrons
questions.answer: Water forms a stronger extended hydrogen-bond network
questions.explanation: Boiling separates molecules; strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding raises the energy required.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A liquid evaporates into a much larger available gas volume. What usually happens to the substance's entropy?
options: It decreases necessarily
It is unchanged because mass is conserved
It becomes zero
It increases
questions.answer: It increases
questions.explanation: The gaseous state allows many more accessible arrangements and molecular positions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, increased pressure at fixed temperature favours which side?
options: Neither side because gases cannot equilibrate
Whichever side contains a catalyst
Ammonia
Nitrogen and hydrogen
questions.answer: Ammonia
questions.explanation: Compression favours the side with fewer gas molecules, which is the ammonia side.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Equal-concentration strong and weak monoprotic acids are compared. Why does the weak acid usually have higher pH?
options: A smaller fraction of its molecules ionises
Each molecule releases more protons
Its concentration must be zero
Its conjugate base is absent
questions.answer: A smaller fraction of its molecules ionises
questions.explanation: Partial ionisation gives a lower hydrogen-ion concentration than a fully dissociated acid of equal concentration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A little acid is added to a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base. Why does pH change only slightly?
options: The solvent loses all polarity
The weak acid becomes a strong acid
The added acid is not conserved
The conjugate base consumes much of the added H+
questions.answer: The conjugate base consumes much of the added H+
questions.explanation: The buffer's base component reacts with added hydrogen ions, limiting the concentration change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A species oxidises another reactant. What happens to that species itself?
options: It cannot change oxidation state
It is reduced
It is also oxidised necessarily
Its electrons vanish
questions.answer: It is reduced
questions.explanation: The oxidising agent accepts electrons and undergoes reduction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why is a salt bridge useful in a galvanic cell?
options: It allows ionic movement that prevents charge buildup
It sends electrons through the solution between electrodes
It replaces both electrodes
It makes the redox reaction nonspontaneous
questions.answer: It allows ionic movement that prevents charge buildup
questions.explanation: Ion migration maintains electrical neutrality as oxidation and reduction proceed in separate compartments.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A molecular-ion region has two peaks two mass units apart in approximately a three-to-one ratio. What evidence would this pattern support?
options: Two carbon atoms being removed successively
A molecule containing only hydrogen
One chlorine atom in the molecular ion
One fluorine atom with two equally common isotopes
questions.answer: One chlorine atom in the molecular ion
questions.explanation: The common chlorine isotopes differ by two mass units and occur in an approximately three-to-one abundance ratio.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A sample gives one spot in one solvent system. Why is that insufficient to prove absolute purity?
options: One spot means the sample has one atom
Different substances can coincide under those conditions
Pure substances always give two spots
Chromatography cannot separate any organic compounds
questions.answer: Different substances can coincide under those conditions
questions.explanation: Co-migration or undetected components can hide impurities, so one result provides limited rather than conclusive evidence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Doubling a reactant concentration doubles the initial rate while other conditions are fixed. What does this support?
options: Second-order dependence on that reactant
Zero-order dependence on that reactant
A negative reaction order necessarily
First-order dependence on that reactant
questions.answer: First-order dependence on that reactant
questions.explanation: A proportional rate change is consistent with a first-power concentration dependence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Why can a small temperature increase greatly accelerate a reaction?
options: The activation energy must rise
The equilibrium constant always becomes one
The fraction of collisions above activation energy increases
Every collision becomes successful
questions.answer: The fraction of collisions above activation energy increases
questions.explanation: The high-energy tail of the molecular energy distribution grows with temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A haloalkane forms an alkene by losing a hydrogen and a halogen from adjacent carbons. Which change distinguishes this process?
options: A carbon-carbon double bond forms
The carbon chain necessarily lengthens
An oxygen atom replaces the halogen
The molecule must become an ionic solid
questions.answer: A carbon-carbon double bond forms
questions.explanation: Elimination removes groups from neighbouring atoms and forms a pi bond.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Under controlled oxidation, a primary alcohol forms an aldehyde. Why is further oxidation often prevented by removing the aldehyde promptly?
options: Aldehydes cannot evaporate
The alcohol changes into a ketone when distilled
Removing product stops all molecular collisions
Aldehydes can oxidise further to acids
questions.answer: Aldehydes can oxidise further to acids
questions.explanation: Separating the aldehyde limits its continued exposure to the oxidising agent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A carbonyl carbon is attacked by a nucleophile. Why?
options: The carbonyl group is nonpolar
The C=O bond makes carbon partially positive
Carbon always carries a full positive charge
Oxygen donates all its electrons permanently
questions.answer: The C=O bond makes carbon partially positive
questions.explanation: Oxygen draws electron density toward itself, making carbon electrophilic.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An ester is hydrolysed under acidic conditions. Which products are expected?
options: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol
Two alkenes
An amine and an alkane
Only carbon dioxide and water
questions.answer: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis reverses ester formation by restoring an acid and alcohol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A student compares rates at two temperatures using different reactant concentrations too. What weakens the conclusion about temperature?
options: A rate comparison requires identical products only
Changing two variables automatically doubles the rate
Concentration is a confounding variable
Temperature can never affect rate
questions.answer: Concentration is a confounding variable
questions.explanation: Both temperature and concentration can affect rate, so their separate effects cannot be isolated in that comparison.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A product yield is lower than the stoichiometric maximum although the limiting reactant is consumed. Which explanation is possible?
options: The balanced equation must contain fractional atoms
Some reactant formed a side product
Mass conservation failed
The limiting reactant was unlimited
questions.answer: Some reactant formed a side product
questions.explanation: Consumption need not all follow the desired pathway; side reactions can lower isolated yield.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: First ionisation energy of boron is lower than beryllium's despite higher nuclear charge. Why?
options: Boron has fewer protons
Beryllium's outer shell is farther from the nucleus
Boron loses an inner 1s electron first
Boron loses a higher-energy 2p electron
questions.answer: Boron loses a higher-energy 2p electron
questions.explanation: Beryllium's filled 2s subshell is relatively stable, while boron's first removed electron is in 2p.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two resonance structures of an ion place charge on different atoms. What is the actual ion best described as?
options: A mixture of different compounds
An ion whose atoms exchange positions
One delocalised structure
A rapid physical oscillation between complete drawings
questions.answer: One delocalised structure
questions.explanation: Resonance drawings represent contributors to one electronic structure; atoms do not switch places.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A process has positive enthalpy change and positive entropy change. Under what condition can it be spontaneous?
options: At sufficiently high temperature
Only at absolute zero
At no temperature
At all temperatures necessarily
questions.answer: At sufficiently high temperature
questions.explanation: In Gibbs energy, the favourable T delta-S term can exceed the positive enthalpy change at high temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A reversible reaction equation is multiplied by two. How does its equilibrium constant change?
options: It doubles
It halves
It stays unchanged
It is squared
questions.answer: It is squared
questions.explanation: Multiplying all stoichiometric coefficients doubles the exponents in the equilibrium expression.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An inert gas is added to a reacting ideal-gas mixture at constant volume and temperature. What happens to equilibrium composition?
options: All reactants are consumed
It is unchanged
It always shifts toward fewer gas molecules
It always shifts toward more gas molecules
questions.answer: It is unchanged
questions.explanation: Reactant and product partial pressures stay unchanged at fixed volume and temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two buffers have the same acid-to-base ratio but different total concentrations. What differs most directly?
options: The more concentrated buffer resists added acid or base better
Only the dilute buffer has a definable pH
The concentrated buffer must have a radically different initial pH
Both can absorb unlimited acid
questions.answer: The more concentrated buffer resists added acid or base better
questions.explanation: Similar ratios give similar pH, but more buffer components provide greater capacity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two metal ions are present, and one reaches its precipitation threshold at a lower added anion concentration. What can careful addition achieve?
options: A change in both metals' atomic numbers
Removal of all anions without solids
Precipitation of one ion before the other
Equal precipitation of both at every concentration
questions.answer: Precipitation of one ion before the other
questions.explanation: Different solubility equilibria can allow selective precipitation before the second salt becomes saturated.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A cell reaction has positive standard cell potential. What follows about standard Gibbs-energy change?
options: It is independent of electron transfer
It is negative
It is positive
It must be zero
questions.answer: It is negative
questions.explanation: The relation delta-G-standard = -nFE-standard gives a negative Gibbs-energy change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Aqueous salt electrolysis is compared with molten-salt electrolysis. Why may the cathode products differ?
options: Ions have no charge in water
Molten salts contain no cations
Electrode reactions never depend on the medium
Water can compete for reduction in the aqueous cell
questions.answer: Water can compete for reduction in the aqueous cell
questions.explanation: Aqueous solutions introduce water as a possible reactant, changing which reduction occurs.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two proposed isomers have the same formula. One predicts fewer distinct proton environments through symmetry. How can NMR help choose between them?
options: Count each hydrogen as a separate signal automatically
Ignore symmetry because all protons have identical shifts
Compare the observed number and pattern of signals with each prediction
Select the isomer with the larger molecular mass
questions.answer: Compare the observed number and pattern of signals with each prediction
questions.explanation: Structural symmetry can make hydrogens equivalent; their predicted signal patterns can distinguish isomers of equal mass.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An observed rate law differs from the coefficients in the overall balanced equation. What is the best inference?
options: The overall equation need not represent one elementary step
The equation violates conservation of mass
The measured concentrations must be zero
All reactions have zero order
questions.answer: The overall equation need not represent one elementary step
questions.explanation: Overall stoichiometry does not determine rate-law exponents unless it describes an appropriate elementary step.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A first-order reactant starts at two different concentrations under identical conditions. How do its half-lives compare?
options: The more concentrated sample has twice the half-life
The less concentrated sample has twice the half-life
Half-life cannot be defined for a chemical reaction
They are equal
questions.answer: They are equal
questions.explanation: A first-order half-life depends on the rate constant, not the initial concentration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A catalyst shortens the time needed to reach equilibrium but leaves final composition unchanged at fixed temperature. Which claim is ruled out by the final result?
options: The uncatalysed reaction can reach the same equilibrium
The catalyst changed the equilibrium constant
The catalyst provides a faster pathway
The catalyst affects both reaction directions
questions.answer: The catalyst changed the equilibrium constant
questions.explanation: A changed equilibrium constant would change the equilibrium relation at that temperature; a catalyst changes kinetics instead.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A molecule has one tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups. What is possible?
options: A pair of nonsuperimposable mirror-image forms
Only one spatial arrangement under all conditions
A required carbon-carbon triple bond
A mandatory ionic lattice
questions.answer: A pair of nonsuperimposable mirror-image forms
questions.explanation: A tetrahedral stereogenic centre can give two enantiomeric arrangements.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Aniline is brominated readily compared with benzene under comparable conditions. Why?
options: Aniline is a saturated hydrocarbon
The benzene ring in aniline has no resonance
The amino group donates electron density into the ring
Nitrogen removes every pi electron
questions.answer: The amino group donates electron density into the ring
questions.explanation: The amino group's resonance donation activates the ring toward electrophilic substitution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A tertiary haloalkane reacts by an SN1 pathway in a suitable polar protic solvent. What most directly favours its first step?
options: Formation of a carbon atom with five permanent bonds
Stabilisation of the tertiary carbocation
Unhindered backside attack at the tertiary carbon
A required free radical
questions.answer: Stabilisation of the tertiary carbocation
questions.explanation: SN1 ionisation is favoured when the resulting carbocation is relatively stabilised.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Both fusion of suitable light nuclei and fission of suitable heavy nuclei can release energy. What common comparison explains this?
options: Both processes always increase total rest mass
Both processes convert every proton into a neutron
Products must have larger individual mass numbers in both cases
Products have greater binding energy per nucleon overall
questions.answer: Products have greater binding energy per nucleon overall
questions.explanation: Moving toward more tightly bound products lowers total rest energy; the difference can appear as released energy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A catalyst is added to a system already at equilibrium. Which combined statement is correct?
options: The equilibrium constant increases while temperature stays fixed
The reverse reaction stops
Both reaction rates increase but equilibrium composition is unchanged
Only the forward rate increases and yield rises
questions.answer: Both reaction rates increase but equilibrium composition is unchanged
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds both directions and does not change the equilibrium constant or equilibrium composition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An overall reaction uses A and B, but its measured rate depends only on A. Why need this not contradict the equation?
options: B may enter after the rate-determining step
B cannot be consumed in the reaction
The balanced equation must determine every rate exponent
A must be a catalyst rather than a reactant
questions.answer: B may enter after the rate-determining step
questions.explanation: Overall stoichiometry and kinetic order describe different aspects; a later step can consume B without controlling rate.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A school programme wants to identify nutritional needs before planning support. Which first step is most useful?
options: Assume all learners have identical needs
Collect relevant dietary and health information
Give every learner the same supplement
Judge nutritional status from appearance alone
questions.answer: Collect relevant dietary and health information
questions.explanation: Assessment establishes needs before an intervention is chosen.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: Two meals supply similar energy, but one includes a wider variety of nutritious foods. What additional advantage may it offer?
options: A broader range of essential nutrients
Guaranteed absence of every nutrient deficiency
Exactly the same micronutrient profile
No need to consider portion size
questions.answer: A broader range of essential nutrients
questions.explanation: Food variety can improve the range of nutrients supplied, while overall adequacy still needs assessment.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A person has adequate energy intake but insufficient iron. Which conclusion is justified?
options: All nutritional requirements must be met
Only low body weight can indicate malnutrition
Iron status can be inferred from height alone
Energy adequacy does not rule out micronutrient deficiency
questions.answer: Energy adequacy does not rule out micronutrient deficiency
questions.explanation: Energy and individual nutrient adequacy are different dimensions of nutrition.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A height measurement is taken once with shoes and once without. Why is the comparison weak?
options: The second measurement is necessarily correct
Shoes affect only body temperature
The measurement conditions changed
Height can never be measured reliably
questions.answer: The measurement conditions changed
questions.explanation: Consistent procedures are needed to distinguish real change from measurement differences.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A learner reports yesterday's food intake from memory. Which limitation should be considered?
options: One day's intake must equal usual intake
Some foods or portions may be forgotten
The method directly measures blood nutrients
The method cannot record any useful information
questions.answer: Some foods or portions may be forgotten
questions.explanation: Recall depends on memory and may not fully capture the day's consumption.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A practitioner uses a laboratory blood measurement alongside a diet history. What does the laboratory result add?
options: A biological measure that can complement reported intake
A complete record of every meal eaten
A direct measure of food affordability
A replacement for all clinical interpretation
questions.answer: A biological measure that can complement reported intake
questions.explanation: Biochemical data and dietary reports provide different, potentially complementary information.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: Why should a visible sign suspected of indicating deficiency be assessed by a qualified professional?
options: Every visible sign identifies exactly one nutrient
Appearance always gives the full diagnosis
Laboratory information is never relevant
Similar signs may have different causes
questions.answer: Similar signs may have different causes
questions.explanation: Clinical signs require context and appropriate interpretation rather than a single-cause assumption.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A family understands nutrition but has limited access to affordable varied food. What factor is highlighted?
options: A biochemical testing error
An inherited inability to choose food
The food environment
Lack of knowledge as the only cause
questions.answer: The food environment
questions.explanation: Availability and affordability can constrain choices independently of knowledge.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A snack label gives nutrients per serving, and a packet contains two servings. What matters when evaluating the whole packet?
options: The nutrient amount becomes unknown
The packet contains twice the listed per-serving amount
The listed amount already describes every packet size
Serving size affects only the packaging
questions.answer: The packet contains twice the listed per-serving amount
questions.explanation: Amounts per serving must be related to the quantity actually consumed.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: Why are repeated age-appropriate growth measurements more informative than one isolated measurement?
options: They show a pattern over time
They remove every source of measurement error
They establish the cause of all growth differences
They replace information about age
questions.answer: They show a pattern over time
questions.explanation: A series can reveal a trajectory that a single observation cannot establish.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A vaccine prepares immune recognition before exposure to a pathogen. Which description fits its purpose?
options: Immediate treatment of every existing infection
Replacement of all other preventive measures
Proof that exposure can never occur
Prevention through developing an immune response
questions.answer: Prevention through developing an immune response
questions.explanation: Vaccination prepares immune defences, though effectiveness and additional measures depend on the disease and vaccine.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: For an infection spread by contaminated hands, why can hand hygiene help?
options: It treats every established illness
It changes an inherited trait
It interrupts a route of transmission
It makes every surface permanently sterile
questions.answer: It interrupts a route of transmission
questions.explanation: Reducing contamination on hands can reduce transfer of relevant pathogens.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A health poster uses unfamiliar technical words for a general student audience. What would improve it?
options: Assume confusion means disinterest
Use clear language while preserving accuracy
Remove the explanation and keep only a slogan
Add more unexplained abbreviations
questions.answer: Use clear language while preserving accuracy
questions.explanation: Accessible wording helps the intended audience understand and use the information.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: Students practise recording health information in class. Which approach best protects privacy?
options: Use fictional cases or appropriately consented, protected data
Display named personal results to everyone
Collect extra sensitive details for curiosity
Share the records in an open group chat
questions.answer: Use fictional cases or appropriately consented, protected data
questions.explanation: Practice should minimise unnecessary disclosure and use appropriate permission and protection.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A school provides safe drinking-water points as well as information about hydration. What does the practical change address?
options: Only the wording of the information
A guarantee that all learners have identical fluid needs
A substitute for maintaining the water supply
An environmental barrier to acting on information
questions.answer: An environmental barrier to acting on information
questions.explanation: Facilities can make a healthy choice more accessible, complementing education.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A healthy-eating lesson recommends varied lunches, but the canteen offers only one option. Which change addresses the practical barrier?
options: Repeat the same message without changing availability
Assume knowledge automatically changes the menu
Measure only how many posters are displayed
Provide a broader range of suitable food choices
questions.answer: Provide a broader range of suitable food choices
questions.explanation: The environment must allow learners to act on the information they receive.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A report says ten students missed breakfast, but does not say how many were surveyed. What is needed to interpret how common this was?
options: The colour of the survey form
The number of questions about exercise
The total number of surveyed students
Only the students' names
questions.answer: The total number of surveyed students
questions.explanation: A count needs the relevant population or sample denominator to be interpreted as a proportion.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.topic: Nutrition information: nutrient versus energy claims
questions.q: A food is advertised as high in one vitamin. Why examine the rest of its nutritional information too?
options: Other nutrients cannot be measured once a vitamin is listed
One nutrient claim does not describe the whole nutritional profile
High vitamin content guarantees balanced nutrition by itself
The claim proves that the product has no energy
questions.answer: One nutrient claim does not describe the whole nutritional profile
questions.explanation: Nutritional evaluation considers the overall composition and context of consumption rather than one promoted feature.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: Two classes complete food diaries for different lengths of time. Why not compare their total recorded food intake directly?
options: The recording durations differ
Longer diaries always show poorer diets
Total intake is independent of time observed
A diary can record only one meal
questions.answer: The recording durations differ
questions.explanation: A fair comparison needs a common time basis as well as comparable reporting methods.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A presenter asks learners to explain a label in their own words after a lesson. What does this check more directly than attendance?
options: Whether they were physically in the room only
Whether every future food choice will change
Whether the label meets all legal requirements
Whether they can interpret the information
questions.answer: Whether they can interpret the information
questions.explanation: Explaining the meaning gives evidence of understanding that presence alone cannot provide.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A food diary suggests low intake, but another assessment gives an inconsistent picture. What is the best response?
options: Diagnose from the diary alone
Assume every assessment measures the same thing
Investigate the discrepancy using complementary evidence
Discard whichever result is less convenient
questions.answer: Investigate the discrepancy using complementary evidence
questions.explanation: Different methods have distinct limitations, and inconsistency calls for investigation.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A scale reads 2 kg even before anyone steps on it. What issue should be corrected?
options: A difference in height reference charts
A zero offset that biases measurements
Random variation in each person's diet
A change in everyone's true mass
questions.answer: A zero offset that biases measurements
questions.explanation: A nonzero baseline introduces systematic measurement error.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: Someone changes meals because they know each meal will be recorded. How can this affect a food diary?
options: Recorded intake may differ from habitual intake
The diary becomes a biochemical measurement
All memory error is eliminated
The diary necessarily overestimates every nutrient
questions.answer: Recorded intake may differ from habitual intake
questions.explanation: Recording can change the behaviour being measured, not just document it.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: Why should an adolescent's BMI be interpreted using an appropriate age-related reference rather than adult cut-offs alone?
options: BMI has no relationship to height
Every adolescent has the same body composition
Adult cut-offs automatically account for all growth stages
Growth and age affect its interpretation
questions.answer: Growth and age affect its interpretation
questions.explanation: Adolescent growth requires an age-appropriate framework and broader clinical context.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A single laboratory value is outside a reference range. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: It identifies every aspect of nutritional status
It makes further assessment unnecessary
It warrants interpretation with clinical and other relevant information
It proves one specific dietary cause
questions.answer: It warrants interpretation with clinical and other relevant information
questions.explanation: A single value can have multiple influences and should not be treated as a complete diagnosis.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A researcher wants usual intake but samples only festival days. What is the main problem?
options: Long-term intake is determined by one event
Those days may not represent routine eating
The food cannot be recorded accurately in principle
Every festival meal has the same nutrients
questions.answer: Those days may not represent routine eating
questions.explanation: Unusual occasions can distort an estimate of habitual intake.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A campaign improves nutrition knowledge but meal choices barely change because healthier options remain unaffordable. What should planners reconsider?
options: Whether the intervention addresses the actual access barrier
Whether knowledge scores should replace all outcomes
Whether cost can be ignored
Whether participants should simply be blamed
questions.answer: Whether the intervention addresses the actual access barrier
questions.explanation: Information alone may not overcome affordability constraints.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A screening result suggests increased risk. What should a health-education explanation emphasise?
options: A positive screen proves the condition
A negative screen rules out every possible condition
Screening replaces qualified evaluation in all cases
Screening identifies a need for further assessment, not a definitive diagnosis by itself
questions.answer: Screening identifies a need for further assessment, not a definitive diagnosis by itself
questions.explanation: Screening and diagnosis have different purposes and levels of certainty.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A factor is associated with a higher probability of disease. What does this mean for an individual?
options: No unexposed person can develop it
The factor alone supplies a diagnosis
Risk may be increased without disease being inevitable
Every exposed person will develop the disease
questions.answer: Risk may be increased without disease being inevitable
questions.explanation: Risk describes probability, not a guaranteed outcome for each person.

questions.subject: Health Sciences
questions.q: A school combines hand hygiene, ventilation and illness reporting where appropriate. What is the rationale?
options: Layering guarantees that no infection will ever occur
Different measures can address different parts of transmission risk
Every measure has exactly the same mechanism
One measure makes all others useless
questions.answer: Different measures can address different parts of transmission risk
