questions.q: Which prediction best distinguishes 'the fault is caused by heat' from 'the fault is random'?
options: The device has a serial number
A fault is inconvenient
Under controlled testing, faults rise when temperature rises
The device sometimes fails
questions.answer: Under controlled testing, faults rise when temperature rises
questions.explanation: A controlled temperature-dependent change is more discriminating than an observation both explanations allow.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: An advert compares this year's total sales with last year's sales per shop. What is the problem?
options: It proves every shop improved
It compares different measures
It necessarily understates growth
Both quantities always have the same unit and basis
questions.answer: It compares different measures
questions.explanation: Total sales and average sales per shop use different denominators and are not directly comparable.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A claim is defended only by saying nobody has disproved it. What is missing?
options: Positive evidence supporting the claim
A longer title
Proof that all alternatives are impossible before any inquiry
A requirement that the claim be accepted
questions.answer: Positive evidence supporting the claim
questions.explanation: Absence of disproof is not sufficient affirmative evidence for a claim.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Three news reports repeat the same anonymous original story. Why may they count as only one evidential source?
options: Three reports are always independent
Repetition guarantees truth
Anonymous reports cannot contain any facts
They may share a single underlying claim
questions.answer: They may share a single underlying claim
questions.explanation: Multiple publications do not provide independent corroboration when all depend on the same source.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A school reports fewer absences after narrowing what counts as an absence. What must be checked before claiming attendance improved?
options: Whether the old report used a larger font
Whether every student changed schools
Whether rates remain lower using a consistent definition
Whether the new term is shorter
questions.answer: Whether rates remain lower using a consistent definition
questions.explanation: A measurement-definition change can produce an apparent improvement without a behavioural change.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A trial shows modest benefit for one age group in one setting. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The setting is irrelevant to interpretation
Benefit was observed for that tested group and setting
The method works for everyone everywhere
The method can never help other groups
questions.answer: Benefit was observed for that tested group and setting
questions.explanation: The conclusion should match the population and conditions actually studied.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: School A has a higher pass rate than B in both a difficult and an easy course. Could B still have the higher overall rate?
options: Yes, if B has a much larger share in the easy course
No, subgroup superiority always fixes the overall order
Yes, but only if pass rates exceed 100 percent
No, because courses cannot have different sizes
questions.answer: Yes, if B has a much larger share in the easy course
questions.explanation: Different weighting of easier and harder courses can reverse an aggregate comparison.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A quantity falls by half, then grows by half of its new value. Why does it not return to its start?
options: The two percentages have different units
Halving and increasing are the same operation
The second change must be negative
The increase uses a smaller base
questions.answer: The increase uses a smaller base
questions.explanation: After the fall, the same percentage represents a smaller absolute amount.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A 20-percent solution is mixed only with pure water. Which proposed final concentration is infeasible without evaporation?
options: 10 percent
5 percent
25 percent
15 percent
questions.answer: 25 percent
questions.explanation: Adding water can dilute the solution but cannot raise its solute proportion.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A driver travels one half of a route at 30 km/h. Could any finite speed on the other half make the overall average 60 km/h?
options: Yes; matching 30 km/h works
No; the first half already uses the entire time budget
Yes; 60 km/h is enough
Yes; 90 km/h always works
questions.answer: No; the first half already uses the entire time budget
questions.explanation: At 30 km/h, half the distance consumes the time allowed for the entire route at 60 km/h.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A firm's average cost per unit is currently 10. Producing one extra unit costs 6 and changes no other cost. What happens to average cost?
options: It decreases
It increases
It stays exactly 10
It becomes exactly 6
questions.answer: It decreases
questions.explanation: An additional observation below the current mean pulls the mean downward.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two branches report percentage growth. Why is averaging those percentages without weights potentially misleading?
options: Growth percentages can never be compared
All branches must have equal growth
The higher percentage always contributes more revenue
Their starting sales may differ
questions.answer: Their starting sales may differ
questions.explanation: Aggregate growth depends on absolute changes relative to total starting sales, which requires baseline weights.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A model's length scale doubles while its density halves. How does its mass change for similar three-dimensional shapes?
options: It stays unchanged
It becomes eight times as large
It becomes four times as large
It doubles
questions.answer: It becomes four times as large
questions.explanation: Volume rises eightfold and density halves, giving four times the mass.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Plan A has a higher fixed charge but a lower cost per use than plan B. What pattern is possible as use increases?
options: They must have equal total charges at all usage levels
B is cheaper initially, but A becomes cheaper after a threshold
A must always be cheaper
B must always be cheaper
questions.answer: B is cheaper initially, but A becomes cheaper after a threshold
questions.explanation: The lower marginal cost can eventually offset A's larger fixed charge.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two positive quantities have a fixed sum. As their difference decreases toward zero, what happens to their product?
options: It increases toward a maximum
It decreases toward zero
It remains constant
It becomes negative
questions.answer: It increases toward a maximum
questions.explanation: For a fixed sum, the product is greatest when the quantities are equal.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two equal-sized square plots have side lengths 2 and 4. Why is their average area not the area of a square with the average side length?
options: Averages cannot apply to lengths
Both squares have equal area
The average side is not between the two sides
Squaring is nonlinear
questions.answer: Squaring is nonlinear
questions.explanation: The mean of squared values differs from the square of the mean when the values vary.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A board begins with an even number of lit lamps. Each move toggles exactly two distinct lamps. Can it end with exactly one lit lamp?
options: Yes; only the positions matter
No; the number of lit lamps never changes at all
No; parity of the lit count is preserved
Yes; one move always suffices
questions.answer: No; parity of the lit count is preserved
questions.explanation: A move changes the count by minus two, zero or plus two, preserving evenness.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Six objects are placed into five boxes. What is unavoidable?
options: A box contains all six objects
At least one box contains two or more objects
Every box contains an object
Exactly one box contains two objects
questions.answer: At least one box contains two or more objects
questions.explanation: If every box held at most one object, only five objects could be placed.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: An integer squared is claimed to leave remainder 2 when divided by 4. What can be concluded?
options: The claim is impossible
The integer must be odd
The integer must be even
The integer must be negative
questions.answer: The claim is impossible
questions.explanation: Even squares are divisible by four, and odd squares leave remainder one.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Why is the product of any three consecutive integers divisible by 6?
options: Every factor is divisible by 6
Their sum must be 6
All three factors are odd
One factor is even and one is divisible by 3
questions.answer: One factor is even and one is divisible by 3
questions.explanation: Consecutive triples include a multiple of three and at least one even integer.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A password uses four distinct digits from a set of four. If the first digit is fixed, what happens to the arrangement count compared with unrestricted first digits?
options: It stays unchanged
It becomes four times larger
It becomes one quarter as large
It becomes one half as large
questions.answer: It becomes one quarter as large
questions.explanation: The four possible first digits have equal numbers of completions, so fixing one selects one quarter.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two identical trophies are distributed to two different people from a group. Why would counting the two recipients in order overcount?
options: The number of people becomes irrelevant
Swapping trophy assignments does not create a distinct outcome
The recipients must be the same person
There are no possible distributions
questions.answer: Swapping trophy assignments does not create a distinct outcome
questions.explanation: Identical trophies make the recipient pair unordered; each pair would be counted twice by order.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Three independent components each have a chance to fail. Why is 'at least one fails' often easiest to calculate using a complement?
options: Subtract the probability that all work from one
Add each failure probability without checking overlaps
Multiply the probabilities that exactly one works
Assume failures are mutually exclusive
questions.answer: Subtract the probability that all work from one
questions.explanation: The complement of at least one failure is no failures, whose probability is a product under independence.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A fair die is rolled, and you learn the result is even. Which information determines the chance it exceeds four?
options: All six outcomes remain in the conditional sample
The die must be rolled again
Odd outcomes become more likely
Only the even outcomes 2, 4 and 6 remain possible
questions.answer: Only the even outcomes 2, 4 and 6 remain possible
questions.explanation: Conditioning removes outcomes inconsistent with the information, leaving one favourable outcome among three.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Ten tickets each have the same winning probability, but their outcomes may be dependent. Which can still be found by adding individual winning probabilities?
options: Probability that at least one wins
Variance of the winning count without more information
Expected number of winning tickets
Probability that every ticket wins
questions.answer: Expected number of winning tickets
questions.explanation: Linearity of expectation applies even when the ticket outcomes are dependent.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A fair coin is tossed independently many times. Why does a past imbalance not force compensating future tosses?
options: The past outcomes must be erased
Future probabilities stay fixed even though long-run proportions may stabilise
The coin changes its fairness after each toss
Long-run balance requires exact alternation
questions.answer: Future probabilities stay fixed even though long-run proportions may stabilise
questions.explanation: Relative frequencies can approach one half without the coin correcting earlier outcomes.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: If A occurs, B occurs; if B occurs, C occurs. C did not occur. What follows?
options: Neither A nor B occurred
A occurred but B did not
B occurred but A did not
A and B both occurred
questions.answer: Neither A nor B occurred
questions.explanation: Absence of C rules out B, and absence of B then rules out A.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A badge is issued if and only if training is completed. Someone has no badge. What follows under the exact rule?
options: They completed training but lost their place in line necessarily
Training may be complete because the rule is only one-way
Everyone has a badge
They have not completed training
questions.answer: They have not completed training
questions.explanation: The biconditional makes training completion sufficient for a badge and badge absence rules it out.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: It is false that both the door and window are open. What is guaranteed?
options: Exactly one is open
The door is closed specifically
At least one of them is not open
Both are closed
questions.answer: At least one of them is not open
questions.explanation: Negating a conjunction gives an inclusive disjunction of the negated components.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Exactly one of A and B is true, and exactly one of B and C is true. How are A and C related?
options: They must have opposite truth values
They have the same truth value
They must both be true
They must both be false
questions.answer: They have the same truth value
questions.explanation: Both are the opposite of B, so they match each other.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: All A are B and all C are B. Both A and C are nonempty. Must A and C overlap?
options: No; they may occupy separate parts of B
Yes; sharing a larger set guarantees overlap
Yes; every A must be C
No; overlap is impossible
questions.answer: No; they may occupy separate parts of B
questions.explanation: Two subsets of the same set may intersect or be disjoint.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Some A are B, and every B is C. What is guaranteed?
options: Every A is C
Every C is A
No A is C
Some A are C
questions.answer: Some A are C
questions.explanation: The known A members that are B must also be C.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Which situation disproves 'If a card is red, it has an even number'?
options: A blue card with an odd number
A red card with an even number
A red card with an odd number
A blue card with an even number
questions.answer: A red card with an odd number
questions.explanation: A conditional fails only when its condition is true and its required consequence is false.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Cards show a colour on one side and a number on the other. To test 'red implies even', which visible types need checking?
options: Only even-number cards
Red cards and odd-number cards
Red cards and even-number cards
Only blue cards
questions.answer: Red cards and odd-number cards
questions.explanation: Red cards may hide odd numbers, and odd cards may hide red; either would violate the rule.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Which is the exact negation of 'Every applicant submitted at least one reference'?
options: At least one applicant submitted no references
No applicant submitted references
Every applicant submitted two references
Most applicants submitted no references
questions.answer: At least one applicant submitted no references
questions.explanation: Negating a universal claim requires at least one case that fails its stated condition.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A always tells the truth; B always lies. One says, 'I am B.' Who could say this consistently?
options: Only A
Only B
Both people
Neither person
questions.answer: Neither person
questions.explanation: A would make a false identity claim, while B would make a true one; both violate their rules.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A precedes C and B precedes C, but no relation between A and B is given. Which order is forced?
options: B is before A
A and B must occur simultaneously
C is after both A and B
A is before B
questions.answer: C is after both A and B
questions.explanation: The constraints place C after each prerequisite without ordering the prerequisites themselves.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two independent jobs need the same single specialist for their full duration. Why can their times not overlap despite logical independence?
options: The specialist can always perform both simultaneously
Resource capacity adds a scheduling constraint
Independence means they require no worker
The shorter job must be cancelled
questions.answer: Resource capacity adds a scheduling constraint
questions.explanation: Lack of task dependencies does not remove a shared exclusive-resource conflict.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A project has a six-day path and a four-day parallel path. The four-day path is shortened by one day. What happens to total time if nothing else changes?
options: It remains six days
It falls to five days
It falls to three days
It rises to seven days
questions.answer: It remains six days
questions.explanation: The unchanged longest path still controls completion time.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A task on a noncritical path has two days of slack. It is delayed one day with no further effects. What follows?
options: The project must be a day late
Every other task must stop
Slack becomes three days
The overall deadline can remain unchanged
questions.answer: The overall deadline can remain unchanged
questions.explanation: A delay within available slack need not extend the project's completion date.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Five distinct people sit around an unlabelled round table. Rotations count as identical, but reflections do not. What can fix rotational overcounting?
options: Remove two people from the table
Count every rotation as a new seating
Hold one chosen person in a fixed reference position
Treat everyone as identical
questions.answer: Hold one chosen person in a fixed reference position
questions.explanation: Fixing one person anchors the arrangement while preserving distinct relative orders.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A list says someone is ranked second, but ties are allowed. Why can their position in a physical queue be uncertain?
options: Rank tells the person's age
Several people may share a rank
Second rank always means exactly one person is ahead
Ties cannot affect ordering
questions.answer: Several people may share a rank
questions.explanation: Rank labels do not necessarily correspond one-to-one with individual positions when ties occur.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two tasks use the same room: one ends at 10:00 and another starts at 10:00. They need a ten-minute reset between them. Is the schedule feasible as stated?
options: No, it lacks the required reset interval
Yes, because their task times do not overlap
Yes, because reset time counts as zero
Only if both tasks are cancelled
questions.answer: No, it lacks the required reset interval
questions.explanation: Feasibility must include setup or transition time, not just task durations.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A must precede B, B must precede C, and C must precede A in a one-time schedule. What is the problem?
options: The tasks must have equal durations
The order is uniquely A, B, C
Only the longest task matters
The dependencies form a cycle
questions.answer: The dependencies form a cycle
questions.explanation: A directed precedence cycle cannot be satisfied by a finite sequential order.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Three people have distinct ages. You know A is older than B. What additional fact is sufficient to identify the oldest?
options: B is younger than C
C is not the youngest
C is younger than A
C is older than B
questions.answer: C is younger than A
questions.explanation: Knowing C is below A puts both others below A; the other facts leave A versus C unresolved.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A schedule requires at least two breaks. Someone inserts three. Which conclusion is justified?
options: All other scheduling requirements are satisfied automatically
The minimum-break requirement is satisfied
The schedule violates the rule because three exceeds two
Exactly two breaks occurred
questions.answer: The minimum-break requirement is satisfied
questions.explanation: At least two permits three, but says nothing about other constraints.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A proposal says replacing paper forms with online forms will reduce total work. Which finding most threatens its assumption?
options: Online submissions still require manual re-entry plus new support tasks
Users like the online colours
Some staff prefer screens
The online form has a title
questions.answer: Online submissions still require manual re-entry plus new support tasks
questions.explanation: If the new process preserves old work and adds tasks, the assumed workload reduction may fail.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Students with more tutoring have lower average marks. Why might concluding tutoring harms performance be mistaken?
options: Tutoring cannot ever have an effect
Low marks necessarily cause every tutoring session
The marks must be incorrect
Students struggling most may seek more tutoring
questions.answer: Students struggling most may seek more tutoring
questions.explanation: Selection into tutoring can reverse the apparent causal interpretation of the association.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: To estimate whether a programme improved outcomes, what missing comparison is central?
options: Whether participants remember the starting date
Whether the programme had a logo
What would have happened to comparable participants without it
Whether its name sounds positive
questions.answer: What would have happened to comparable participants without it
questions.explanation: Causal impact is the difference between observed outcomes and a credible no-programme counterfactual.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A trial's control group starts using the treatment too. What can happen to the estimated difference?
options: The treatment is proven ineffective
It may be diluted toward no difference
It must become infinitely large
Randomisation removes the issue automatically
questions.answer: It may be diluted toward no difference
questions.explanation: If controls receive the treatment's benefits, between-group contrast can shrink.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Why can blinding outcome assessors improve a trial even when participants cannot be blinded?
options: It reduces assessment influenced by knowledge of treatment assignment
It guarantees the treatment works
It makes all outcomes objective automatically
It replaces the need for a comparison group
questions.answer: It reduces assessment influenced by knowledge of treatment assignment
questions.explanation: Blinded assessment limits expectation-related judgement differences between groups.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A researcher tests many unrelated hypotheses and reports only the significant one. What is a concern?
options: More tests guarantee every result is true
Unreported tests cannot affect interpretation
Significance proves practical importance
A chance finding may be presented as unusually strong evidence
questions.answer: A chance finding may be presented as unusually strong evidence
questions.explanation: Searching many tests raises the chance of an apparently positive result unless multiplicity is addressed.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A business study examines only firms still operating. What can be missed?
options: The existence of businesses
All measures of present revenue
Patterns among firms that failed
Any information about surviving firms
questions.answer: Patterns among firms that failed
questions.explanation: Excluding failures can distort conclusions about which past practices predict success.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A medical observational study finds sicker patients received a stronger treatment and had worse outcomes. What must be considered?
options: All patients were randomly assigned
Initial illness severity may explain both treatment choice and outcome
The treatment is certainly harmful
Severity is irrelevant once treatment is recorded
questions.answer: Initial illness severity may explain both treatment choice and outcome
questions.explanation: Treatment selection based on severity confounds a simple treated-versus-untreated comparison.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A policy applies to one region but not a similar neighbouring region. What strengthens a causal comparison of later changes?
options: Evidence that their pre-policy trends were similar
Different outcome definitions in each region
Ignoring all earlier data
Choosing only the most favourable month
questions.answer: Evidence that their pre-policy trends were similar
questions.explanation: Comparable prior trends support, though do not guarantee, the untreated region as a counterfactual.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A plausible mechanism explains why an intervention could work. Why is outcome evidence still needed?
options: Mechanisms are always false
Outcomes cannot be observed
Any plausible story proves effectiveness
A plausible mechanism does not establish the real-world net effect
questions.answer: A plausible mechanism does not establish the real-world net effect
questions.explanation: Other processes, implementation limits or opposing effects may prevent the predicted benefit.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A rare event triggers an alarm that also has occasional false positives. Why can many alarms be false even when the alarm is fairly accurate?
options: Rare events cannot trigger alarms
All alarms must be false
Non-events are far more common
Accuracy makes base rates irrelevant
questions.answer: Non-events are far more common
questions.explanation: A large number of non-events can generate many false positives despite a small false-positive rate.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A sensor repeatedly reports almost the same value, but calibration shows a fixed offset. What does this indicate?
options: Random variation is the only issue
High precision with systematic inaccuracy
Low precision with perfect accuracy
Both precision and accuracy are guaranteed
questions.answer: High precision with systematic inaccuracy
questions.explanation: Closely clustered readings are precise, while the offset makes them inaccurate.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A school rewards number of books borrowed as a measure of reading. Why could the metric improve without reading increasing?
options: Students may borrow more without reading more
Borrowing and reading are identical acts
Metrics cannot influence behaviour
Every borrowed book must be fully read
questions.answer: Students may borrow more without reading more
questions.explanation: A proxy can be optimized in ways that do not improve the underlying goal.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A hospital's infection rate falls while its infection count stays fixed. What change alone could explain this?
options: Fewer patients were included
The same denominator was used
Every infection became more severe
More patients were included in the denominator
questions.answer: More patients were included in the denominator
questions.explanation: A fixed numerator divided by a larger denominator produces a lower rate.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two unbiased surveys use the same method, but one has a much larger random sample. What is generally expected?
options: Guaranteed removal of all systematic bias
A necessarily different population mean
Less sampling uncertainty in the larger survey
No possible error in the larger survey
questions.answer: Less sampling uncertainty in the larger survey
questions.explanation: Larger random samples generally reduce sampling variability but do not eliminate bias or uncertainty.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two measurements share the same faulty calibration reference. Why does agreement between them give limited reassurance?
options: Their errors must cancel
They can share the same systematic error
Agreement always proves truth
Independent calibration is irrelevant
questions.answer: They can share the same systematic error
questions.explanation: Common-source errors can make multiple readings agree while all are wrong.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Average performance improves after the lowest-performing participants leave. What cannot be inferred from the average alone?
options: That the remaining individuals improved
That the group's membership changed
That low performers left
That the reported average rose
questions.answer: That the remaining individuals improved
questions.explanation: A composition change can raise the group average without any person's performance changing.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A report says risk fell by 50 percent. Why is the original risk needed to judge the absolute reduction?
options: Relative reductions are always fraudulent
Absolute reduction always equals fifty percentage points
The original risk must be one hundred percent
Half of a tiny risk differs greatly from half of a large risk
questions.answer: Half of a tiny risk differs greatly from half of a large risk
questions.explanation: The baseline converts relative change into an absolute probability difference.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A forecast gives a single expected value for a highly variable outcome. What additional information most improves planning?
options: More decimal places without new data
A guarantee based only on confidence of tone
A plausible range or distribution of outcomes
A more decorative chart title
questions.answer: A plausible range or distribution of outcomes
questions.explanation: Planning needs the spread and possible extremes, not just a central estimate.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A prediction model is evaluated using information that would only become available after the event. What is wrong?
options: The number of features no longer matters
The evaluation overstates usable predictive performance
Later information makes all forecasts fairer
The model must be causal
questions.answer: The evaluation overstates usable predictive performance
questions.explanation: Real-time prediction cannot use future information, so leakage makes the test unrealistically easy.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A labelled solid is rotated without reflection. Which relation among labels must remain unchanged?
options: Which faces share an edge
Which label appears uppermost
Which face points toward the viewer
Which side of the page holds each label
questions.answer: Which faces share an edge
questions.explanation: Rigid rotation preserves adjacency while changing orientation to the observer.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A right-handed screw shape is mirrored. Why cannot rotation alone generally restore its original handedness?
options: Rotation changes every length
All reflected objects are larger
The mirrored object must be flat
Reflection changes chirality while rotation preserves it
questions.answer: Reflection changes chirality while rotation preserves it
questions.explanation: Chiral objects and their mirror images cannot be superimposed by rigid rotation alone.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A cube face shares edges with four other faces. What relationship has it with the one remaining face?
options: They are the same face
They meet along one edge
They are opposite
They share two edges
questions.answer: They are opposite
questions.explanation: Each cube face has four adjacent faces and one opposite face.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A plane cuts a sphere away from its centre but still through its interior. How does the section compare with a central section?
options: It has the same radius necessarily
It is a smaller circle
It is a larger circle
It is a triangle
questions.answer: It is a smaller circle
questions.explanation: The section radius decreases as the cutting plane moves away from the sphere's centre.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A straight route is blocked by a wall with one opening. Why might the shortest allowed path change when the opening moves?
options: The feasible crossing point changes
Straight lines stop being shortest between free points
Distance becomes independent of endpoints
All routes become equal
questions.answer: The feasible crossing point changes
questions.explanation: An obstacle constrains allowed paths, so the location of its opening affects the optimum.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two rectangles have the same perimeter but different side proportions. Which has greater area as the proportions approach a square?
options: The more elongated rectangle
Their areas must be equal
The one with the smaller width always
The more nearly square rectangle
questions.answer: The more nearly square rectangle
questions.explanation: At fixed perimeter, balancing the side lengths increases their product.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A box's volume exceeds an object's volume. Why does that not guarantee the object fits?
options: The box must be spherical
A smaller volume always means greater width
Its dimensions or shape may prevent placement
Volume never affects fit
questions.answer: Its dimensions or shape may prevent placement
questions.explanation: Volume is necessary context but does not capture all geometric dimension constraints.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A shape is reflected in two perpendicular lines through one point. What transformation results?
options: No change for every shape
A half-turn about their intersection
A single reflection in either line
A doubling of scale
questions.answer: A half-turn about their intersection
questions.explanation: Two perpendicular reflections compose to a rotation through twice the angle between the lines.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two labels lie at positions exchanged by a shape's symmetry. Without any external reference, what can that imply?
options: The geometry alone may not distinguish their roles
The labels must have identical spelling
The shape has no dimensions
Every possible label position is equivalent
questions.answer: The geometry alone may not distinguish their roles
questions.explanation: A symmetry can make positions structurally equivalent unless extra information breaks it.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A simple closed curve is drawn on a plane. A path starts inside and ends outside without touching the curve's endpoints, since it has none. What must the path do?
options: Remain entirely inside
Remain entirely outside
Avoid the boundary necessarily
Cross the boundary at least once
questions.answer: Cross the boundary at least once
questions.explanation: Moving from interior to exterior requires passing through the separating boundary.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two proposed rules agree on every observed term but predict different next terms. What observation would distinguish them?
options: The rule with fewer written letters alone
Repeating the existing terms unchanged
The next term at which their predictions differ
Another observation on which they agree
questions.answer: The next term at which their predictions differ
questions.explanation: A discriminating test targets a point where competing predictions diverge.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A puzzle move always preserves the sum of two counters. A target state has a different sum from the start. What follows?
options: The move rule must change the sum after a while
The target is unreachable under those moves
Enough moves always reach it
Only an odd number of moves reaches it
questions.answer: The target is unreachable under those moves
questions.explanation: An invariant cannot change, so a target violating it is inaccessible.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A positive sequence adds a fixed positive fraction of its current value each step. Why do its absolute increments grow?
options: Each increment is based on a larger current value
The fraction changes automatically
The sequence is arithmetic
The first term must be zero
questions.answer: Each increment is based on a larger current value
questions.explanation: Constant proportional growth generates increasing absolute additions as the base grows.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A device returns to its initial state every four steps. What can be concluded after fourteen steps from its start?
options: Its state matches the start necessarily
Its state matches one step
Its state cannot repeat
Its state matches that after two steps
questions.answer: Its state matches that after two steps
questions.explanation: Fourteen consists of three complete cycles plus two steps.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A code stores a check value calculated from its data. Why can that help detect some errors?
options: The data no longer need transmission
Check values make random noise impossible
A changed message may no longer agree with the check value
Every error is guaranteed to be corrected
questions.answer: A changed message may no longer agree with the check value
questions.explanation: Redundant constraints can reveal inconsistencies, though their detection power depends on the scheme.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A code maps two different original symbols to the same encoded symbol with no extra context. What is lost?
options: The existence of the original alphabet
Unique decoding
The ability to encode either symbol
All message length
questions.answer: Unique decoding
questions.explanation: A shared code output cannot identify which of the two original symbols produced it.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A sorting rule works on all tested lists, which happened to be already sorted. What is the strongest next test?
options: An unsorted list chosen to challenge the rule
Another identical sorted list
An empty description with no input
A longer title for the rule
questions.answer: An unsorted list chosen to challenge the rule
questions.explanation: A test should exercise the unverified behaviour rather than repeat cases that do not challenge it.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Every neighbouring pair in a numerical list is in ascending order. What follows for the whole list?
options: Only the first pair is ordered
The last value must be smallest
The values must be consecutive integers
The list is ascending
questions.answer: The list is ascending
questions.explanation: Transitivity of numerical order extends the pairwise condition through the entire list.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Choosing the best-looking immediate option gives a poor final outcome in a constrained puzzle. What does this demonstrate?
options: The immediate option was necessarily measured incorrectly
Future constraints never matter
Local improvement need not yield a global optimum
All optimization is impossible
questions.answer: Local improvement need not yield a global optimum
questions.explanation: An early choice can restrict later possibilities, making local and global objectives diverge.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: An algorithm decreases a nonnegative integer by at least one on every continuing step. Why must it terminate?
options: The initial integer must be one
The integer cannot decrease indefinitely while staying nonnegative
Every algorithm terminates
The steps must all take equal time
questions.answer: The integer cannot decrease indefinitely while staying nonnegative
questions.explanation: A strictly decreasing nonnegative integer is a finite descent measure.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Plan A is no worse than B on every relevant criterion and strictly better on one, with criteria preferred in the stated directions. What is B?
options: Dominated by A
Guaranteed optimal
Incomparable to A
Always cheaper than A
questions.answer: Dominated by A
questions.explanation: A offers at least equal performance everywhere and an improvement somewhere, so B has no advantage under these criteria.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two options have equal expected payoff, but one can cause an unaffordable loss. Why might a decision-maker reasonably reject it?
options: Equal expected value means equal outcomes in every case
Risk has no relation to possible losses
The safer option must have a higher mean
Expected value alone omits risk tolerance and constraints
questions.answer: Expected value alone omits risk tolerance and constraints
questions.explanation: A severe downside can violate practical constraints despite an acceptable average payoff.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two backup suppliers depend on the same single factory. Why may they offer little protection against factory failure?
options: The factory must have unlimited capacity
Supplier names determine independence
Their failures share a common cause
Two suppliers always eliminate risk
questions.answer: Their failures share a common cause
questions.explanation: Apparent supplier diversity does not remove a shared upstream dependency.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A fully booked workshop accepts a new session by cancelling an existing one. What cost should the choice include?
options: Zero, because the room already exists
The benefit lost from the cancelled session
Only the new session's direct expense
All expenses ever incurred by the workshop
questions.answer: The benefit lost from the cancelled session
questions.explanation: At full capacity, using the slot displaces an alternative with value.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A free perfectly accurate forecast is available before a reversible choice. Why can it never make the best achievable expected outcome worse?
options: The decision-maker can ignore it if unhelpful
It forces a different action every time
It changes the underlying event probabilities automatically
Every forecast guarantees a positive payoff
questions.answer: The decision-maker can ignore it if unhelpful
questions.explanation: Having optional information expands or preserves available decision strategies.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A plan is optimal for one exact demand estimate but fails if demand is slightly higher. What would a robust alternative seek?
options: A better-looking point estimate only
Zero demand in every scenario
Maximum complexity regardless of need
Acceptable performance across plausible demand levels
questions.answer: Acceptable performance across plausible demand levels
questions.explanation: Robust design considers uncertainty rather than optimizing solely for one assumed value.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A production line has one slow stage and several much faster stages. Why may speeding a fast stage not improve final output?
options: Faster stages create negative output
All queues must vanish immediately
The unchanged slow stage still limits throughput
Every stage always limits output equally
questions.answer: The unchanged slow stage still limits throughput
questions.explanation: System throughput is constrained by the bottleneck, so nonbottleneck improvements may not help.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A controller makes large corrections before earlier corrections have taken effect. What risk follows?
options: A permanently constant output
Overshooting and oscillation
Perfect stability necessarily
Elimination of all uncertainty
questions.answer: Overshooting and oscillation
questions.explanation: Delayed feedback can cause repeated overcorrection and unstable swings.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two uncertain plans offer similar benefits, but one can be cheaply reversed after learning more. What advantage does it have?
options: It preserves flexibility under uncertainty
It guarantees the highest final benefit
It removes the need to compare outcomes
It makes future information worthless
questions.answer: It preserves flexibility under uncertainty
questions.explanation: Low reversal cost allows adaptation when new information changes the preferred choice.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A feasible design cannot improve speed without worsening cost, and cannot reduce cost without worsening speed. What does this indicate?
options: It must be dominated
It is necessarily the only feasible design
It is optimal for every person's preferences
It may lie on a Pareto frontier
questions.answer: It may lie on a Pareto frontier
questions.explanation: A nondominated trade-off can be efficient without being uniquely preferred under all weightings.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: An argument says a source is reliable because it says it is reliable. What independent support is missing?
options: A more confident tone
A longer biography with no verification
Evidence of reliability beyond the source's own claim
A repeated version of the same statement
questions.answer: Evidence of reliability beyond the source's own claim
questions.explanation: The conclusion is being used to justify itself rather than supported independently.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A speaker says, 'Either accept this exact plan or accept complete failure,' while other plans are possible. What is the flaw?
options: It uses no nouns
It excludes viable alternatives
It presents too many choices
It proves the plan cannot work
questions.answer: It excludes viable alternatives
questions.explanation: A false dichotomy narrows the options unjustifiably to two extremes.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: An employment rate rises after many unemployed people leave the measured population. Why can this overstate local job creation?
options: The rate can rise through denominator composition without new jobs
Every departure creates a job
Employment counts and rates are identical
Migration cannot affect statistics
questions.answer: The rate can rise through denominator composition without new jobs
questions.explanation: Removing unemployed people can raise the employed share without increasing employed numbers.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Two studies conflict: one is large and well-controlled, the other small and heavily confounded. Why not simply count one vote each?
options: The smaller study is always false
Large studies cannot be wrong
Study conclusions are determined by majority vote
Their evidential quality differs
questions.answer: Their evidential quality differs
questions.explanation: Evidence should be weighed by design, uncertainty and relevance, not just counted.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A model predicts rain well using umbrella sales. Why might increasing umbrella sales not cause rain?
options: Rain cannot be predicted
Sales records contain no information
Prediction does not establish a causal intervention effect
Useful predictors must always be causes
questions.answer: Prediction does not establish a causal intervention effect
questions.explanation: A variable can signal an outcome through association without causing it.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A teaching method works in a small specialist school with unusually high staff support. What is needed before generalising to all schools?
options: A guarantee that small studies always generalise
Evidence about performance under other staffing and school conditions
Only a new school name
An assumption that all settings are identical
questions.answer: Evidence about performance under other staffing and school conditions
questions.explanation: Context and implementation conditions may modify the method's effectiveness elsewhere.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: One verified black swan is found. What happens to the claim 'all swans are white' compared with seeing many white swans?
options: The black swan disproves it; many white swans alone do not prove it
Both observations prove it
Neither observation is relevant
White swans disprove it but black swans confirm it
questions.answer: The black swan disproves it; many white swans alone do not prove it
questions.explanation: A universal claim is refuted by one counterexample but not established by a finite collection of confirming cases alone.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A highly flexible model fits past data perfectly but performs poorly on new cases. What is the likely issue?
options: Insufficient fit to the old sample
Proof that prediction is impossible
A need to reuse the test outcomes during training
Overfitting to sample-specific patterns
questions.answer: Overfitting to sample-specific patterns
questions.explanation: A model may capture noise rather than stable relationships, reducing generalisation.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: A screening process lowers its threshold for flagging cases while underlying measurements stay the same. What trade-off is generally expected?
options: Perfect accuracy automatically
No change in any classification
More true cases detected and more false positives
Fewer true cases detected and fewer false positives
questions.answer: More true cases detected and more false positives
questions.explanation: A more permissive threshold flags more cases, increasing sensitivity while usually reducing specificity.

questions.subject: Aptitude
questions.q: Strong independent evidence contradicts a previously reasonable conclusion. Which response best reflects sound reasoning?
options: Accept the opposite with infinite certainty after any weak claim
Revise confidence in proportion to the new evidence
Preserve certainty because the conclusion came first
Treat every prior belief as worthless forever
questions.answer: Revise confidence in proportion to the new evidence
questions.explanation: Rational updating balances the strength of prior and new evidence rather than freezing or overcorrecting belief.
